@@@ rt-oc-001-intervals-are-open-or-closed.md
---
title: Open intervals are open and closed intervals are closed
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 1
tags: open set, closed set, epsilon definition, intervals
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

A subset $U\subset\mathbb{R}$ is **open** if for every $x\in U$ there is $\varepsilon>0$ such that $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subset U$. A subset $F\subset\mathbb{R}$ is **closed** if $\mathbb{R}\setminus F$ is open.

1. Show that $(a,b)$ is open.
2. Show that $[a,b]$ is closed, and that $(a,+\infty)$ is open while $[a,+\infty)$ is closed.
3. Show that $[0,1)$ is neither open nor closed.

## Hint

For part 1, take $\varepsilon=\min(x-a,\;b-x)$. For part 2, describe the complement of $[a,b]$ as a union of two open intervals. For part 3, find one point where openness fails and one where closedness fails.

## Solution

**Idea.** Everything follows from the definition. The only work is to choose the $\varepsilon$ (it depends on the point) and to make sure the neighbourhood really stays inside the set.

**Step 1: $(a,b)$ is open.** Let $x\in(a,b)$. Then $x-a>0$ and $b-x>0$, so $\varepsilon=\min(x-a,b-x)>0$. If $|y-x|<\varepsilon$, then
$$y>x-\varepsilon\ge x-(x-a)=a\qquad\text{and}\qquad y<x+\varepsilon\le x+(b-x)=b,$$
so $y\in(a,b)$. Hence $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subset(a,b)$.

**Step 2: closed intervals and half-lines.**
- $\mathbb{R}\setminus[a,b]=(-\infty,a)\cup(b,+\infty)$. The same argument as in Step 1 (with $\varepsilon=a-x$ for $x<a$, and $\varepsilon=x-b$ for $x>b$) shows that each of these two half-lines is open, and a union of open sets is open (if $x$ belongs to the union, it belongs to one of the sets, and the $\varepsilon$ of that set works). So $[a,b]$ is closed.
- $(a,+\infty)$ is open: for $x>a$ take $\varepsilon=x-a$.
- $\mathbb{R}\setminus[a,+\infty)=(-\infty,a)$ is open, so $[a,+\infty)$ is closed.

**Step 3: $[0,1)$ is neither.**
- *Not open*: the point $0$ belongs to $[0,1)$, but for every $\varepsilon>0$ the number $-\varepsilon/2$ lies in $(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ and not in $[0,1)$.
- *Not closed*: its complement is $(-\infty,0)\cup[1,\infty)$, which is not open: the point $1$ belongs to it, but for every $\varepsilon>0$ the number $1-\tfrac12\min(\varepsilon,1)$ lies in $(1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)$ and in $[0,1)$, hence not in the complement.

**Common mistake.** "Open" and "closed" are not opposites. A set can be both ($\emptyset$ and $\mathbb{R}$, see the problem on clopen sets) or neither ($[0,1)$). Openness is a property of each point of the set having room around it; closedness is a property of the *complement*.

**Remark.** The same $\varepsilon$ cannot be chosen uniformly: for $(0,1)$ the admissible $\varepsilon$ at the point $x$ tends to $0$ as $x\to0$ or $x\to1$. That is why an open set can fail to be "uniformly" open, and why the distinction between open and closed intervals matters in analysis.

@@@ topology-R-open-ball.md

title: Open balls in ℝ
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l1
difficulty: 1
order: 2
tags: open ball, interval, topology
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

For $a\in\mathbb{R}$ and $r>0$, describe the open ball $B(a,r)$ and show it is an open set.

## Hint

$B(a,r)=\{x:|x-a|<r\}=]a-r,a+r[$.

## Solution

**Identification.** $B(a,r)$ is the open interval $]a-r,a+r[$.

**Openness.** Every point of $]a-r,a+r[$ has a small ball around it contained in $]a-r,a+r[$ (previous exercise).

**Conclusion.** Open balls are open sets; they are the building blocks of the topology of $\mathbb{R}$.

@@@ topology-R-closed-definition.md
---
title: Closed sets
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l1
difficulty: 1
order: 3
tags: closed sets, complement, definition
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Define a closed set in $\mathbb{R}$ and give two examples and one counterexample.

## Hint

Closed = complement is open.

## Solution

**Definition.** $F\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is closed iff $\mathbb{R}\setminus F$ is open.

**Examples.** $\emptyset$, $\mathbb{R}$, $[0,1]$, singletons $\{a\}$.

**Counterexample.** $]0,1]$ is neither open nor closed: it is not open (0 is a boundary point) and its complement $]-\infty,0]\cup]1,+\infty[$ is not open.

**Conclusion.** Some sets are neither open nor closed.

@@@ topology-R-boundary.md
---
title: Interior, closure, boundary
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l1
difficulty: 1
order: 4
tags: interior, closure, boundary
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

For $A=]0,1]\cup\{2\}$, compute the interior, closure, and boundary of $A$.

## Hint

$\mathring A$ = union of open subsets of $A$; $\overline A$ = smallest closed set containing $A$; $\partial A=\overline A\setminus\mathring A$.

## Solution

**Interior.** $\mathring A=]0,1[$: $1$ is not interior (every ball around $1$ hits the complement), $2$ is not interior (isolated).

**Closure.** $\overline A=[0,1]\cup\{2\}$: the limit points of $]0,1]$ are in $[0,1]$; $2$ is already in $A$.

**Boundary.** $\partial A=\{0,1,2\}$.

**Conclusion.** Interior $]0,1[$, closure $[0,1]\cup\{2\}$, boundary $\{0,1,2\}$.

@@@ rt-oc-002-unions-and-intersections.md
---
title: Finite intersections, infinite unions: what is allowed
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 1
order: 7
tags: open sets, closed sets, unions, intersections, counterexamples
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

1. Show that an arbitrary union of open sets is open, and that a finite intersection of open sets is open.
2. Deduce the dual statements for closed sets: an arbitrary intersection of closed sets is closed, and a finite union of closed sets is closed.
3. Give an infinite intersection of open sets which is not open, and an infinite union of closed sets which is not closed.

## Hint

For the intersection of two open sets, take the smaller of the two $\varepsilon$'s. For part 2, use De Morgan's laws: the complement of a union is the intersection of the complements.

## Solution

**Idea.** The proof of part 1 is a bookkeeping exercise with $\varepsilon$'s. The point is that "take the minimum of finitely many positive numbers" is again positive, but this fails for infinitely many.

**Step 1: unions.** Let $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ be open sets and $x\in\bigcup_iU_i$. Then $x\in U_{i_0}$ for some $i_0$, and there is $\varepsilon>0$ with $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subset U_{i_0}\subset\bigcup_iU_i$.

**Step 1': finite intersections.** Let $U_1,\dots,U_n$ be open and $x\in\bigcap_kU_k$. For each $k$ choose $\varepsilon_k>0$ with $(x-\varepsilon_k,x+\varepsilon_k)\subset U_k$, and put $\varepsilon=\min_k\varepsilon_k$. This is a minimum of **finitely many** positive numbers, hence $\varepsilon>0$, and $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subset U_k$ for every $k$.

**Step 2: closed sets.** If $(F_i)$ are closed, then
$$\mathbb{R}\setminus\bigcap_iF_i=\bigcup_i(\mathbb{R}\setminus F_i)$$
is a union of open sets, hence open. Similarly $\mathbb{R}\setminus(F_1\cup\dots\cup F_n)=\bigcap_k(\mathbb{R}\setminus F_k)$ is a finite intersection of open sets.

**Step 3: counterexamples.**
- $\bigcap_{n\ge1}\left(-\tfrac1n,\tfrac1n\right)=\{0\}$. Each interval is open but $\{0\}$ is not open (no interval around $0$ is contained in $\{0\}$). Here $\varepsilon_n=\tfrac1n$ and $\inf_n\varepsilon_n=0$: the minimum trick fails.
- $\bigcup_{n\ge2}\left[\tfrac1n,1\right]=(0,1]$. Each $[\tfrac1n,1]$ is closed but $(0,1]$ is not closed ($0$ is a limit of points of the set and is not in it). Another example: $\bigcup_{x\in(0,1)}\{x\}=(0,1)$, a union of singletons (which are closed).

**Remark.** These two properties (arbitrary unions, finite intersections) are exactly the axioms of a *topology*. Everything in this chapter uses only them and the definition of open sets in $\mathbb{R}$.

@@@ rt-oc-003-closed-sets-and-sequences.md
---
title: Closed sets are the sets that contain their limits
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 8
tags: closed set, sequences, characterisation
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Prove that $F\subset\mathbb{R}$ is closed if and only if every convergent sequence $(x_n)$ of elements of $F$ has its limit in $F$.

## Hint

($\Rightarrow$) If the limit $x$ were outside $F$, a neighbourhood of $x$ would miss $F$ — but the sequence enters this neighbourhood. ($\Leftarrow$) Argue by contradiction: if the complement is not open, build a sequence of points of $F$ converging to a point of the complement.

## Solution

**Idea.** A point outside a closed set has some room around it; a sequence converging to this point must eventually use that room. Conversely, failing to have room means being approximated by points of $F$.

**($\Rightarrow$)** Let $F$ be closed, $x_n\in F$, $x_n\to x$. Suppose $x\notin F$. Since $\mathbb{R}\setminus F$ is open, there is $\varepsilon>0$ with $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subset\mathbb{R}\setminus F$. By convergence, there is $N$ such that $|x_n-x|<\varepsilon$ for $n\ge N$, hence $x_N\notin F$. This contradicts $x_N\in F$. So $x\in F$.

**($\Leftarrow$)** Assume $F$ contains the limit of each of its convergent sequences. We prove that $U=\mathbb{R}\setminus F$ is open. Suppose not: there is $x\in U$ such that for every $\varepsilon>0$ the interval $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)$ is not contained in $U$, i.e. meets $F$. Taking $\varepsilon=\tfrac1n$, we get $x_n\in F$ with $|x_n-x|<\tfrac1n$. Then $x_n\to x$, so $x\in F$ by hypothesis, contradicting $x\in U$.

**Example of use.** $\mathbb{N}$ is closed: a convergent sequence of integers is eventually constant (its terms are within $\tfrac12$ of each other for large $n$), so its limit is an integer. $\{1/n\}$ is not closed: $\tfrac1n\to0\notin\{1/n\}$.

**Common mistake.** The statement concerns *convergent* sequences. A sequence in a closed set need not converge (e.g. $x_n=n$ in $\mathbb{N}$), and nothing is claimed in that case.

**Remark.** This is the characterisation one uses in practice: to show $F=\{x:f(x)\le c\}$ is closed for a continuous $f$, take $x_n\to x$ with $f(x_n)\le c$ and pass to the limit.

@@@ rt-oc-004-interior-closure-boundary-of-classical-sets.md
---
title: Interior, closure and boundary of five classical sets
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 1
order: 10
tags: interior, closure, boundary, rationals, integers
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Determine the interior $\mathring A$, the closure $\overline A$ and the boundary $\partial A=\overline A\setminus\mathring A$ of
1. $A=\mathbb{Q}$,
2. $A=\mathbb{Z}$,
3. $A=(0,1]$,
4. $A=\{1/n:n\ge1\}$,
5. $A=(0,1)\cup(1,2)$.

Recall: $x\in\mathring A$ iff some $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subset A$; $x\in\overline A$ iff every $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)$ meets $A$.

## Hint

For $\mathbb{Q}$, use that every interval contains both a rational and an irrational number. For $\{1/n\}$, look at what happens near $0$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Test the two definitions on well-chosen points. The "bad" points are the ones where the structure of the set changes.

**1. $A=\mathbb{Q}$.** Every non-empty open interval contains an irrational number, so no interval is contained in $\mathbb{Q}$: $\mathring A=\emptyset$. Every non-empty open interval contains a rational number, so every real is in the closure: $\overline A=\mathbb{R}$. Hence $\partial A=\mathbb{R}$.

**2. $A=\mathbb{Z}$.** An interval around an integer $k$ contains non-integers, so $\mathring A=\emptyset$. $\mathbb{Z}$ is closed (a point $x\notin\mathbb{Z}$ has distance $\min(x-\lfloor x\rfloor,\lceil x\rceil-x)>0$ to $\mathbb{Z}$), so $\overline A=\mathbb{Z}$. Hence $\partial A=\mathbb{Z}$.

**3. $A=(0,1]$.** The open interval $(0,1)\subset A$ is open, so $(0,1)\subset\mathring A$. The point $1$ is not interior since $1+\varepsilon/2\notin A$; the point $0\notin A$ is not interior. So $\mathring A=(0,1)$. For the closure: $0$ is adherent since $\tfrac1n\in A$ and $\tfrac1n\to0$, and $A\cup\{0\}=[0,1]$ is closed, so $\overline A=[0,1]$. Hence $\partial A=\{0,1\}$.

**4. $A=\{1/n\}$.** No interval is contained in a countable set, so $\mathring A=\emptyset$. Since $\tfrac1n\to0$, $0\in\overline A$; and $A\cup\{0\}$ is closed (a point $x\ne0$ not of the form $1/n$ has a neighbourhood meeting at most finitely many $\tfrac1n$, so we can shrink the neighbourhood to avoid them). So $\overline A=A\cup\{0\}$ and $\partial A=\overline A=A\cup\{0\}$.

**5. $A=(0,1)\cup(1,2)$.** $A$ is open, so $\mathring A=A$. The closure is $[0,2]$ (the point $1$ is adherent from both sides). Hence $\partial A=\{0,1,2\}$.

**Common mistake.** "The boundary of $(0,1)\cup(1,2)$ is $\{0,2\}$" forgets that $1$ is a boundary point: it is in the closure, and not in the interior.

**Remark.** Notice the two extremes: $\mathbb{Q}$ has empty interior and full closure (it is *dense with empty interior*), whereas $\mathbb{Z}$ has empty interior and is closed (it is *nowhere dense*). Both have non-empty boundary equal to the whole closure.

@@@ rt-oc-005-accumulation-points-and-isolated-points.md
---
title: Accumulation points, isolated points and the derived set
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 17
tags: accumulation point, isolated point, derived set
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

A point $x\in\mathbb{R}$ is an **accumulation point** of $A$ if every interval $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)$ contains a point of $A$ different from $x$. The set of accumulation points is the **derived set** $A'$. A point of $A$ which is not an accumulation point of $A$ is **isolated**.

1. Find $A'$ and the isolated points of $A=\mathbb{Z}$, $A=\mathbb{Q}$, $A=\{1/n:n\ge1\}$, $A=(0,1)\cup\{2\}$.
2. Show that $x\in A'$ iff there is a sequence of **pairwise distinct** points of $A$ converging to $x$, iff every interval around $x$ contains infinitely many points of $A$.
3. Show that $A'$ is always closed.

## Hint

For 2, build the sequence by successively choosing points closer and closer to $x$, using at each step that the interval $(x-\delta,x+\delta)$ with $\delta$ smaller than the distance to the previous point contains a new point. For 3, show that $\mathbb{R}\setminus A'$ is open.

## Solution

**1. Examples.**
- $\mathbb{Z}$: no point has other integers arbitrarily close, so $A'=\emptyset$ and every point is isolated.
- $\mathbb{Q}$: every interval contains infinitely many rationals, so $A'=\mathbb{R}$; there is no isolated point.
- $\{1/n\}$: $A'=\{0\}$ since $\tfrac1n\to0$ and the other points have a neighbourhood containing only finitely many $\tfrac1k$. All the points $\tfrac1n$ are isolated, and $0\notin A$.
- $(0,1)\cup\{2\}$: $A'=[0,1]$ ($0$ and $1$ are limits of points of $(0,1)$), and the only isolated point is $2$.

**2. Equivalences.** We prove that the following are equivalent: (a) $x\in A'$; (b) there is a sequence of pairwise distinct points of $A$ converging to $x$; (c) every interval around $x$ contains infinitely many points of $A$.

*(a) $\Rightarrow$ (b).* Choose $a_1\in A\setminus\{x\}$ with $|a_1-x|<1$. Having chosen $a_1,\dots,a_n$, let $\delta=\min\left(\tfrac1{n+1},|a_1-x|,\dots,|a_n-x|\right)>0$ and pick $a_{n+1}\in A\setminus\{x\}$ with $|a_{n+1}-x|<\delta$. The $a_n$ are pairwise distinct (their distances to $x$ strictly decrease) and $a_n\to x$.

*(b) $\Rightarrow$ (c).* Let $(a_n)$ be pairwise distinct and $a_n\to x$, and let $J$ be an interval around $x$. Since $a_n\to x$, all but finitely many terms lie in $J$; among those, only finitely many can be equal to $x$; so infinitely many distinct points of $A$ lie in $J$.

*(c) $\Rightarrow$ (a).* If every interval around $x$ contains infinitely many points of $A$, it contains in particular one different from $x$, so $x\in A'$.

**3. $A'$ is closed.** Let $x\notin A'$. There is $\varepsilon>0$ such that $J=(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)$ satisfies $J\cap A\subset\{x\}$. We show $J\cap A'=\emptyset$, which proves that $\mathbb{R}\setminus A'$ is open. Let $y\in J$. If $y=x$, then $y\notin A'$ by assumption. If $y\ne x$, put $\eta=\min\bigl(|y-x|,\ y-(x-\varepsilon),\ (x+\varepsilon)-y\bigr)>0$. Then $(y-\eta,y+\eta)\subset J$ and $x\notin(y-\eta,y+\eta)$, so $(y-\eta,y+\eta)\cap A\subset J\cap A\setminus\{x\}=\emptyset$. Hence $y\notin A'$.

**Common mistake.** "$A'$ is the set of limits of sequences of $A$." This is wrong: *every* point of $A$ is the limit of the constant sequence, but isolated points of $A$ are not accumulation points. One needs sequences of pairwise distinct points, or sequences with $a_n\ne x$.

**Remark.** The closure is $\overline A=A\cup A'$. This formula shows that closed sets are exactly the sets with $A'\subset A$ (they "contain all their accumulation points").

@@@ rt-oc-006-four-descriptions-of-the-closure.md
---
title: Four equivalent descriptions of the closure
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 11
tags: closure, adherent point, sequences, distance to a set
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

For $A\subset\mathbb{R}$ non-empty and $x\in\mathbb{R}$, prove that the following are equivalent:
1. every interval $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)$ meets $A$;
2. $x$ is the limit of a sequence of elements of $A$;
3. $d(x,A):=\inf_{a\in A}|x-a|=0$;
4. $x$ belongs to every closed set containing $A$.

The set of such $x$ is called the closure $\overline A$. Conclude that $\overline A$ is the smallest closed set containing $A$.

## Hint

Prove $1\Rightarrow2\Rightarrow3\Rightarrow1$, then $2\Rightarrow4$ using the sequential characterisation of closed sets, and $4\Rightarrow$ closedness of the set defined by 1.

## Solution

**Idea.** The first three descriptions are the same idea in three languages (neighbourhoods, sequences, distances). The fourth is the "global" definition of the closure as an intersection.

**$1\Rightarrow2$.** For each $n$, the interval $(x-\tfrac1n,x+\tfrac1n)$ contains some $a_n\in A$; then $|a_n-x|<\tfrac1n$ so $a_n\to x$.

**$2\Rightarrow3$.** If $a_n\to x$, then $d(x,A)\le|x-a_n|\to0$, so $d(x,A)=0$.

**$3\Rightarrow1$.** If $d(x,A)=0$, then for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is $a\in A$ with $|x-a|<\varepsilon$ (by definition of the infimum), so the interval meets $A$.

**$2\Rightarrow4$.** Let $F\supset A$ be closed and $a_n\to x$ with $a_n\in A\subset F$. By the sequential characterisation of closed sets, $x\in F$.

**$4\Rightarrow1$.** Let $C$ be the set of points satisfying 1. We show that $C$ is closed and contains $A$; then 4 gives that $x\in C$. $A\subset C$: take $\varepsilon$ arbitrary, $a\in(a-\varepsilon,a+\varepsilon)\cap A$. $C$ closed: let $y\notin C$, so some $(y-\varepsilon,y+\varepsilon)$ misses $A$; every point $z$ of this interval has a smaller interval around it, contained in $(y-\varepsilon,y+\varepsilon)$, which also misses $A$, so $z\notin C$. Thus $\mathbb{R}\setminus C$ is open.

**Conclusion.** The set $C=\overline A$ is closed, contains $A$, and is contained in every closed set containing $A$ (this is item 4): it is the smallest one.

**Remark.** Description 3 is the most useful for estimates: to show $x\in\overline A$ it suffices to find points of $A$ at distance as small as we wish. Description 2 is the one to use for continuity arguments ($f(\overline A)\subset\overline{f(A)}$).

@@@ rt-oc-007-the-interior-is-the-largest-open-subset.md
---
title: The interior as the largest open subset
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 12
tags: interior, complement, duality
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Let $A\subset\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathring A=\{x:\exists\varepsilon>0,\ (x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subset A\}$.

1. Show that $\mathring A$ is open and that it contains every open set contained in $A$.
2. Prove the duality formulas $\mathring A=\mathbb{R}\setminus\overline{\mathbb{R}\setminus A}$ and $\overline A=\mathbb{R}\setminus\operatorname{int}(\mathbb{R}\setminus A)$.
3. Compute $\mathring A$ for $A=[0,1]\cup\{2\}\cup(3,4)$.

## Hint

For 1, if $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subset A$, show that every point of this interval is itself interior. For 2, translate "an interval around $x$ is contained in $A$" as "an interval around $x$ does not meet $\mathbb{R}\setminus A$".

## Solution

**1. $\mathring A$ is open.** Let $x\in\mathring A$ and $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subset A$. Each $y$ in this interval has a smaller interval $(y-\eta,y+\eta)\subset(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subset A$ (take $\eta=\min(y-x+\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon-y)$), so $y\in\mathring A$. Thus $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subset\mathring A$.

**Largest.** If $U\subset A$ is open and $x\in U$, there is an interval around $x$ inside $U\subset A$, so $x\in\mathring A$. Hence $U\subset\mathring A$.

**2. Duality.** Let $B=\mathbb{R}\setminus A$. Then
$$x\in\mathring A\iff\exists\varepsilon,\ (x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\cap B=\emptyset\iff x\notin\overline B,$$
by description 1 of the closure. This gives the first formula. Applying it to $B$ gives $\operatorname{int}B=\mathbb{R}\setminus\overline A$, i.e. $\overline A=\mathbb{R}\setminus\operatorname{int}(\mathbb{R}\setminus A)$.

**3. Computation.** $A=[0,1]\cup\{2\}\cup(3,4)$. The open set $(0,1)\cup(3,4)\subset A$. The endpoints $0,1$ fail ($0-\varepsilon/2\notin A$), $2$ is isolated and $3,4\notin A$. So
$$\mathring A=(0,1)\cup(3,4).$$

**Remark.** These formulas say that "interior" and "closure" are two faces of the same operation, exchanged by complement. Any statement about closures has a dual statement about interiors; for instance $\overline{A\cup B}=\overline A\cup\overline B$ is dual to $\operatorname{int}(A\cap B)=\mathring A\cap\mathring B$ (see the next two problems).

@@@ rt-oc-008-closure-of-a-union-and-of-an-intersection.md
---
title: Closure of a union, closure of an intersection
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 13
tags: closure, union, intersection, counterexample
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

1. Prove $\overline{A\cup B}=\overline A\cup\overline B$.
2. Prove $\overline{A\cap B}\subset\overline A\cap\overline B$ and show by an example that the inclusion can be strict.
3. Does the formula of part 1 extend to infinite unions? Examine $A_n=\{1/n\}$.

## Hint

For 1, use the sequence characterisation of the closure. For 2, take two disjoint open intervals with a common endpoint.

## Solution

**1. Union.** ($\supset$) $A\subset A\cup B$, so $\overline A\subset\overline{A\cup B}$ (monotonicity of the closure); likewise for $B$. ($\subset$) Let $x\in\overline{A\cup B}$ and $a_n\in A\cup B$, $a_n\to x$. Infinitely many of the $a_n$ lie in $A$, or infinitely many lie in $B$. In the first case they form a subsequence in $A$ converging to $x$, so $x\in\overline A$; in the second case $x\in\overline B$.

**2. Intersection.** From $A\cap B\subset A$, we get $\overline{A\cap B}\subset\overline A$, and similarly for $B$; hence the inclusion. *Strictness:* take $A=(0,1)$ and $B=(1,2)$. Then $A\cap B=\emptyset$ so $\overline{A\cap B}=\emptyset$, but $\overline A\cap\overline B=[0,1]\cap[1,2]=\{1\}$.

**3. Infinite unions.** The inclusion $\bigcup_n\overline{A_n}\subset\overline{\bigcup_nA_n}$ holds in general, but the reverse inclusion fails: with $A_n=\{1/n\}$, $\overline{A_n}=A_n$ and $\bigcup_n\overline{A_n}=\{1/n:n\ge1\}$, whereas $\overline{\bigcup_nA_n}=\{1/n\}\cup\{0\}$ contains $0$. The finite case works because a sequence in a finite union has a *subsequence* in one of the pieces.

**Common mistake.** Writing $\overline{A\cap B}=\overline A\cap\overline B$. The error is usually invisible with intervals which overlap; test with disjoint sets that touch, or with $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ (the intersection is empty but both closures are $\mathbb{R}$).

**Remark.** An easy equality case: if $B$ is open, then $\overline{A\cap B}\supset\overline A\cap B$. Indeed let $x\in\overline A\cap B$; since $B$ is open there is $\varepsilon>0$ with $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subset B$, and since $x\in\overline A$ every neighbourhood of $x$ meets $A$, hence meets $A\cap B$; so $x\in\overline{A\cap B}$. This is the key to "localisation" arguments.

@@@ rt-oc-009-interior-of-an-intersection-and-of-a-union.md
---
title: Interior of an intersection, interior of a union
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 14
tags: interior, union, intersection, counterexample
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

1. Prove $\operatorname{int}(A\cap B)=\mathring A\cap\mathring B$.
2. Prove $\mathring A\cup\mathring B\subset\operatorname{int}(A\cup B)$ and show by an example that the inclusion can be strict.
3. Show that $\bigcap_n\operatorname{int}(A_n)$ can differ from $\operatorname{int}(\bigcap_nA_n)$ for infinitely many sets, but that $\operatorname{int}(\bigcap_nA_n)\subset\bigcap_n\operatorname{int}(A_n)$ always holds.

## Hint

For 1, intersect two intervals around $x$. For 2, try $A=[0,1]$, $B=[1,2]$, or the rational/irrational pair.

## Solution

**1.** ($\subset$) $A\cap B\subset A$ so $\operatorname{int}(A\cap B)\subset\mathring A$; same for $B$. ($\supset$) If $x\in\mathring A\cap\mathring B$, there are $\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2>0$ with $(x-\varepsilon_1,x+\varepsilon_1)\subset A$ and $(x-\varepsilon_2,x+\varepsilon_2)\subset B$. With $\varepsilon=\min(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2)$, $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subset A\cap B$.

**2.** The inclusion follows from monotonicity: $\mathring A\subset\operatorname{int}(A\cup B)$ and likewise for $B$. *Strictness:* $A=[0,1]$, $B=[1,2]$. Then $\mathring A\cup\mathring B=(0,1)\cup(1,2)$ while $A\cup B=[0,2]$ has interior $(0,2)\ni1$. A more drastic example: $A=\mathbb{Q}$, $B=\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ have empty interiors but $A\cup B=\mathbb{R}$.

**3. Infinite families.** The inclusion $\operatorname{int}\left(\bigcap_nA_n\right)\subset\bigcap_n\operatorname{int}(A_n)$ follows from monotonicity as before: $\bigcap_nA_n\subset A_m$ gives $\operatorname{int}(\bigcap_nA_n)\subset\operatorname{int}(A_m)$ for each $m$. It can be strict: take the open sets $A_n=\left(-\tfrac1n,\tfrac1n\right)$. Then $\operatorname{int}A_n=A_n$ and $\bigcap_n\operatorname{int}A_n=\bigcap_nA_n=\{0\}$, whereas $\operatorname{int}\left(\bigcap_nA_n\right)=\operatorname{int}\{0\}=\emptyset$. So $\bigcap_n\operatorname{int}(A_n)=\{0\}\ne\emptyset=\operatorname{int}\left(\bigcap_nA_n\right)$.

**Remark.** Summary: interior commutes with finite intersections (not with unions), closure commutes with finite unions (not with intersections); the two statements are dual under complement. For infinite families neither commutes in general.

@@@ rt-oc-010-the-only-clopen-subsets-of-the-real-line.md
---
title: The only subsets of ℝ that are both open and closed
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 22
tags: clopen, connectedness, supremum
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Show that the only subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ which are both open and closed are $\emptyset$ and $\mathbb{R}$.

## Hint

Suppose $A$ is open and closed, $a\in A$, $b\notin A$ with $a<b$. Look at $s=\sup\{x\in[a,b]:[a,x]\subset A\}$ and use both properties at the point $s$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Walk from a point of $A$ towards a point outside $A$. The last point where we are still in $A$ must be both in $A$ (closedness) and a boundary point (impossible for an open set). This is the real-line version of the intermediate value theorem.

**Setup.** Let $A$ be clopen, $A\ne\emptyset$, $A\ne\mathbb{R}$. Take $a\in A$ and $b\notin A$. If $b<a$, replace $A$ by $\mathbb{R}\setminus A$ (also clopen) and rename the two points: then $a\in A$, $b\notin A$ and $a<b$.

**The set $S$.** Let $S=\{x\in[a,b]:[a,x]\subset A\}$. It contains $a$ and is bounded by $b$; let $s=\sup S\in[a,b]$.

**Step 1: $s\in A$.** If $s=a$ this is clear. If $s>a$, every $t\in[a,s)$ is below some element of $S$, so $t\in A$. Thus $s_n=s-\tfrac1n\in A$ for $n$ large, and $s_n\to s$. Since $A$ is closed, $s\in A$. Hence $[a,s]\subset A$, i.e. $s\in S$.

**Step 2: $s<b$.** Since $[a,s]\subset A$ and $b\notin A$, $s\ne b$, so $s<b$.

**Step 3: contradiction.** Since $A$ is open and $s\in A$, there is $\delta>0$ with $(s-\delta,s+\delta)\subset A$. Let $x=\min(s+\delta/2,b)>s$. Then $[a,x]=[a,s]\cup(s,x]\subset A$, so $x\in S$ and $x>s=\sup S$. This is absurd.

**Conclusion.** No such $A$ exists, so a clopen set is $\emptyset$ or $\mathbb{R}$.

**Remark.** This property is called *connectedness* of $\mathbb{R}$. It is *equivalent* to the completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ (we used the supremum): in $\mathbb{Q}$, the set $\mathbb{Q}\cap(-\infty,\sqrt2)$ is both open and closed in $\mathbb{Q}$. The problem on the relative topology explores this.

@@@ rt-oc-011-open-sets-are-countable-unions-of-disjoint-intervals.md
---
title: Every open subset of ℝ is a countable union of disjoint open intervals
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 4
order: 23
tags: structure of open sets, connected components, countability
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Let $U\subset\mathbb{R}$ be open.

1. Show that $U$ is a union of pairwise disjoint open intervals (bounded or not).
2. Show that there are at most countably many of them.
3. Show that this decomposition is unique.

## Hint

Define on $U$ the relation $x\sim y\iff$ the closed segment between $x$ and $y$ is contained in $U$. Show that it is an equivalence relation whose classes are open intervals. For countability, associate to each class a rational number it contains.

## Solution

**Idea.** The equivalence classes ("components") of $U$ are the maximal intervals contained in $U$. They are open because $U$ is, they are disjoint because they are classes, and each contains a rational number, which gives an injection into $\mathbb{Q}$.

**Step 1: the relation.** For $x,y\in U$ write $x\sim y$ if the closed segment $[\min(x,y),\max(x,y)]\subset U$. *Reflexive* and *symmetric* are clear. *Transitive:* if $[x,y]$ and $[y,z]$ (in whatever order) are contained in $U$, then the segment between $x$ and $z$ is contained in the union of these two segments, hence in $U$.

**Step 2: each class $C$ is an interval.** If $x<z$ are in $C$ and $x<y<z$, then $[x,z]\subset U$ (as $x\sim z$), so $y\in U$ and $[x,y]\subset[x,z]\subset U$: $y\sim x$ and $y\in C$.

**Step 3: each class is open.** Let $x\in C$. As $U$ is open, $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subset U$ for some $\varepsilon$. For every $y$ in this interval, the segment between $x$ and $y$ is inside the interval, so $y\sim x$. Hence $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subset C$.

An open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ which is an interval has the form $(a,b)$ with $-\infty\le a<b\le+\infty$ (a bounded-below interval which contained its left endpoint $a$ would not be open at $a$).

**Step 4: countability.** Each class is a non-empty open interval, so it contains a rational number. Choose one, $q(C)\in C\cap\mathbb{Q}$. Since the classes are disjoint, $C\mapsto q(C)$ is injective into the countable set $\mathbb{Q}$. So there are at most countably many classes.

**Step 5: uniqueness.** Suppose $U=\bigsqcup_jI_j$ with $I_j$ pairwise disjoint open intervals. Two points in the same $I_j$ are equivalent (the segment between them lies in $I_j$). Two points in different intervals are not. Indeed let $x\in I_j$, $y\in I_k$, $k\ne j$, and say $x<y$ (the case $y<x$ is symmetric). Let $b=\sup I_j\in(x,+\infty]$. Since $y\notin I_j$ and $y>x$, we have $y\ge b$, so $b$ is finite, $b\in[x,y]$, and $b\notin I_j$ because $I_j$ is open. Suppose $[x,y]\subset U$. Then $b\in I_m$ for some $m\ne j$. As $I_m$ is open, it contains points $t<b$ arbitrarily close to $b$, and these lie in $I_j$ as soon as $t>x$ (since $(x,b)\subset I_j$). This contradicts $I_j\cap I_m=\emptyset$. So $x\not\sim y$, and the $I_j$ are exactly the classes.

**Remark.** The classes are called the *connected components* of $U$. This structure result is specific to $\mathbb{R}$: in $\mathbb{R}^2$ open sets are not unions of disjoint discs or rectangles. It explains why closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are exactly "$\mathbb{R}$ minus a countable family of disjoint open intervals", the construction used for the Cantor set.

@@@ rt-oc-012-a-dense-open-set-of-small-total-length.md
---
title: A dense open set of arbitrarily small total length
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l3
difficulty: 4
order: 24
tags: dense open set, countable cover, compactness, nowhere dense
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Enumerate the rationals as $q_1,q_2,\dots$ and, for $0<\varepsilon<\tfrac14$, put
$$O_\varepsilon=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\left(q_n-\varepsilon2^{-n},\ q_n+\varepsilon2^{-n}\right).$$

1. Show that $O_\varepsilon$ is open and dense in $\mathbb{R}$, and that the sum of the lengths of its intervals is at most $2\varepsilon$.
2. Show that $K=[0,1]\setminus O_\varepsilon$ is a non-empty closed set with empty interior.
3. Conclude that a closed set with empty interior can be "large": $K$ is not contained in any countable union of open intervals of total length $<1-2\varepsilon$.

## Hint

For 2, if $K$ were empty then $[0,1]\subset O_\varepsilon$ and by compactness finitely many of the intervals would cover $[0,1]$. A finite family of intervals covering $[0,1]$ must have total length at least $1$.

## Solution

**Idea.** The intervals are centred at *all* rationals, so $O_\varepsilon$ is dense; but their lengths decrease geometrically, so the total is tiny. The complement in $[0,1]$ must therefore be non-empty, closed, and cannot contain any interval (since it misses a dense set).

**1. Open, dense, small.** $O_\varepsilon$ is a union of open intervals, hence open. It contains $\mathbb{Q}$, so it is dense. The total length is $\sum_n2\varepsilon2^{-n}=2\varepsilon$.

**2. $K$ is closed, non-empty, with empty interior.**
- *Closed:* $K=[0,1]\cap(\mathbb{R}\setminus O_\varepsilon)$ is an intersection of two closed sets.
- *Empty interior:* if an interval $(a,b)\subset K\subset\mathbb{R}\setminus O_\varepsilon$ existed, it would contain a rational, which lies in $O_\varepsilon$. Contradiction.
- *Non-empty:* this follows from part 3 below (with the empty family of extra intervals): if $K=\emptyset$, then $[0,1]\subset O_\varepsilon$ and the lemma gives a contradiction.

**Lemma.** If finitely many open intervals $J_1,\dots,J_m$ cover $[0,L]$ ($L>0$), then their total length is at least $L$.
*Proof.* Induction on $m$. Let $J=(c,d)$ be one of the intervals containing $L$, so $d>L$. If $c<0$, then $d-c>L$ and we are done. If $c\ge0$, the points of $[0,c]$ are not in $J$, so the other $m-1$ intervals cover $[0,c]$. If $c=0$ the length of $J$ is $d>L$. If $c>0$, by the induction hypothesis (applied to $m-1$ intervals and $L=c$) their total length is at least $c$. For $m=1$ this case cannot occur, since $J$ alone covers $[0,L]$ and so $c<0$. The total is at least $c+(d-c)=d>L$. $\square$

**3. Interpretation.** $K$ is compact, being closed and bounded. Suppose $K$ is covered by open intervals $L_1,L_2,\dots$ (countably many) of total length $\ell$. Then $[0,1]=K\cup([0,1]\cap O_\varepsilon)$ is covered by the $L_j$ together with the intervals defining $O_\varepsilon$; by compactness of $[0,1]$ finitely many of these intervals suffice, and by the lemma their total length is at least $1$. This total length is at most $\ell+2\varepsilon$, so $\ell\ge1-2\varepsilon$. In particular, applied to the empty family of $L_j$, $K\ne\emptyset$ since $2\varepsilon<1$. Thus $K$ is a closed set with empty interior that cannot be covered by intervals of total length less than $1-2\varepsilon$.

**Remark.** This gives a "fat" nowhere dense set, in contrast to the Cantor ternary set which has length $0$. It also shows that "dense" and "small" are compatible for open sets, a fact that surprises people at first and is the basis of many measure-theoretic counterexamples.

@@@ rt-oc-013-sums-of-open-sets-and-of-closed-sets.md
---
title: The sum A + B of two subsets of ℝ
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 27
tags: sum of sets, closed sets, compact sets, counterexample
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

For $A,B\subset\mathbb{R}$ let $A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,\ b\in B\}$.

1. Show that if $A$ is open and $B$ is arbitrary non-empty, then $A+B$ is open.
2. Show that if $A$ is closed and $B$ is compact, then $A+B$ is closed.
3. Show that the sum of two closed sets need not be closed, using $A=\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,3,\dots\}$ and $B=\{-n+\tfrac1n:n\ge2\}$.

## Hint

For 1, write $A+B=\bigcup_{b\in B}(A+b)$ and use that translations map open sets to open sets. For 2, use a convergent sequence $a_n+b_n$ and extract a subsequence from $(b_n)$.

## Solution

**1.** For fixed $b$, $A+b=\{a+b:a\in A\}$ is open: if $a+b\in A+b$ and $(a-\varepsilon,a+\varepsilon)\subset A$, then $(a+b-\varepsilon,a+b+\varepsilon)\subset A+b$. Then $A+B=\bigcup_{b\in B}(A+b)$ is a union of open sets.

**2.** Let $z_n=a_n+b_n\to z$ with $a_n\in A$, $b_n\in B$. Since $B$ is compact, $(b_n)$ has a subsequence $b_{n_k}\to b\in B$. Then $a_{n_k}=z_{n_k}-b_{n_k}\to z-b$ and, $A$ being closed, $z-b\in A$. So $z=(z-b)+b\in A+B$. By the sequential characterisation, $A+B$ is closed.

**3. The counterexample.**
- *$A=\mathbb{N}$ is closed:* its points are at distance at least $1$ from each other, so it has no accumulation point.
- *$B$ is closed:* the consecutive points of $B$ satisfy $\bigl(-n+\tfrac1n\bigr)-\bigl(-(n+1)+\tfrac1{n+1}\bigr)=1+\tfrac1n-\tfrac1{n+1}>1$, so the distance between two distinct points of $B$ is at least $1$. So $B$ is discrete, unbounded in one direction, with no accumulation point; it is closed.
- *$A+B$ is not closed:* $n+\bigl(-n+\tfrac1n\bigr)=\tfrac1n\in A+B$ for all $n\ge2$, and $\tfrac1n\to0$. But $0\notin A+B$: $m+(-n+\tfrac1n)=0$ would give $\tfrac1n=n-m\in\mathbb{Z}$, which is impossible for $n\ge2$.

**Common mistake.** Believing that "closed + closed = closed" because $A+B$ is the image of $A\times B$ under addition. The image of a closed set under a continuous map is not closed in general; compactness of one factor is what saves the day.

**Remark.** The result in part 2 holds in any normed space; in part 3, the sets are closed and unbounded, and the escape of both to infinity creates the missing limit point.

@@@ rt-oc-014-open-closed-or-neither-a-classification.md
---
title: Open, closed or neither? A classification exercise
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 1
order: 20
tags: open set, closed set, classification, continuity
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

For each set, decide whether it is open, closed, both, or neither, and justify.

1. $\{x:x^2<2\}$.
2. $\{x:|x-1|\le2\}$.
3. $\{x:\sin x>0\}$.
4. $\{x:x^3-x\ge0\}$.
5. $\bigcup_{n\ge1}\left(n,\,n+\tfrac1n\right)$.
6. $\{x:\lfloor x\rfloor\text{ is even}\}$.
7. $\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]$.
8. $\{0,1\}$.

## Hint

Solve inequalities explicitly: the sets in 1–4 are unions of intervals. For 5–7, test the endpoints of the pieces.

## Solution

**Idea.** Rewrite each set as a union of intervals and check the endpoints.

1. $x^2<2\iff x\in(-\sqrt2,\sqrt2)$. **Open** (and not closed, as $\sqrt2$ is a limit not in the set).
2. $|x-1|\le2\iff x\in[-1,3]$. **Closed** (not open: $3$ has no interval around it inside the set).
3. $\sin x>0\iff x\in\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}(2k\pi,(2k+1)\pi)$. A union of open intervals: **open**, not closed (the endpoints $2k\pi$ are limits not in the set).
4. $x^3-x=x(x-1)(x+1)\ge0$. A sign table gives $x\in[-1,0]\cup[1,+\infty)$. **Closed**, not open (at $0$ points to the right are not in the set).
5. A union of open intervals: **open**. It is not closed: $n\ge1$ is the limit of the points $n+\tfrac1{k}$ ($k$ large), which lie in $(n,n+\tfrac1n)$, but $n$ itself is in none of the intervals: if $m<n$ then $n\ge m+1\ge m+\tfrac1m$, and if $m\ge n$ then $n\le m$, so $n\notin(m,m+\tfrac1m)$. (Moreover the intervals $(n,n+\tfrac1n)$ are pairwise disjoint.)
6. $\lfloor x\rfloor$ even $\iff x\in\bigcup_k[2k,2k+1)$. **Neither**: not open because $2k$ belongs to the set while points just to its left do not ($\lfloor x\rfloor=2k-1$ is odd); not closed because $2k+1$ is a limit of points $2k+1-\tfrac1m$ of the set, and $2k+1$ is not in it.
7. $\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]$: **neither**. Not open (no interval is made of rationals only), not closed (its closure is $[0,1]$, which contains irrational numbers).
8. $\{0,1\}$: **closed**, not open. A finite set is closed because its complement is a finite union of open intervals.

**Shortcut for 1–4.** A set $\{x:f(x)<c\}$ or $\{x:f(x)>c\}$ is open if $f$ is continuous (it is the preimage of an open set); a set $\{x:f(x)\le c\}$ or $\{x:f(x)\ge c\}$ is closed. This explains the answers to 1, 2, 3 and 4 at once, but remember that the converse statements ("not closed", "not open") need an explicit argument.

**Common mistake.** In 4, forgetting that the inequality is non-strict: the zeros $-1,0,1$ are part of the set, which makes it closed.

@@@ rt-oc-015-f-sigma-and-g-delta-sets.md
---
title: Countable unions of closed sets and countable intersections of open sets
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 29
tags: F-sigma, G-delta, distance function, rationals
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

A set is an **$F_\sigma$** if it is a countable union of closed sets, and a **$G_\delta$** if it is a countable intersection of open sets.

1. Show that every open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is an $F_\sigma$ and every closed subset is a $G_\delta$.
2. Show that $\mathbb{Q}$ is an $F_\sigma$ and that $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ is a $G_\delta$.
3. Determine the set of points of continuity of $f=\mathbf 1_{\mathbb{Q}}$ and check that it is a $G_\delta$.

## Hint

For 1, if $U\ne\mathbb{R}$ is open, write $U=\bigcup_n\{x:d(x,\mathbb{R}\setminus U)\ge\tfrac1n\}$. For 2, a countable set is a countable union of singletons.

## Solution

**Idea.** Closed sets can be approximated from outside by open "thickenings" $\{d(x,F)<\tfrac1n\}$, and open sets from inside by closed "shrinkings" $\{d(x,U^c)\ge\tfrac1n\}$.

**1. Open $\Rightarrow F_\sigma$.** Let $U\ne\mathbb{R}$ be open and $F=\mathbb{R}\setminus U\ne\emptyset$. The function $x\mapsto d(x,F)$ is continuous (it is 1-Lipschitz). Therefore $F_n=\{x:d(x,F)\ge\tfrac1n\}$ is closed. Moreover $d(x,F)>0\iff x\notin F$ (as $F$ is closed), so $\bigcup_nF_n=U$. (If $U=\mathbb{R}$ then $U=\bigcup_n[-n,n]$.)

**1'. Closed $\Rightarrow G_\delta$.** Let $F$ be closed, non-empty. The sets $U_n=\{x:d(x,F)<\tfrac1n\}$ are open and $\bigcap_nU_n=\{x:d(x,F)=0\}=F$. (If $F=\emptyset$, then $F=\bigcap_n\emptyset$ is an intersection of open sets.) This is also obtained from the first part by taking complements.

**2. Rationals.** $\mathbb{Q}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb{Q}}\{q\}$ is a countable union of closed sets (singletons), so an $F_\sigma$. Its complement is the intersection of the open sets $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{q\}$, so $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}=\bigcap_q(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{q\})$ is a $G_\delta$.

**3. Continuity points of $\mathbf 1_{\mathbb{Q}}$.** This function is continuous nowhere (every interval contains rationals and irrationals), so the set of continuity points is $\emptyset$, which is a $G_\delta$. A more interesting example is Thomae's function ($f(p/q)=1/q$ in lowest terms, $f=0$ on irrationals), which is continuous exactly on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$.

**Remark.** It is a theorem (using the Baire category theorem) that the set of continuity points of *any* function $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a $G_\delta$, and that $\mathbb{Q}$ is **not** a $G_\delta$; so no function is continuous exactly on $\mathbb{Q}$. This is the explanation of the contrast between $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ in the previous parts.

@@@ rt-oc-016-relative-topology-open-and-closed-in-a-subset.md
---
title: Open and closed relative to a subset
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 28
tags: relative topology, subspace, clopen, rationals
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Let $X\subset\mathbb{R}$. A subset $V\subset X$ is **open in $X$** if $V=U\cap X$ for some open $U\subset\mathbb{R}$, and **closed in $X$** if $X\setminus V$ is open in $X$.

1. Show that $[0,1)$ is open in $X=[0,1]$ but not open in $\mathbb{R}$.
2. Show that $V$ is closed in $X$ iff $V=F\cap X$ for some closed $F\subset\mathbb{R}$.
3. Show that in $X=\mathbb{Z}$ every subset is open and closed.
4. In $X=\mathbb{Q}$, show that $V=\mathbb{Q}\cap(-\sqrt2,\sqrt2)$ is both open and closed in $\mathbb{Q}$. Why does this not contradict the fact that $\mathbb{R}$ has no non-trivial clopen set?

## Hint

For part 1: $[0,1)=(-1,1)\cap[0,1]$. For part 4: $V=\mathbb{Q}\cap(-\sqrt2,\sqrt2)=\mathbb{Q}\cap[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]$ because $\pm\sqrt2\notin\mathbb{Q}$.

## Solution

**Idea.** "Open" is not an intrinsic property of a set: it depends on the ambient space in which we look at it. Relative topology tells us how to restrict the notion to a subset.

**1.** $[0,1)=(-1,1)\cap[0,1]$ with $(-1,1)$ open in $\mathbb{R}$: open in $X=[0,1]$. It is not open in $\mathbb{R}$ since $0\in[0,1)$ has no neighbourhood inside it.

**2.** $X\setminus V$ is open in $X$ iff $X\setminus V=U\cap X$ with $U$ open, iff $V=X\setminus U=(\mathbb{R}\setminus U)\cap X=F\cap X$ with $F=\mathbb{R}\setminus U$ closed. (We used that for $V\subset X$, $X\setminus(U\cap X)=X\cap(\mathbb{R}\setminus U)$.)

**3. $X=\mathbb{Z}$.** For $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, $\{k\}=\left(k-\tfrac12,k+\tfrac12\right)\cap\mathbb{Z}$ is open in $\mathbb{Z}$. Any subset is a union of singletons, hence open in $\mathbb{Z}$. By complement, any subset is also closed in $\mathbb{Z}$. (The topology on $\mathbb{Z}$ is called *discrete*.)

**4. $\mathbb{Q}$.** $V=\mathbb{Q}\cap(-\sqrt2,\sqrt2)$ is open in $\mathbb{Q}$. Also $V=\mathbb{Q}\cap[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]$ since $\pm\sqrt2\notin\mathbb{Q}$, so $V$ is closed in $\mathbb{Q}$. It is a non-empty proper subset of $\mathbb{Q}$ ($0\in V$ and $2\notin V$). So $\mathbb{Q}$ has non-trivial clopen subsets: it is *disconnected*.

**No contradiction.** In the proof for $\mathbb{R}$, we took the supremum of a set of reals and this supremum exists in $\mathbb{R}$. In $\mathbb{Q}$, the corresponding "supremum" would be $\sqrt2$, which is not a rational: completeness is exactly what makes $\mathbb{R}$ connected.

**Common mistake.** Saying "$[0,1)$ is not open" without specifying the ambient space. Always say "open in $\mathbb{R}$" or "open in $[0,1]$".

**Remark.** The relative topology is the one induced by the distance $|x-y|$ restricted to $X$: the "open ball" of centre $x\in X$ and radius $\varepsilon$ in $X$ is $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\cap X$.

@@@ rt-oc-017-open-sets-and-sequences.md
---
title: A sequential characterisation of open sets
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 9
tags: open set, sequences, characterisation
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Prove that $U\subset\mathbb{R}$ is open if and only if for every $x\in U$ and every sequence $(x_n)$ converging to $x$, the terms $x_n$ belong to $U$ for all large enough $n$.

## Hint

($\Rightarrow$) Use the $\varepsilon$ given by openness and the definition of convergence. ($\Leftarrow$) If $U$ is not open, find $x\in U$ and points $y_n\notin U$ with $y_n\to x$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Openness means "there is room around each point". A sequence converging to the point must eventually use that room; conversely, lack of room is witnessed by a sequence escaping from $U$.

**($\Rightarrow$)** Let $U$ be open, $x\in U$ and $x_n\to x$. There is $\varepsilon>0$ with $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subset U$. By convergence, there is $N$ with $|x_n-x|<\varepsilon$ for $n\ge N$, so $x_n\in U$ for $n\ge N$.

**($\Leftarrow$)** Suppose the sequential condition holds but $U$ is not open. Then there is $x\in U$ such that no interval $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)$ is contained in $U$. For each $n$, choose $y_n\in(x-\tfrac1n,x+\tfrac1n)\setminus U$. Then $y_n\to x$, but $y_n\notin U$ for **every** $n$, contradicting the hypothesis.

**Example.** The set $(0,+\infty)$ is open: if $x>0$ and $x_n\to x$ then eventually $x_n>x/2>0$. The set $[0,+\infty)$ is not: the sequence $-\tfrac1n\to0\in[0,\infty)$ but never enters the set.

**Common mistake.** Dropping the word "eventually". For an open set it is false that *all* terms of the sequence are in $U$: for $U=(0,1)$ and the sequence $-5,\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\dots$ with limit $\tfrac12\in U$, the first term is not in $U$.

**Remark.** Together with the previous characterisation of closed sets, this gives a dictionary: closed $\leftrightarrow$ "limits stay in", open $\leftrightarrow$ "convergent sequences enter".

@@@ rt-oc-018-the-distance-to-a-set.md
---
title: The distance function d(x, A)
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 25
tags: distance to a set, Lipschitz, closure, Bolzano-Weierstrass
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

For a non-empty $A\subset\mathbb{R}$ put $d(x,A)=\inf_{a\in A}|x-a|$.

1. Show that $|d(x,A)-d(y,A)|\le|x-y|$ for all $x,y$. Deduce that $d(\cdot,A)$ is continuous.
2. Show that $d(x,A)=0\iff x\in\overline A$ and that $d(x,A)=d(x,\overline A)$.
3. If $A$ is closed, show that the infimum is attained: there is $a\in A$ with $|x-a|=d(x,A)$. Show by an example that $a$ need not be unique and that the infimum need not be attained if $A$ is not closed.

## Hint

For 1: $|x-a|\le|x-y|+|y-a|$. For 3: take a minimising sequence, which is bounded, and extract a convergent subsequence.

## Solution

**1.** For every $a\in A$, $d(x,A)\le|x-a|\le|x-y|+|y-a|$. Taking the infimum over $a\in A$: $d(x,A)\le|x-y|+d(y,A)$. Exchanging $x,y$ gives the other inequality. So $d(\cdot,A)$ is $1$-Lipschitz, in particular continuous.

**2.** $d(x,A)=0\iff x\in\overline A$ is description 3 of the closure. For the second claim, $A\subset\overline A$ so $d(x,\overline A)\le d(x,A)$. Conversely, for $b\in\overline A$ and $\eta>0$ there is $a\in A$ with $|a-b|<\eta$, so $d(x,A)\le|x-a|\le|x-b|+\eta$; letting $\eta\to0$ and taking the infimum over $b$, $d(x,A)\le d(x,\overline A)$.

**3. Attainment.** Let $A$ be closed and $a_n\in A$ with $|x-a_n|\to d=d(x,A)$. The sequence $(a_n)$ is bounded (it lies in $[x-d-1,x+d+1]$ for large $n$), so by Bolzano–Weierstrass a subsequence converges to some $a$. Since $A$ is closed, $a\in A$, and $|x-a|=\lim|x-a_{n_k}|=d$.

**Examples.**
- *Non-uniqueness:* $A=\{-1,1\}$ and $x=0$: both points are at distance $1$.
- *Not attained when $A$ is not closed:* $A=(0,1)$ and $x=-1$: $d(x,A)=1$ but no point of $A$ is at distance $1$ ($0\notin A$).

**Remark.** The function $d(\cdot,A)$ is the standard way of converting a closed set into the *zero set of a continuous function*. See the problem on zero sets and the problem on $G_\delta$ sets, where it is used.

@@@ rt-oc-019-two-closed-sets-at-distance-zero.md
---
title: Disjoint closed sets can be arbitrarily close
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 26
tags: distance between sets, closed sets, compact sets, separation
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

For non-empty $A,B\subset\mathbb{R}$ define $d(A,B)=\inf\{|a-b|:a\in A,\ b\in B\}$.

1. Give two disjoint closed sets $A,B$ with $d(A,B)=0$.
2. Show that if $A$ is closed and $B$ is compact and they are disjoint, then $d(A,B)>0$.
3. Deduce that two disjoint closed sets with one of them compact can be separated by two disjoint open sets.

## Hint

For 1, use $A=\mathbb{N}$ and $B=\{n+\tfrac1n:n\ge2\}$. For 2, use the continuous function $b\mapsto d(b,A)$ on the compact set $B$.

## Solution

**1.** $A=\mathbb{N}$ and $B=\{n+\tfrac1n:n\ge2\}$. Both are closed: for $\mathbb{N}$, distinct points are at distance $\ge1$; for $B$, which is increasing, the difference of consecutive terms is $1-\tfrac1{n(n+1)}\ge\tfrac56$ (as $n\ge2$), so distinct points of $B$ are at distance $\ge\tfrac56$. A set whose distinct points are at distance $\ge\delta>0$ has no accumulation point, hence contains all of them and is closed. They are disjoint, as $n+\tfrac1n\notin\mathbb{Z}$ for $n\ge2$. But $|(n+\tfrac1n)-n|=\tfrac1n\to0$, so $d(A,B)=0$.

**2.** The function $f(b)=d(b,A)$ is continuous and, $A$ being closed, $f(b)>0$ for every $b\in B$ (since $b\notin A=\overline A$). A continuous function that is positive on a compact set has a positive minimum $m=f(b_0)$ (extreme value theorem). Hence $d(A,B)=\inf_{b\in B}d(b,A)=m>0$.

**3. Separation.** Let $r=d(A,B)/2>0$ and put
$$U=\{x:d(x,A)<r\},\qquad V=\{x:d(x,B)<r\}.$$
These are open (preimages of open sets by continuous functions), contain $A$, resp. $B$, and are disjoint: if $x\in U\cap V$, there would be $a\in A$, $b\in B$ with $|x-a|<r$, $|x-b|<r$, so $|a-b|<2r=d(A,B)$, absurd.

**Common mistake.** Thinking that "disjoint closed sets are at positive distance". It fails in general when neither set is compact, as part 1 shows (both sets are unbounded). Another classical counterexample: the graph of $y=\tfrac1x$ and the $x$-axis in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

**Remark.** Part 3 holds for arbitrary disjoint closed sets in $\mathbb{R}$ (it is the property "normal"), with $U=\{x:d(x,A)<d(x,B)\}$ and $V=\{x:d(x,B)<d(x,A)\}$. The distance-based $r$-neighbourhood construction above needs a compact set.

@@@ rt-oc-020-the-boundary-of-a-set.md
---
title: Properties of the boundary
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 15
tags: boundary, closure, interior, clopen sets
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

For $A\subset\mathbb{R}$, $\partial A=\overline A\setminus\mathring A$.

1. Show that $\partial A=\overline A\cap\overline{\mathbb{R}\setminus A}$, that $\partial A$ is closed, and that $\partial A=\partial(\mathbb{R}\setminus A)$.
2. Show that $\partial(A\cup B)\subset\partial A\cup\partial B$ and give an example of strict inclusion.
3. Show that $\partial(\partial A)\subset\partial A$ and find $A$ with $\partial(\partial A)\ne\partial A$.
4. Show that $\partial A=\emptyset$ iff $A\in\{\emptyset,\mathbb{R}\}$.

## Hint

For 1, use $\mathring A=\mathbb{R}\setminus\overline{\mathbb{R}\setminus A}$. For 3, use the closedness of $\partial A$. For 4, use the clopen problem.

## Solution

**1.** $\mathring A=\mathbb{R}\setminus\overline{\mathbb{R}\setminus A}$, so $\overline A\setminus\mathring A=\overline A\cap\overline{\mathbb{R}\setminus A}$. This is an intersection of two closed sets, hence closed. The formula is symmetric in $A$ and $\mathbb{R}\setminus A$ (the closure of the complement of the complement is $\overline A$), so $\partial A=\partial(\mathbb{R}\setminus A)$.

**2. Union.** If $x\in\partial(A\cup B)$, then $x\in\overline{A\cup B}=\overline A\cup\overline B$ and every interval around $x$ meets $\mathbb{R}\setminus(A\cup B)$. Say $x\in\overline A$. If $x\in\mathring A$, an interval around $x$ would lie in $A\subset A\cup B$, so $x\in\operatorname{int}(A\cup B)$, contradicting $x\in\partial(A\cup B)$. Hence $x\in\overline A\setminus\mathring A=\partial A$; similarly if $x\in\overline B$. *Strictness:* take $A=[0,1]$ and $B=(1,2]$: $\partial A=\{0,1\}$, $\partial B=\{1,2\}$, but $A\cup B=[0,2]$ has boundary $\{0,2\}\subsetneq\{0,1,2\}$.

**3.** $\partial A$ is closed, so $\overline{\partial A}=\partial A$, and $\partial(\partial A)=\overline{\partial A}\setminus\operatorname{int}(\partial A)\subset\partial A$. *Strict example:* $A=\mathbb{Q}$. Then $\partial A=\mathbb{R}$ (problem on classical sets) and $\partial(\partial A)=\partial\mathbb{R}=\emptyset\ne\mathbb{R}$. For $A=\mathbb{Z}$: $\partial A=\mathbb{Z}$ and $\partial\partial A=\mathbb{Z}$ (here equality).

**4.** $\partial A=\emptyset$ means $\overline A=\mathring A$; since $\mathring A\subset A\subset\overline A$, $A=\overline A=\mathring A$ is both closed and open, hence $\emptyset$ or $\mathbb{R}$. Conversely $\partial\emptyset=\partial\mathbb{R}=\emptyset$.

**Remark.** A standard fact used implicitly in part 3: *the boundary of a closed set has empty interior*. Indeed, let $F$ be closed and let $J$ be a non-empty open interval with $J\subset\partial F$. Since $\partial F\subset F$ (as $F$ is closed), $J\subset F$. But $J\subset\partial F\subset\overline{\mathbb{R}\setminus F}$ means every point of $J$ is a limit of $\mathbb{R}\setminus F$, contradicting the fact that $F$ is closed and $J\subset F$ is open. So $\operatorname{int}(\partial F)=\emptyset$.

It follows that the operation $\partial$ stabilises after one step on closed sets: for $F$ closed, $\partial F$ is closed with empty interior, so $\partial(\partial F)=\overline{\partial F}\setminus\operatorname{int}(\partial F)=\partial F\setminus\emptyset=\partial F$. In particular $\partial(\partial A)=\partial\partial A$ for every $A$ such that $\partial A$ is closed (which is always the case), but $\partial(\partial A)$ need not equal $\partial A$ (as the case $A=\mathbb{Q}$ shows).

@@@ rt-oc-021-derived-sets-and-the-derived-set-of-the-derived-set.md
---
title: Iterating the derived set
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l3
difficulty: 4
order: 17
tags: derived set, accumulation points, iteration
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Let $A'$ denote the derived set (set of accumulation points) of $A$.

1. Show that $(A\cup B)'=A'\cup B'$ and that $A\subset B\Rightarrow A'\subset B'$.
2. Show that $(A')'\subset A'$.
3. Let $A=\left\{\tfrac1m+\tfrac1{mn}:m,n\ge1\right\}$. Determine $A'$ and $A''=(A')'$.

## Hint

For 2, recall that $A'$ is closed. For 3, think of $A$ as a set of sequences: for fixed $m$, the elements $\tfrac1m+\tfrac1{mn}$ decrease to $\tfrac1m$ as $n\to\infty$.

## Solution

**1.** If $A\subset B$, any interval around $x$ containing a point of $A$ other than $x$ contains a point of $B$ other than $x$: $A'\subset B'$. For the union, $A'\cup B'\subset(A\cup B)'$ follows from monotonicity. Conversely, suppose $x\notin A'\cup B'$. There are $\varepsilon_A,\varepsilon_B>0$ such that $(x-\varepsilon_A,x+\varepsilon_A)\cap A\subset\{x\}$ and $(x-\varepsilon_B,x+\varepsilon_B)\cap B\subset\{x\}$. With $\varepsilon=\min(\varepsilon_A,\varepsilon_B)$, $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\cap(A\cup B)\subset\{x\}$, so $x\notin(A\cup B)'$.

**2.** $A'$ is closed, so it contains all its accumulation points: $(A')'\subset A'$.

**3. The example.** For fixed $m$, the points $a_{m,n}=\tfrac1m+\tfrac1{mn}$ ($n\ge1$) are pairwise distinct and converge to $\tfrac1m$. Hence $\tfrac1m\in A'$. Also $a_{m,n}\le\tfrac2m$ so the points with large $m$ are near $0$, and there are infinitely many of them: $0\in A'$.

*No other accumulation point:* let $x\in A'$ and choose distinct points of $A$ converging to $x$. Write them as $a_{m_k,n_k}$. If some $m$ occurs for infinitely many $k$, these points are distinct, so their $n_k$ are distinct and tend to $\infty$, hence they converge to $\tfrac1m$ and $x=\tfrac1m$. Otherwise each $m$ occurs finitely often, so $m_k\to\infty$ and $0<a_{m_k,n_k}\le\tfrac2{m_k}\to0$, i.e. $x=0$. Therefore
$$A'=\left\{\tfrac1m:m\ge1\right\}\cup\{0\}.$$
By the example of the problem on the derived set, the derived set of $\{1/m\}\cup\{0\}$ is $\{0\}$. So
$$A''=\{0\},\qquad A'''=\emptyset.$$

**Remark.** The sets $A\supset A'\supset A''\supset\cdots$ form a decreasing chain; the first $k$ for which $A^{(k)}=\emptyset$ measures how "complicated" $A$ is. Cantor discovered this construction (derived sets of arbitrary ordinal rank) while studying the uniqueness of trigonometric series: the origin of set theory.

@@@ rt-oc-022-isolated-points-are-countable.md
---
title: A set has at most countably many isolated points
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 18
tags: isolated points, countability, rational intervals
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Let $A\subset\mathbb{R}$ be any subset. Show that the set $I$ of isolated points of $A$ is at most countable. Deduce that an uncountable set $A$ has uncountably many accumulation points belonging to $A$.

## Hint

For each isolated point $x$, choose an interval with rational endpoints containing $x$ and no other point of $A$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Isolated points can be "separated" from each other by small intervals, and there are only countably many intervals with rational endpoints. This is a typical *Lindelöf-type* argument.

**Step 1: the map.** Let $x\in I$. There is $\varepsilon>0$ with $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\cap A=\{x\}$. Choose rationals $p,q$ with $x-\varepsilon<p<x<q<x+\varepsilon$. Then $(p,q)\cap A=\{x\}$. Define $\phi(x)=(p,q)\in\mathbb{Q}^2$ (choosing one such pair for each $x$).

**Step 2: injectivity.** If $\phi(x)=\phi(y)=(p,q)$ then $x,y\in(p,q)\cap A=\{x\}$, so $y=x$. So $\phi:I\to\mathbb{Q}\times\mathbb{Q}$ is injective.

**Step 3: conclusion.** $\mathbb{Q}\times\mathbb{Q}$ is countable, so $I$ is at most countable.

**Consequence.** If $A$ is uncountable, then $A\setminus I$ is uncountable (a countable set plus a countable set is countable). A point of $A\setminus I$ is a point of $A$ which is an accumulation point of $A$: $A\cap A'=A\setminus I$ is uncountable.

**Common mistake.** Trying to prove the claim by saying "the isolated points can be enumerated from left to right". The set of isolated points need not be well-ordered like $\mathbb{N}$ (think of $\{1/n\}\cup\{-1/n\}$, or of $\mathbb{Q}$ plus something); the injection into $\mathbb{Q}^2$ avoids this issue.

**Remark.** The statement is false in general topological spaces; it uses the fact that $\mathbb{R}$ has a *countable base* of open sets (intervals with rational endpoints).

@@@ rt-oc-023-a-perfect-set-is-uncountable.md
---
title: A non-empty closed set without isolated points is uncountable
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l3
difficulty: 4
order: 19
tags: perfect set, nested intervals, uncountability, Cantor
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

A subset $P\subset\mathbb{R}$ is **perfect** if it is closed, non-empty and has no isolated point. Prove that a perfect set is uncountable. Deduce that a non-empty countable closed subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has an isolated point.

## Hint

Suppose $P=\{x_1,x_2,\dots\}$. Build nested bounded open intervals $V_n$ meeting $P$ with $x_n\notin\overline{V_{n+1}}$ and $\overline{V_{n+1}}\subset V_n$, then use Cantor's nested compact sets theorem.

## Solution

**Idea.** This is Cantor's diagonal-type argument: a countable list cannot exhaust a set in which every point can be approximated by others. At each step we dodge the next listed point.

**Setup.** Assume by contradiction that $P$ is countable and write $P=\{x_1,x_2,x_3,\dots\}$ (it is infinite since a finite non-empty set has isolated points).

**Step 1: $V_1$.** Take $p_1\in P$ with $p_1\ne x_1$ (possible: $x_1$ is not isolated, so there are other points of $P$). Choose a bounded open interval $V_1\ni p_1$ with $x_1\notin\overline{V_1}$.

**Step 2: induction.** Suppose $V_n$ is a bounded open interval with $V_n\cap P\ne\emptyset$. Pick $p\in V_n\cap P$. Since $p$ is not isolated, $V_n\cap P$ contains infinitely many points, in particular a point $p_{n+1}\ne x_{n+1}$. Choose a bounded open interval $V_{n+1}\ni p_{n+1}$ with
$$\overline{V_{n+1}}\subset V_n,\qquad x_{n+1}\notin\overline{V_{n+1}}.$$

**Step 3: the nested compact sets.** Let $K_n=\overline{V_n}\cap P$. Each $K_n$ is closed and bounded (intersection of two closed sets, one bounded), hence compact; it is non-empty (it contains $p_n$); and $K_{n+1}\subset\overline{V_{n+1}}\subset V_n$ gives $K_{n+1}\subset K_n$. By Cantor's theorem (a decreasing sequence of non-empty compact sets has non-empty intersection), there is $x\in\bigcap_nK_n\subset P$.

**Step 4: contradiction.** Since $x\in P$, $x=x_k$ for some $k$. But $x\in K_k\subset\overline{V_k}$, whereas $x_k\notin\overline{V_k}$ by construction. Absurd. Hence $P$ is uncountable.

**Deduction.** If $F\ne\emptyset$ is closed and countable, it cannot be perfect, so it has an isolated point.

**Remark.** The Cantor ternary set is a perfect set, and it has empty interior: so closed sets without isolated points need not contain intervals. Together with the previous problem, this shows that an uncountable closed set has uncountably many points of accumulation (the *perfect set theorem* says even more: a closed uncountable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is the union of a perfect set and a countable set).

@@@ rt-oc-024-closed-sets-are-zero-sets-of-continuous-functions.md
---
title: Closed sets are zero sets of continuous functions
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 30
tags: closed set, zero set, continuous function, distance to a set
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

1. Show that for every closed $F\subset\mathbb{R}$ there is a continuous $f:\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty)$ with $F=\{x:f(x)=0\}$.
2. Show that for every open $U\subset\mathbb{R}$ there is a continuous $g:\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty)$ with $U=\{x:g(x)>0\}$.
3. Conversely, show that for continuous $f$, the set $\{f=0\}$ is closed and $\{f>0\}$ is open.

## Hint

Use $f(x)=d(x,F)$ when $F\ne\emptyset$, and treat $F=\emptyset$ separately. For 2, apply 1 to the complement.

## Solution

**1.** If $F=\emptyset$, take $f\equiv1$. Otherwise, define $f(x)=d(x,F)$. It is continuous (1-Lipschitz), non-negative, and $f(x)=0\iff x\in\overline F=F$.

**2.** Apply part 1 to the closed set $\mathbb{R}\setminus U$: we get $g\ge0$ continuous with $g=0$ exactly on $\mathbb{R}\setminus U$, so $g>0$ exactly on $U$.

**3.** If $f$ is continuous, $\{f=0\}=f^{-1}(\{0\})$ and $\{f>0\}=f^{-1}((0,\infty))$ are the preimages of a closed set, resp. an open set. Directly for the sequence characterisation: if $x_n\to x$ and $f(x_n)=0$ then $f(x)=\lim f(x_n)=0$; and if $f(x)>0$ then by continuity $f>\tfrac{f(x)}2$ on a neighbourhood of $x$.

**Consequence.** A subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is closed iff it is the zero set of a continuous function. In particular the Cantor set, $\mathbb{Z}$ or $\{1/n\}\cup\{0\}$ are zero sets of explicit continuous functions, e.g. $\mathbb{Z}$ is the zero set of $\sin(\pi x)$.

**Remark.** This is a manifestation of the fact that, for metric spaces, topology can be recovered from continuous functions; it also gives a quick proof that $\{x:f(x)\le c\}$ is closed for any continuous $f$ (zero set of $\max(f-c,0)$).

@@@ rt-oc-025-locally-finite-unions-of-closed-sets.md
---
title: When is an infinite union of closed sets closed?
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l3
difficulty: 4
order: 31
tags: locally finite family, union of closed sets, counterexamples
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

A family $(F_i)_{i\in I}$ of subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ is **locally finite** if every point has a neighbourhood $(x-\delta,x+\delta)$ which meets only finitely many $F_i$.

1. Show that the union of a locally finite family of closed sets is closed.
2. Deduce that $\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}[n,n+\tfrac12]$ is closed.
3. Show that the family $\{[\tfrac1n,1]\}_{n\ge2}$ is not locally finite and that its union is not closed.

## Hint

Show that the complement is open: at a point $x\notin\bigcup F_i$, take the neighbourhood that meets only finitely many $F_i$, and shrink it to avoid each of them.

## Solution

**Idea.** For finitely many closed sets, "shrinking to avoid each of them" is possible by taking the smallest radius. Local finiteness reduces the infinite case to the finite case near each point.

**1. Proof.** Let $x\notin\bigcup_iF_i$. By local finiteness there is $\delta>0$ and finitely many indices $i_1,\dots,i_k$ such that $(x-\delta,x+\delta)\cap F_i=\emptyset$ for all other $i$. For each $j\le k$, $F_{i_j}$ is closed and $x\notin F_{i_j}$, so there is $\delta_j>0$ with $(x-\delta_j,x+\delta_j)\cap F_{i_j}=\emptyset$. With $\eta=\min(\delta,\delta_1,\dots,\delta_k)>0$ we get $(x-\eta,x+\eta)\cap F_i=\emptyset$ for all $i$. So $\mathbb{R}\setminus\bigcup F_i$ is open.

**2.** The intervals $[n,n+\tfrac12]$ form a locally finite family: the neighbourhood $(x-\tfrac14,x+\tfrac14)$ meets at most two of them. Each is closed, hence so is the union.

**3. A non-example.** The point $0$ has no neighbourhood meeting only finitely many of the sets $[\tfrac1n,1]$ (any $(-\delta,\delta)$ contains $\tfrac1n$ for large $n$). The union is $\bigcup_{n\ge2}[\tfrac1n,1]=(0,1]$ (each point $x\in(0,1]$ lies in $[\tfrac1n,1]$ for $n\ge\max(2,1/x)$, and $0$ lies in none), which is not closed.

**Common mistake.** Local finiteness is a property of the *family*, not of the sets. The family $\{\{1/n\}\}_{n\ge1}$ consists of closed singletons and its union $\{1/n\}$ is not closed, while the family $\{\{n\}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is locally finite and its union $\mathbb{N}$ is closed.

**Remark.** Locally finite families also behave well for closures: $\overline{\bigcup F_i}=\bigcup\overline{F_i}}$. This is the kind of property one needs for gluing continuous functions defined on closed pieces.

@@@ rt-oc-026-true-or-false-open-and-closed-sets.md
---
title: True or false? Ten statements on open and closed sets
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-open-closed
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 21
tags: true or false, counterexamples, open sets, closed sets
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Decide whether each statement is true or false. Give a proof or a counterexample.

1. Every finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is closed.
2. A subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is open if and only if it is not closed.
3. An infinite union of closed sets is closed.
4. If $A$ is open, then $\overline A$ is open.
5. If $A$ is closed and non-empty, then $\mathring A$ is non-empty.
6. $\operatorname{int}(\overline A)=\mathring A$ for every $A$.
7. $\overline{\mathring A}=\overline A$ for every $A$.
8. The boundary of any subset is closed.
9. A non-empty closed bounded set has a largest and a smallest element.
10. If $A\subset B$ then $A'\subset B'$ (derived sets).

## Hint

For the false statements, the sets $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$, $(0,1)$, $[0,1)$ and $\{0\}$ are enough.

## Solution

**1. True.** A finite set $\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}$ is a finite union of singletons, and a singleton is closed (its complement is $(-\infty,a)\cup(a,\infty)$).

**2. False.** $\emptyset$ and $\mathbb{R}$ are both open and closed; $[0,1)$ is neither.

**3. False.** $\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{1/n\}$ is a union of closed sets (singletons) but it is not closed since $0$ is a limit not in it.

**4. False.** $A=(0,1)$ is open but $\overline A=[0,1]$ is not open.

**5. False.** $A=\mathbb{Z}$ is closed non-empty and has empty interior.

**6. False.** $A=\mathbb{Q}$: $\overline A=\mathbb{R}$ so $\operatorname{int}\overline A=\mathbb{R}\ne\emptyset=\mathring A$. (Another example: $A=(0,1)\cup(1,2)$: $\operatorname{int}\overline A=(0,2)\ne A$.)

**7. False.** $A=\{0\}$: $\mathring A=\emptyset$ so $\overline{\mathring A}=\emptyset\ne\{0\}=\overline A$.

**8. True.** $\partial A=\overline A\cap\overline{\mathbb{R}\setminus A}$ is an intersection of closed sets.

**9. True.** Let $F$ be closed, non-empty and bounded. $s=\sup F$ exists by completeness; for each $n$ there is $x_n\in F$ with $s-\tfrac1n<x_n\le s$, so $x_n\to s$ and $s\in F$ since $F$ is closed. Same for the infimum. (This fails without closedness: $(0,1)$ has no maximum; or without boundedness: $\mathbb{N}$ has no maximum.)

**10. True.** An interval around $x$ containing a point of $A\setminus\{x\}$ contains a point of $B\setminus\{x\}$.

**Score.** Four true ($1,8,9,10$) and six false ($2$–$7$).

**Remark.** When facing "true or false?", first try the extreme examples $\emptyset$, $\mathbb{R}$, singletons, $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$, $(0,1)$, $[0,1)$, $\{1/n\}$: these cover nearly all the pathologies of the real line.
@@@ rt-sq-001-adherent-values-of-an-alternating-sequence.md
---
title: Adherent values of an alternating sequence
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-sequences
level: l2
difficulty: 1
order: 1
tags: adherent value, cluster value, subsequence
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

A real number $x$ is an **adherent value** (or cluster value) of a sequence $(u_n)$ if some subsequence $(u_{n_k})$ converges to $x$. Find all adherent values of
$$u_n=(-1)^n\left(1+\frac1n\right),\qquad n\ge1,$$
and prove your answer.

## Hint

Look separately at the terms with $n$ even and the terms with $n$ odd.

To prove that no other value is adherent, recall that any infinite set of indices contains infinitely many even indices or infinitely many odd indices (or both).

## Solution

**Idea.** The sequence splits into two convergent subsequences with different limits. Every subsequence is then forced to "choose a side".

**Step 1: two limits are adherent.**
- For even indices $n=2k$: $u_{2k}=1+\frac1{2k}\to1$. So $1$ is an adherent value.
- For odd indices $n=2k+1$: $u_{2k+1}=-1-\frac1{2k+1}\to-1$. So $-1$ is an adherent value.

**Step 2: no other adherent value.** Let $(u_{n_k})$ be a subsequence converging to some $x$. The indices $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ form an infinite set, so at least one of the two parities occurs infinitely often.
- If infinitely many $n_k$ are even, those terms form a subsequence of $(u_{2k})$, which converges to $1$. A subsequence of a convergent sequence has the same limit, and a subsequence of $(u_{n_k})$ also converges to $x$. By uniqueness of limits, $x=1$.
- If infinitely many $n_k$ are odd, the same argument gives $x=-1$.

**Conclusion.** The set of adherent values is $\{-1,1\}$. In particular the sequence does not converge (a convergent sequence has exactly one adherent value, its limit).

**Remark.** The sequence is bounded, and $\limsup u_n=1$, $\liminf u_n=-1$ (see the problem on $\limsup$). A common mistake is to say "the adherent values are the terms $u_n$ themselves". The adherent values are *limits* of subsequences, and the terms $u_n$ themselves ($\pm(1+1/n)$) are not adherent values.

@@@ rt-sq-002-two-descriptions-of-adherent-values.md
---
title: Two descriptions of adherent values
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-sequences
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 2
tags: adherent value, subsequence, epsilon characterisation
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Let $(u_n)$ be a real sequence and $x\in\mathbb{R}$. Prove that the following are equivalent.
1. $x$ is the limit of some subsequence of $(u_n)$.
2. For every $\varepsilon>0$ and every $N\in\mathbb{N}$, there is $n\ge N$ with $|u_n-x|<\varepsilon$.

## Hint

For $(1)\Rightarrow(2)$, use the definition of a limit for the subsequence and the fact that $n_k\ge k$.

For $(2)\Rightarrow(1)$, build the indices $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ one at a time, using $\varepsilon=1/k$ at step $k$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Condition (2) says "every neighbourhood of $x$ contains terms of arbitrarily high index", i.e. infinitely many terms. This is the form that is easiest to check; condition (1) is the form that is easiest to use.

**$(1)\Rightarrow(2)$.** Let $u_{n_k}\to x$ with $n_1<n_2<\cdots$. Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and $N$. By the definition of convergence there is $K$ such that $|u_{n_k}-x|<\varepsilon$ for all $k\ge K$. Since $n_k\ge k$ (strictly increasing integers), choosing $k=\max(K,N)$ gives $n_k\ge N$ and $|u_{n_k}-x|<\varepsilon$. So $n=n_k$ works.

**$(2)\Rightarrow(1)$.** We construct the subsequence by induction.
- Apply (2) with $\varepsilon=1$ and $N=0$: there is $n_1$ with $|u_{n_1}-x|<1$.
- Suppose $n_1<\dots<n_{k-1}$ are built. Apply (2) with $\varepsilon=\frac1k$ and $N=n_{k-1}+1$: there is $n_k\ge n_{k-1}+1$ with $|u_{n_k}-x|<\frac1k$.

The indices are strictly increasing, so $(u_{n_k})$ is a subsequence, and $|u_{n_k}-x|<\frac1k\to0$. Hence $u_{n_k}\to x$.

**Remark.** The role of "$N$" in (2) is essential. If we only asked for *some* $n$ with $|u_n-x|<\varepsilon$, every term of the sequence would qualify (take $\varepsilon$ larger than $|u_n-x|$ and $x=u_n$), and the notion would be empty. A common mistake is to confuse "$x$ is an adherent value of the sequence" with "$x$ is an adherent point of the set $\{u_n\}$". These differ. For $u_n=1/n$, the set $\{u_n\}=\{1,1/2,1/3,\dots\}$ has adherent points $\{0\}\cup\{1,1/2,1/3,\dots\}$ (each term is trivially an adherent point of the set, and $0$ is a limit point), whereas the sequence $(u_n)$ has only the adherent value $0$. The two notions must be distinguished.

@@@ rt-sq-003-adherent-values-of-a-periodic-sequence-with-a-perturbation.md
---
title: Adherent values of cos(nπ/3) + 1/n
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-sequences
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 3
tags: adherent value, periodic sequence, residue classes
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Determine the set of adherent values of
$$u_n=\cos\frac{n\pi}3+\frac1n,\qquad n\ge1.$$

## Hint

$\cos\frac{n\pi}3$ only depends on $n$ modulo $6$. Split the indices into the $6$ residue classes.

## Solution

**Idea.** A sequence made of a periodic part and a part tending to $0$ has, as adherent values, exactly the values taken by the periodic part.

**Step 1: the periodic part.** Since $\cos\frac{(n+6)\pi}3=\cos\left(\frac{n\pi}3+2\pi\right)=\cos\frac{n\pi}3$, the values for $n\equiv r\pmod 6$, $r=0,\dots,5$, are
$$\cos0=1,\ \cos\tfrac\pi3=\tfrac12,\ \cos\tfrac{2\pi}3=-\tfrac12,\ \cos\pi=-1,\ \cos\tfrac{4\pi}3=-\tfrac12,\ \cos\tfrac{5\pi}3=\tfrac12.$$
So the periodic part takes exactly the four values $\{1,\tfrac12,-\tfrac12,-1\}$.

**Step 2: each of these four is adherent.** For a residue class $r$, consider the subsequence $n=6k+r$ (with $k$ large so that $n\ge1$). Then $u_{6k+r}=\cos\frac{r\pi}3+\frac1{6k+r}\to\cos\frac{r\pi}3$. So each value $\cos\frac{r\pi}3$ is an adherent value.

**Step 3: there is no other.** Let $u_{n_k}\to x$. The indices $n_k$ fall into $6$ residue classes, so some class $r$ contains infinitely many $n_k$. Along those indices, $u_{n_k}\to\cos\frac{r\pi}3$ (Step 2), and a subsequence of a convergent sequence has the same limit, so $x=\cos\frac{r\pi}3$.

**Conclusion.** The set of adherent values is $\left\{-1,-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,1\right\}$.

**Remark.** The general principle (pigeonhole on residue classes) is used constantly. Here it shows $\limsup u_n=1$ and $\liminf u_n=-1$. Note that the perturbation $\frac1n$ is irrelevant for the set of adherent values, but it matters for another question: the values $u_n$ themselves are never equal to $-\tfrac12$ or $\tfrac12$ exactly for $n\ge1$. Adherent values need not be values of the sequence.

@@@ rt-sq-004-an-enumeration-of-the-rationals.md
---
title: Every point of [0,1] is an adherent value of an enumeration of the rationals
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-sequences
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 4
