Conversely if $\omega_f(x)=0$, given $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta$ with $\sup<\varepsilon$, in particular $|f(y)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ for $y\in(x-\delta,x+\delta)$.

**2. Openness.** Let $\omega_f(x)<\varepsilon$. Choose $\delta>0$ with $\sup\{|f(y)-f(z)|:y,z\in(x-\delta,x+\delta)\}<\varepsilon$. If $x'\in(x-\delta,x+\delta)$, pick $\delta'>0$ with $(x'-\delta',x'+\delta')\subset(x-\delta,x+\delta)$; the supremum over the smaller interval is also $<\varepsilon$, so $\omega_f(x')<\varepsilon$. Hence $\{\omega_f<\varepsilon\}$ contains a neighbourhood of each of its points: it is open.

By part 1,
$$\mathrm{Cont}(f)=\{\omega_f=0\}=\bigcap_{n\ge1}\{\omega_f<\tfrac1n\},$$
a countable intersection of open sets: a $G_\delta$.

**3.** If $f$ were continuous exactly on $\mathbb{Q}$, then $\mathbb{Q}=\mathrm{Cont}(f)$ would be a $G_\delta$, contradicting problem 22.

**4. Thomae.** *Discontinuity at $p/q$:* $f(p/q)=\frac1q>0$ while irrational numbers arbitrarily close to $p/q$ give $f=0$, so $f$ is not continuous at $p/q$. *Continuity at an irrational $x$:* let $\varepsilon>0$ and choose $N$ with $\frac1N<\varepsilon$. The rationals in $(x-1,x+1)$ with denominator $\le N$ form a finite set (for each denominator there are finitely many fractions in a bounded interval), and $x$ is not among them. Take $0<\delta\le1$ so small that $(x-\delta,x+\delta)$ avoids this finite set. Then for $y$ in this interval, either $y$ is irrational and $f(y)=0=f(x)$, or $y=p/q$ in lowest terms with $q>N$ and $f(y)=\frac1q<\frac1N<\varepsilon$.

**Common mistake.** Thinking the set of continuity points can be an arbitrary set: Baire says it cannot be $\mathbb{Q}$, and in general it is always a $G_\delta$. Conversely every $G_\delta$ is the set of continuity points of some function (a harder theorem).

**Remark.** Combining parts 2 and 3 we see a strict asymmetry between $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$: one can have a function continuous exactly on the irrationals (Thomae), but never exactly on the rationals.

@@@ rt-dn-024-a-meagre-set-of-full-measure.md
---
title: R is the union of a meagre set and a null set
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-density
level: m1
difficulty: 5
order: 24
tags: meagre, null set, dense G delta, category versus measure
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

A set $N\subset\mathbb{R}$ is **null** if for every $\varepsilon>0$ it can be covered by countably many intervals of total length $<\varepsilon$.

Prove that $\mathbb{R}=A\cup B$ where $A$ is meagre and $B$ is null. Deduce that $B$ is a dense, uncountable, null $G_\delta$ set.

## Hint

Enumerate $\mathbb{Q}=\{q_1,q_2,\dots\}$, put $U_m=\bigcup_n\big(q_n-2^{-n-m},q_n+2^{-n-m}\big)$ and $B=\bigcap_mU_m$.

## Solution

**Idea.** $U_m$ is a dense open set (it contains all rationals) with tiny total length; the intersection $B$ is large topologically (comeagre) and tiny metrically (null).

**$U_m$ is open and dense.** It is a union of open intervals and contains $\mathbb{Q}$, hence is dense.

**$B$ is null.** For each $m$, the intervals defining $U_m$ have total length at most $\sum_{n\ge1}2\cdot2^{-n-m}=2^{1-m}$. Since $B\subset U_m$ for all $m$, for $\varepsilon>0$ choose $m$ with $2^{1-m}<\varepsilon$: $B$ is covered by countably many intervals of total length $<\varepsilon$.

**$A=\mathbb{R}\setminus B$ is meagre.**
$$A=\mathbb{R}\setminus\bigcap_mU_m=\bigcup_m(\mathbb{R}\setminus U_m).$$
Each $\mathbb{R}\setminus U_m$ is closed, and its interior is empty because $U_m$ is dense. So it is nowhere dense, and $A$ is a countable union of nowhere dense sets.

**Properties of $B$.** It is a $G_\delta$ by construction. It is dense, being a countable intersection of dense open sets (Baire, problem 20). It is uncountable: if it were countable, $\mathbb{R}=A\cup B$ would be meagre (countable sets are meagre), contradicting Baire.

**Common mistake.** Category and measure are *unrelated* notions of "small" or "large": $B$ is large for category ($\mathbb{R}\setminus B$ meagre) and small for measure ($B$ null), while $A$ is the opposite. One should never use one to deduce the other.

**Remark.** So $\mathbb{R}$ can be split into two pieces, one negligible for category and the other negligible for measure. In particular "almost every" in the sense of measure and "generic" in the sense of category can be about disjoint sets.

@@@ rt-dn-025-perfect-sets-are-uncountable.md
---
title: A non-empty perfect set is uncountable
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-density
level: m1
difficulty: 5
order: 25
tags: perfect set, uncountable, nested compact sets
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

A set $P\subset\mathbb{R}$ is **perfect** if it is closed and has no isolated point. Prove that a non-empty perfect set $P$ is uncountable.

## Hint

Suppose $P=\{x_1,x_2,\dots\}$. Build open intervals $V_1\supset\overline{V_2}\supset\overline{V_3}\supset\cdots$ meeting $P$ such that $x_n\notin\overline{V_{n+1}}$. Intersect the compact sets $\overline{V_n}\cap P$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Because $P$ has no isolated points, each of its points can be "avoided" inside a smaller neighbourhood still meeting $P$; nested compact sets then produce a point of $P$ that avoids every $x_n$.

**Preliminary.** Since $P$ has no isolated point, every non-empty open interval $V$ meeting $P$ contains *infinitely many* points of $P$. Indeed let $x\in V\cap P$. As $x$ is not isolated, every $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood contains a point of $P$ other than $x$; shrinking $\varepsilon$ we get infinitely many distinct points of $P$ in $V$.

**Suppose $P$ countable.** $P$ is infinite (it is non-empty without isolated points), so $P=\{x_1,x_2,\dots\}$.

*Construction.* Let $V_1$ be an open interval around $x_1$. Suppose $V_n$ is an open interval with $V_n\cap P\ne\emptyset$. By the preliminary remark pick $y\in V_n\cap P$ with $y\ne x_n$. Choose an open interval $V_{n+1}\ni y$ so small that $\overline{V_{n+1}}\subset V_n$ and $x_n\notin\overline{V_{n+1}}$ (possible because $y\ne x_n$ and $V_n$ is open).

*The nested compact sets.* Let $K_n=\overline{V_n}\cap P$. Each $K_n$ is compact (closed and bounded, intersection of two closed sets, one of them bounded) and non-empty (it contains $V_n\cap P\ne\emptyset$), and $K_{n+1}\subset\overline{V_{n+1}}\cap P\subset V_n\cap P\subset K_n$. By the nested compact sets theorem $\bigcap_nK_n\ne\emptyset$; let $x$ be in it. Then $x\in P$, so $x=x_k$ for some $k$. But $x\in K_{k+1}\subset\overline{V_{k+1}}$ and $x_k\notin\overline{V_{k+1}}$ by construction: contradiction. Hence $P$ is uncountable.

**Common mistake.** The hypothesis "closed" is used to get compactness of the $K_n$; the hypothesis "no isolated point" gives the room to avoid $x_n$. Without the second one the statement fails ($\{0\}$ is closed and countable), without the first as well ($\mathbb{Q}$ has no isolated point but is countable).

**Remark.** This applies to the Cantor set (problem 13), giving uncountability without ternary expansions. A stronger theorem (Cantor–Bendixson) says that every closed subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is the union of a perfect set and a countable set.

@@@ rt-dn-026-a-fat-cantor-set.md
---
title: A fat Cantor set: nowhere dense with positive measure
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-density
level: l3
difficulty: 4
order: 26
tags: fat Cantor set, Smith-Volterra-Cantor, measure, nowhere dense
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Construct $F=\bigcap_nF_n$ as follows: $F_0=[0,1]$, and to get $F_n$ from $F_{n-1}$ remove from the middle of each of the $2^{n-1}$ intervals of $F_{n-1}$ an open interval of length $4^{-n}$.

1. Show that the construction is possible: the intervals of $F_n$ have length $\ell_n=\dfrac{2^n+1}{2\cdot4^n}$ and $\ell_{n-1}>4^{-n}$.
2. Show that $F$ is closed, has empty interior, and that the total length of the removed intervals is $\frac12$, so $F$ has measure $\frac12$.
3. Show that $F$ has no isolated point (so it is perfect and uncountable).

## Hint

Compute $\ell_n$ by the recurrence $\ell_n=\frac{\ell_{n-1}-4^{-n}}2$ and verify the closed form by induction. Compute the removed length as a geometric series.

## Solution

**Idea.** The Cantor set removes a fraction $\frac13$ at each stage and loses everything; removing instead smaller and smaller intervals ($4^{-n}$, summable) keeps a positive part, while still destroying every interval.

**1. Lengths.** The $2^{n-1}$ intervals of $F_{n-1}$ each have length $\ell_{n-1}$. We remove from each an open middle interval of length $4^{-n}$, and two intervals of equal length remain, $\ell_n=\frac{\ell_{n-1}-4^{-n}}2$, with $\ell_0=1$. Claim: $\ell_n=\frac{2^n+1}{2\cdot4^n}$. For $n=0$: $\frac{2}{2}=1$ ✓. If true for $n-1$,
$$\ell_n=\frac12\left(\frac{2^{n-1}+1}{2\cdot4^{n-1}}-\frac1{4^n}\right)=\frac12\cdot\frac{2(2^{n-1}+1)-1}{4^n}=\frac{2^n+1}{2\cdot4^n}.$$
Feasibility: $\ell_{n-1}=\frac{2^{n-1}+1}{2\cdot4^{n-1}}=\frac{2(2^{n-1}+1)}{4^n}>\frac1{4^n}$. (First values: $\frac38,\frac5{32},\frac9{128}$.)

**2. Properties.**
*Closed:* intersection of the closed sets $F_n$. *Empty interior:* an interval contained in $F$ lies in $F_n$ for every $n$, hence in an interval of length $\ell_n\to0$; so its length is $0$.
*Removed length:* at stage $n$ we remove $2^{n-1}$ intervals of length $4^{-n}$, total $2^{n-1}4^{-n}=2^{-n-1}$. Summing,
$$\sum_{n\ge1}2^{-n-1}=\frac12.$$
So $[0,1]\setminus F$ is a disjoint union of open intervals of total length $\frac12$ and $F$ has measure $1-\frac12=\frac12$. Consistently, $2^n\ell_n=\frac{2^n+1}{2^{n+1}}\to\frac12$.

**3. No isolated point.** Let $x\in F$ and $n\ge1$. Then $x$ lies in an interval $I$ of $F_n$ of length $\ell_n$. The two endpoints of $I$ belong to $F$ (an endpoint of an interval of $F_n$ is never removed later: later removals are in the open middle parts). One of them, call it $e$, is different from $x$ and satisfies $|e-x|\le\ell_n$. So $x$ is a limit of points of $F$ different from $x$ as $n\to\infty$.

**Common mistake.** "Nowhere dense $\Rightarrow$ measure zero" is false: $F$ is nowhere dense (closed with empty interior) but has measure $\frac12$. Category and measure are independent ideas of size.

**Remark.** Taking $\alpha 4^{-n}$ with $\alpha\in(0,2)$ in place of $4^{-n}$ gives a fat Cantor set of any measure $1-\frac\alpha2$. The indicator function of $F$ is a bounded function that is Lebesgue integrable but not Riemann integrable: its set of discontinuities is $F$, of positive measure.

@@@ rt-dn-027-countable-closed-sets.md
---
title: Countable closed sets and their derived sets
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-density
level: l3
difficulty: 4
order: 27
tags: countable closed sets, derived set, isolated points, scattered sets
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

For $A\subset\mathbb{R}$ let $A'$ be the set of accumulation points of $A$ (the *derived set*).

1. Show that every non-empty countable closed set has an isolated point.
2. Construct a countable closed set $K$ such that $K'\ne\emptyset$ and $K''\ne\emptyset$.
3. Show that $\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]$ is countable but not closed and has no isolated point, and explain why this does not contradict part 1.

## Hint

For part 1, use problem 25. For part 2, put a sequence converging to $1/n$ near each $1/n$.

## Solution

**Idea.** A countable closed set is "scattered": it must have isolated points. One can iterate: remove them, take the derived set, and so on.

**1.** Let $F$ be a non-empty countable closed set. If $F$ had no isolated point it would be perfect (closed, non-empty, no isolated point), hence uncountable by problem 25: contradiction.

**2. An example.** For $n\ge1$ and $m\ge1$ put $a_{n,m}=\frac1n+\frac1{mn^3}$, and let
$$K=\{0\}\cup\{\tfrac1n:n\ge1\}\cup\{a_{n,m}:n,m\ge1\}.$$
$K$ is countable.

*Local structure.* For $n\ge2$, $\frac1n+\frac1{n^3}<\frac1{n-1}$ (since $\frac1{n(n-1)}>\frac1{n^3}$). So the points $a_{n,m}$ lie in the open interval $(\frac1n,\frac1n+\frac1{n^3}]$ which is contained in $(\frac1n,\frac1{n-1})$. Within this interval the points $a_{n,m}$ form a sequence converging to $\frac1n$ (as $m\to\infty$) and they are all distinct from $\frac1n$ and from each other. The remaining points of $K$ — namely $0$, the $\frac1k$ for $k\ne n$, and the $a_{k,m}$ for $k\ne n$ — all lie outside $(\frac1n,\frac1{n-1})$ except for the endpoints $\frac1n$ and $\frac1{n-1}$, and only $\frac1n$ is in $K$.

*Closedness.* Let $x\notin K$. We exhibit an open neighbourhood of $x$ meeting $K$ at most at one point, hence $x$ is not an accumulation point of $K$.

- If $x<0$ or $x>1$, then $\min(|x|,|x-1|)>0$ and $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)$ misses $K$.
- If $x\in[\frac1{n+1},\frac1n]$ for some $n\ge1$ with $x\notin\{\frac1{n+1},\frac1n\}$, then $x$ lies strictly inside $(\frac1{n+1},\frac1n)$. But $(\frac1{n+1},\frac1n)$ meets $K$ only in the cluster $\{a_{n,m}\}_m$ (which lies in $(\frac1n,\frac1n+\frac1{n^3})$ and is disjoint from $(\frac1{n+1},\frac1n)$), and the cluster at level $n+1$ (which lies in $(\frac1{n+1},\frac1{n+1}+\frac1{(n+1)^3})$, also disjoint from $(\frac1{n+1},\frac1n)$ because $\frac1{n+1}+\frac1{(n+1)^3}<\frac1n$ for $n\ge1$). So $(\frac1{n+1},\frac1n)\cap K=\emptyset$ — in particular $x$ is not an accumulation point of $K$.
- If $x\in(\frac1n,\frac1n+\frac1{n^3})$ for some $n\ge1$ with $x\notin\{a_{n,m}\}_m$, then $x\ne\frac1n$; take $\varepsilon=\min\{|x-\frac1n|,|x-\frac1n-\frac1{n^3}|,\min_m|x-a_{n,m}|\}$ (the last minimum is over the finitely many $a_{n,m}$ with $|x-a_{n,m}|\le|x-\frac1n|$, which is finite because $a_{n,m}\to\frac1n$). Then $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\cap K\subseteq\{x\}$ (or is empty), so $x$ is not an accumulation point of $K$.
- If $x=\frac1n$ or $x=0$, then $x\in K$ — so it is not in $\mathbb{R}\setminus K$ to begin with.

Hence every point of $\mathbb{R}\setminus K$ is at positive distance from $K$ (locally), which means $\mathbb{R}\setminus K$ is open, i.e. $K$ is closed.

*Derived sets.* The accumulation points of $K$ are $0$ and the points $\frac1n$: indeed, each $\frac1n$ is the limit of $(a_{n,m})_m$, and $0$ is the limit of $(\frac1n)_n$. No other point can be an accumulation point by the local structure above. So $K'=\{0\}\cup\{\frac1n:n\ge1\}$. Then each $\frac1n$ is isolated in $K'$, and $0$ is the limit of the $\frac1n$, so $K''=\{0\}$. Finally, $0$ is isolated in $K''=\{0\}$, so $K'''=\emptyset$.

**3.** $\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]$ is countable, dense in $[0,1]$ (so every point of $[0,1]$, rational or not, is an accumulation point) and has no isolated point; it is not closed (its closure is $[0,1]$). Part 1 applies to *closed* countable sets only; closedness is exactly what makes problem 25 applicable.

**Common mistake.** Believing that "countable and without isolated points" is impossible. It is impossible only for closed sets; $\mathbb{Q}$ is the standard counterexample otherwise.

**Remark.** Iterating $F\mapsto F'$ (transfinitely) terminates at $\emptyset$ for every countable closed set; the number of steps is its *Cantor–Bendixson rank*. The set $K$ above has rank $3$. This is the historical origin of ordinal numbers.

@@@ rt-dn-028-a-dense-uncountable-null-meagre-set.md
---
title: A set that is dense, uncountable, null and meagre
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-density
level: m1
difficulty: 5
order: 28
tags: Cantor set, translations, meagre, null, dense
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Let $E=C+\mathbb{Q}=\{c+q:c\in C,\ q\in\mathbb{Q}\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb{Q}}(C+q)$, where $C$ is the Cantor set.

1. Show that $E$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$ and uncountable.
2. Show that $E$ is meagre and null.
3. Deduce that $\mathbb{R}\setminus E$ is dense, and that $E\ne\mathbb{R}$.

## Hint

$0\in C$, so $\mathbb{Q}\subset E$. For part 2, $C+q$ is a translate of a closed nowhere dense null set; use countable unions. For part 3 use Baire.

## Solution

**Idea.** Countably many translates of a thin set remain thin (meagre and null) but now their union is dense because the translation vectors form a dense set.

**1. Dense, uncountable.** Since $0\in C$, $E\supset\mathbb{Q}+0=\mathbb{Q}$, which is dense (problem 1). Also $E\supset C$, which is uncountable (problem 14).

**2. Meagre.** Each $C+q$ is the image of $C$ under the homeomorphism $x\mapsto x+q$, so it is closed with empty interior, i.e. nowhere dense. $E$ is a countable union of nowhere dense sets: meagre (problem 19).

**Null.** Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Enumerate $\mathbb{Q}=\{q_1,q_2,\dots\}$. By problem 13, $C$ is covered by finitely many intervals of total length $<\varepsilon2^{-j}$ for any $j$; translating them by $q_j$ we cover $C+q_j$ by intervals of total length $<\varepsilon2^{-j}$. All these intervals together cover $E$ and have total length less than $\sum_j\varepsilon2^{-j}=\varepsilon$.

**3. The complement.** $E$ is meagre, so $\mathbb{R}\setminus E$ is dense: otherwise some open interval $I$ would be contained in $E$, hence meagre, contradicting Baire (problem 20). Also $E\ne\mathbb{R}$, since $\mathbb{R}$ is not meagre.

**Common mistake.** "Dense" and "meagre" are not contradictory: a set can be dense and still nowhere large in the Baire sense, as $\mathbb{Q}$ and $E$ show. What cannot be is a meagre set that contains an interval.

**Remark.** The set $E$ is an $F_\sigma$, since it is a countable union of closed sets $C+q$, and it is not a $G_\delta$ (a dense $G_\delta$ is comeagre, whereas $E$ is meagre). It is therefore a natural example of a dense $F_\sigma$ set with dense complement, both uncountable, with complement of full measure and comeagre.
@@@ rt-ct-01-continuity-through-open-sets.md
---
title: Continuity through open sets
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: l2
difficulty: 1
order: 1
tags: continuity, preimage, open sets, epsilon-delta
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$. Prove that $f$ is continuous if and only if $f^{-1}(U)$ is open for every open set $U\subset\mathbb{R}$. Deduce that $f^{-1}(F)$ is closed for every closed set $F$.

## Hint

For "$\Rightarrow$", take $x\in f^{-1}(U)$ and put a small interval around $f(x)$ inside $U$.

For "$\Leftarrow$", apply the hypothesis to the open interval $U=(f(x)-\varepsilon,f(x)+\varepsilon)$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Continuity at $x$ says "points close to $x$ are sent close to $f(x)$". Open sets are exactly the sets in which every point has a whole interval of room around it. Preimages translate one statement into the other.

Recall: $U$ is *open* if for each $a\in U$ there is $r>0$ with $(a-r,a+r)\subset U$; $f$ is *continuous at $x$* if for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $|y-x|<\delta\Rightarrow|f(y)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$.

**Step 1: continuous $\Rightarrow$ preimages of open sets are open.** Let $U$ be open and $x\in f^{-1}(U)$, so $f(x)\in U$. Since $U$ is open there is $\varepsilon>0$ with $(f(x)-\varepsilon,f(x)+\varepsilon)\subset U$. By continuity at $x$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $|y-x|<\delta$ implies $f(y)\in(f(x)-\varepsilon,f(x)+\varepsilon)\subset U$, that is $y\in f^{-1}(U)$. So $(x-\delta,x+\delta)\subset f^{-1}(U)$. As $x$ was arbitrary, $f^{-1}(U)$ is open.

**Step 2: preimages of open sets open $\Rightarrow$ continuous.** Fix $x$ and $\varepsilon>0$. The interval $U=(f(x)-\varepsilon,f(x)+\varepsilon)$ is open, so $f^{-1}(U)$ is open and contains $x$. Hence there is $\delta>0$ with $(x-\delta,x+\delta)\subset f^{-1}(U)$, which says exactly: $|y-x|<\delta\Rightarrow|f(y)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$.

**Step 3: closed sets.** If $F$ is closed then $\mathbb{R}\setminus F$ is open and
$$f^{-1}(F)=\mathbb{R}\setminus f^{-1}(\mathbb{R}\setminus F),$$
which is the complement of an open set, hence closed.

**Common mistake.** The statement is about **preimages**. Images of open sets need not be open: $f(x)=x^2$ sends the open set $(-1,1)$ onto $[0,1)$, and a constant function sends $\mathbb{R}$ to a point.

**Remark.** This characterisation does not mention distances at all: it only uses which sets are open. That is why continuity makes sense in an arbitrary topological space. If $f$ is only defined on a subset $A\subset\mathbb{R}$, the correct statement is that $f^{-1}(U)$ is *open in $A$*, i.e. of the form $A\cap V$ with $V$ open in $\mathbb{R}$.

@@@ rt-ct-02-zero-sets-and-sublevel-sets.md
---
title: Zero sets and level sets of continuous functions
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: l2
difficulty: 1
order: 2
tags: closed sets, open sets, continuous functions, compact sets
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Let $f,g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous.

1. Show that $\{f=0\}$ and $\{f\le g\}$ are closed, and that $\{f>0\}$ and $\{f<g\}$ are open.
2. Show that $A=\{x:x^3-3x+1>0\}$ is open and that $S=\{x:x^2+\sin x\le3\}$ is compact and non-empty.
3. Show that the set of fixed points of a continuous $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is closed. Is it always non-empty?

## Hint

Write each set as a preimage of an open or closed set under a continuous function (such as $f-g$). For $S$, first bound $|x|$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Every set defined by a strict inequality between continuous quantities is open, every set defined by a non-strict inequality or an equality is closed. This follows from the preimage characterisation of continuity.

**1.** The function $h=f-g$ is continuous. Then
- $\{f=0\}=f^{-1}(\{0\})$ is closed, because $\{0\}$ is closed;
- $\{f\le g\}=h^{-1}((-\infty,0])$ is closed;
- $\{f>0\}=f^{-1}((0,\infty))$ is open;
- $\{f<g\}=h^{-1}((-\infty,0))$ is open.

**2. The set $A$.** $A=p^{-1}((0,\infty))$ with $p(x)=x^3-3x+1$ continuous (a polynomial). So $A$ is open. (It is not a finite union of intervals you must compute: openness is automatic.)

**The set $S$.** Let $q(x)=x^2+\sin x$, continuous. Then $S=q^{-1}((-\infty,3])$ is closed. It is bounded: if $x\in S$ then $x^2\le3-\sin x\le4$, so $|x|\le2$. A closed bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is compact (Heine–Borel). It is non-empty since $q(0)=0\le3$.

**3. Fixed points.** The set $\{f(x)=x\}=\{f=g\}$ with $g(x)=x$ is closed by part 1. It can be empty: $f(x)=x+1$ has no fixed point. It is non-empty if $f$ maps a bounded closed interval $[a,b]$ into itself (the intermediate value theorem applied to $f(x)-x$); this is the content of a separate problem.

**Common mistake.** Arbitrary intersections of open sets need not be open: $\bigcap_n(-1/n,1/n)=\{0\}$. This is why equalities such as $\{f=0\}=\bigcap_n\{|f|<1/n\}$ give a closed set, not an open one.

**Remark.** The compactness of $S$ is useful in practice: a continuous function on $S$ attains its maximum and minimum, even though $S$ was only described by an inequality.

@@@ rt-ct-03-what-continuous-maps-preserve.md
---
title: What continuous maps do and do not preserve
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 3
tags: continuous images, counterexamples, compact, connected, open, closed
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Decide whether each statement is true or false for continuous functions $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$. Prove the true ones and give a counterexample to the false ones.

1. The image of an open set is open.
2. The image of a closed set is closed.
3. The image of a bounded set is bounded.
4. The image of a compact set is compact.
5. The image of an interval is an interval.
6. The preimage of a compact set is compact.
7. The preimage of a bounded set is bounded.

## Hint

For the false ones, think of $x^2$, $e^x$ and $\sin$.

For the true ones, use sequences (for compactness) and the intermediate value theorem (for intervals).

## Solution

**Idea.** Continuity controls **preimages of open and closed sets** and the images of **compact** and **connected** sets. Everything else typically fails.

**1. False.** $f(x)=x^2$ maps the open set $(-1,1)$ onto $[0,1)$, which is not open. Even simpler: a constant function maps $\mathbb{R}$ to a single point.

**2. False.** $f(x)=e^x$ maps the closed set $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$, not closed. Another example: $f(x)=\frac1{1+x^2}$ maps the closed set $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,1]$.

**3. True.** Let $A$ be bounded, say $A\subset[-M,M]$. The interval $[-M,M]$ is compact, so $f([-M,M])$ is compact by the argument of part 4 below, hence bounded, and $f(A)\subset f([-M,M])$ is bounded. (This uses that $f$ is defined and continuous on all of $\mathbb{R}$: $\tan$ on $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ or $\frac1x$ on $(0,1)$ have unbounded images of bounded sets, but they are not defined and continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.)

**4. True.** Let $K$ be compact and $(y_n)$ a sequence in $f(K)$, $y_n=f(x_n)$ with $x_n\in K$. By compactness a subsequence $x_{n_k}\to x\in K$. By continuity, $y_{n_k}=f(x_{n_k})\to f(x)\in f(K)$. So every sequence in $f(K)$ has a subsequence converging in $f(K)$: $f(K)$ is compact. (In $\mathbb{R}$: compact means closed and bounded.)

**5. True.** Let $I$ be an interval, $f(a)<c<f(b)$ with $a,b\in I$. The intermediate value theorem applied on the segment between $a$ and $b$ (contained in $I$) gives a point $x$ with $f(x)=c$. So $f(I)$ contains every value between two of its values, which characterises intervals.

**6. False.** $f=\sin$ and $K=\{0\}$: $f^{-1}(K)=\pi\mathbb{Z}$ is closed but unbounded, so not compact.

**7. False.** Same example: $f^{-1}(\{0\})=\pi\mathbb{Z}$, or $f^{-1}([-1,1])=\mathbb{R}$.

**When does it work?** If $|f(x)|\to\infty$ as $|x|\to\infty$ (for example $f(x)=x^2$), then preimages of bounded sets are bounded, preimages of compact sets are compact and images of closed sets are closed.

**Remark.** The slogan: *continuous images preserve compactness and connectedness, continuous preimages preserve closedness and openness.* Mixing these up is the most frequent error in this chapter.

@@@ rt-ct-04-closed-graph.md
---
title: Continuous functions have a closed graph (and conversely?)
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 4
tags: closed graph, continuity, boundedness, compactness
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

For $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ let $\Gamma_f=\{(x,f(x)):x\in\mathbb{R}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ be its graph.

1. Show that if $f$ is continuous then $\Gamma_f$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^2$.
2. Show that the converse is false: $f(x)=1/x$ for $x\ne0$, $f(0)=0$ has a closed graph but is not continuous.
3. Show that if $\Gamma_f$ is closed and $f$ is bounded on bounded sets, then $f$ is continuous.

## Hint

Part 1: take a convergent sequence of points of the graph.

Part 3: take $x_n\to x$ and a subsequence of $f(x_n)$ that converges.

## Solution

**Idea.** The graph being closed is a "sequential" statement: whenever $(x_n,f(x_n))\to(x,y)$, we must have $y=f(x)$. This is almost continuity, except that it does not exclude $f(x_n)\to\infty$.

**1.** Let $(x_n,f(x_n))\to(x,y)$. Then $x_n\to x$, so $f(x_n)\to f(x)$ by continuity, and $f(x_n)\to y$ by assumption. By uniqueness of limits $y=f(x)$, so $(x,y)\in\Gamma_f$.

**2.** The function $f$ is not continuous at $0$ ($f(1/n)=n\to\infty\ne f(0)$). Let $(x_n,f(x_n))\to(x,y)$ with $y\in\mathbb{R}$.
- If $x\ne0$, then $x_n\ne0$ for large $n$ and $f(x_n)=1/x_n\to1/x$, so $y=1/x=f(x)$.
- If $x=0$: if $x_n\ne0$ for infinitely many $n$, then along those $n$ we have $|f(x_n)|=1/|x_n|\to\infty$, contradicting convergence to $y\in\mathbb{R}$. So $x_n=0$ for all large $n$, and $y=\lim f(x_n)=f(0)=0$.

In all cases $(x,y)\in\Gamma_f$: the graph is closed.

**3.** Let $x_n\to x$. The sequence $(x_n)$ is bounded, hence so is $(f(x_n))$. Suppose $f(x_n)\not\to f(x)$. Then there are $\varepsilon>0$ and a subsequence with $|f(x_{n_k})-f(x)|\ge\varepsilon$. By Bolzano–Weierstrass, a further subsequence satisfies $f(x_{n_{k_j}})\to y$, with $|y-f(x)|\ge\varepsilon$. Then $(x_{n_{k_j}},f(x_{n_{k_j}}))\to(x,y)$, and closedness of $\Gamma_f$ gives $y=f(x)$: contradiction.

**Common mistake.** Do not believe that "closed graph $\Leftrightarrow$ continuous". The missing ingredient is boundedness: the graph of $1/x$ escapes to infinity near $0$ without leaving the closed set.

**Remark.** The closed graph theorem of functional analysis states that the converse holds for *linear* maps between Banach spaces, with no boundedness assumption: the linear structure supplies the missing control.

@@@ rt-ct-05-determined-by-a-dense-set.md
---
title: A continuous function is determined by its values on a dense set
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 5
tags: density, rational numbers, Cauchy functional equation, continuity
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

1. Let $f,g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous and $D\subset\mathbb{R}$ dense with $f=g$ on $D$. Show that $f=g$.
2. Find all **continuous** $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ for all $x,y$.
3. Find all continuous $f$ with $f\!\left(\frac{x+y}2\right)=\frac{f(x)+f(y)}2$.

## Hint

Part 1: approximate any $x$ by points of $D$. Part 2: first prove $f(q)=qf(1)$ for $q\in\mathbb{Q}$.

## Solution

**Idea.** If two continuous functions agree on a dense set, the density lets us reach every point as a limit of points where they agree, and continuity passes the equality to the limit.

**1.** Let $x\in\mathbb{R}$. Since $D$ is dense there is a sequence $d_n\in D$ with $d_n\to x$. By continuity, $f(x)=\lim f(d_n)=\lim g(d_n)=g(x)$.

**2. Rational values.** Put $c=f(1)$.
- $f(0)=f(0+0)=2f(0)$ gives $f(0)=0$.
- By induction $f(nx)=nf(x)$ for $n\in\mathbb{N}$, so $f(n)=nc$.
- $f(-x)=-f(x)$ because $f(x)+f(-x)=f(0)=0$; hence $f(n)=nc$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}$.
- For $q=m/n$ with $n\ge1$: $nf(m/n)=f(m)=mc$, so $f(m/n)=cm/n$.

So $f$ and $x\mapsto cx$ are continuous and agree on the dense set $\mathbb{Q}$. By part 1, $f(x)=cx$ for all $x$. Conversely every $x\mapsto cx$ works.

**3. Midpoint equation.** Replace $f$ by $h(x)=f(x)-f(0)$, which satisfies the same equation with $h(0)=0$. Taking $y=0$: $h(x/2)=h(x)/2$. Then
$$h(x+y)=2h\!\left(\tfrac{x+y}2\right)=h(x)+h(y),$$
so $h$ is continuous and additive, hence $h(x)=cx$ by part 2. Therefore $f(x)=cx+d$: exactly the affine functions.

**Remark.** Continuity is essential in part 2. Using a Hamel basis of $\mathbb{R}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ (and the axiom of choice) one constructs additive functions that are not linear; their graphs are dense in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Even a mild regularity assumption (continuity at one point, monotonicity, boundedness on an interval, measurability) is enough to force linearity.

@@@ rt-ct-06-the-real-line-and-the-interval.md
---
title: The real line is homeomorphic to an open interval
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 6
tags: homeomorphism, open intervals, explicit bijections
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

A **homeomorphism** is a continuous bijection whose inverse is continuous.

1. Show that $f(x)=\dfrac12+\dfrac{x}{2(1+|x|)}$ is a homeomorphism from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,1)$ and find its inverse.
2. Deduce that any two open intervals (bounded or not) are homeomorphic.
3. Is $f^{-1}$ uniformly continuous? Is $f$?

## Hint

Solve $y=\frac12+\frac{x}{2(1+|x|)}$ for $x$: set $t=2y-1$, so $t=\frac{x}{1+|x|}$ lies in $(-1,1)$.

## Solution

**Idea.** The function $x\mapsto\frac x{1+|x|}$ squeezes the whole line into $(-1,1)$ while remaining strictly increasing and continuous. An affine map then moves $(-1,1)$ to $(0,1)$.

**1. $f$ is a bijection onto $(0,1)$.** Let $\varphi(x)=\frac{x}{1+|x|}$. It is continuous, odd, and
$$\varphi(x)=\frac{x}{1+x}=1-\frac1{1+x}\ \text{ for }x\ge0,$$
which is strictly increasing from $0$ to $1^-$; by oddness it is strictly increasing from $-1^+$ to $0$ on $x\le0$. So $\varphi$ is a strictly increasing continuous bijection $\mathbb{R}\to(-1,1)$ (the intermediate value theorem gives surjectivity). Its inverse is
$$\varphi^{-1}(t)=\frac{t}{1-|t|}\qquad(|t|<1).$$
Check: for $t\ge0$, $x=\frac t{1-t}$ gives $\frac{x}{1+x}=\frac{t/(1-t)}{1/(1-t)}=t$.

**The inverse of $f$.** Since $f=\frac12(1+\varphi)$, we get $f^{-1}(y)=\varphi^{-1}(2y-1)=\dfrac{2y-1}{1-|2y-1|}$ for $y\in(0,1)$. It is continuous on $(0,1)$ because $|2y-1|<1$ there. So $f$ is a homeomorphism.

**2. Other intervals.**
- $(a,b)\cong(0,1)$ by the affine map $x\mapsto\frac{x-a}{b-a}$.
- $(a,\infty)\cong(0,\infty)\cong\mathbb{R}$ via $x\mapsto\ln(x-a)$.
- $(-\infty,b)\cong(0,\infty)$ via $x\mapsto b-x$.

Compositions and inverses of homeomorphisms are homeomorphisms, so all open intervals are homeomorphic.

**3. Uniform continuity.** $f$ is uniformly continuous: it is $\frac12$-Lipschitz, because $\varphi'(x)=\frac1{(1+|x|)^2}\in(0,1]$. But $f^{-1}$ is not: $f^{-1}(y)\to+\infty$ as $y\to1^-$, so it is unbounded on a bounded interval, which a uniformly continuous function on $(0,1)$ cannot be.

**Remark.** Being homeomorphic is a topological property: it forgets distances, boundedness and completeness. $\mathbb{R}$ is complete and unbounded, $(0,1)$ is incomplete and bounded, yet they are topologically the same. The next problem shows what *is* topological: compactness.

@@@ rt-ct-07-compactness-distinguishes-intervals.md
---
title: Compactness distinguishes [0,1] from (0,1) and from the real line
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 7
tags: homeomorphism, compactness, topological invariant
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Prove that $[0,1]$ is not homeomorphic to $(0,1)$, and not homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}$. Can there be a continuous **bijection** from $[0,1]$ onto $(0,1)$?

## Hint

Continuous images of compact sets are compact. Is $(0,1)$ compact? Find a sequence in $(0,1)$ with no subsequence converging in $(0,1)$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Compactness is a *topological invariant*: if $h:X\to Y$ is a homeomorphism, then $X$ compact implies $Y=h(X)$ compact, and conversely. So it suffices to find a compact and a non-compact space.

**Step 1: $[0,1]$ is compact.** It is closed and bounded (Heine–Borel); equivalently every sequence in $[0,1]$ has a subsequence converging in $[0,1]$ (Bolzano–Weierstrass).

**Step 2: $(0,1)$ is not compact.** The sequence $x_n=1/(n+1)\in(0,1)$ converges to $0$, so every subsequence converges to $0\notin(0,1)$. No subsequence converges in $(0,1)$.

**Step 3: $\mathbb{R}$ is not compact.** The sequence $x_n=n$ has no convergent subsequence (it is unbounded).

**Step 4: conclusion.** If $h:[0,1]\to(0,1)$ (or $\to\mathbb{R}$) were a continuous map onto, the image $h([0,1])$ would be compact (continuous image of a compact set). But $(0,1)$ and $\mathbb{R}$ are not compact. So there is not even a continuous **surjection** from $[0,1]$ onto $(0,1)$ or onto $\mathbb{R}$, let alone a homeomorphism.

**Answer to the last question.** No continuous bijection $[0,1]\to(0,1)$ exists, for the reason above.

**Remark.** The converse direction is different: there are continuous surjections from non-compact intervals onto $[0,1]$ (for instance $x\mapsto\sin^2x$ from $\mathbb{R}$), and even continuous bijections from a non-compact set onto $[0,1]$ (see the problem on continuous bijections that are not homeomorphisms). The invariant is "compactness", not "boundedness": $\mathbb{R}\cong(0,1)$ although one is bounded and the other is not.

@@@ rt-ct-08-removing-a-point.md
---
title: Telling intervals apart by removing a point
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 8
tags: homeomorphism, connectedness, cut points, intervals
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Show that $(0,1)$, $[0,1)$ and $[0,1]$ are pairwise non-homeomorphic. Show also that $[0,1)$ and $(0,1]$ are homeomorphic.

## Hint

Compactness separates $[0,1]$ from the others. To separate $(0,1)$ from $[0,1)$, remove one point and ask whether what remains is connected. Recall: a subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is connected iff it is an interval.

## Solution

**Idea.** A homeomorphism $h:X\to Y$ restricts to a homeomorphism $X\setminus\{p\}\to Y\setminus\{h(p)\}$. So a property such as "removing the point $p$ leaves a connected set" is preserved.

**Step 1: $[0,1]$ versus the others.** $[0,1]$ is compact, $(0,1)$ and $[0,1)$ are not ($x_n=1-\frac1{n+1}\to1\notin[0,1)$, and $\frac1{n+1}\to0\notin(0,1)$). Compactness is a topological invariant, so $[0,1]$ is homeomorphic to neither.

**Step 2: $(0,1)$ versus $[0,1)$.** Suppose $h:[0,1)\to(0,1)$ is a homeomorphism. Let $q=h(0)$. Then $h$ restricts to a homeomorphism
$$[0,1)\setminus\{0\}=(0,1)\ \longrightarrow\ (0,1)\setminus\{q\}=(0,q)\cup(q,1).$$
The left side is an interval, hence connected, so its continuous image $(0,q)\cup(q,1)$ would be connected. But a connected subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is an interval and $(0,q)\cup(q,1)$ is not (it misses the point $q$ between two of its points). Contradiction.

**Step 3: $[0,1)\cong(0,1]$.** The map $x\mapsto1-x$ is a homeomorphism (it is its own inverse and continuous).

**Why connectedness of $(0,q)\cup(q,1)$ fails, concretely.** Choose $a\in(0,q)$, $b\in(q,1)$. The intermediate value theorem applied to the identity function would produce a point $q$ in the set: it is not there.

**Remark.** This "cut point" technique shows that the interval $(0,1)$ is not homeomorphic to a circle (removing one point from a circle leaves a connected set, removing a point from an interval does not), and more generally that $\mathbb{R}$ is not homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^2$ (removing a point disconnects the line but not the plane).

@@@ rt-ct-09-open-maps-on-the-line.md
---
title: Continuous open maps of the line are strictly monotone
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: m1
difficulty: 4
order: 9
tags: open maps, monotonicity, injectivity, intermediate value theorem
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

A map $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is **open** if it sends open sets to open sets.

1. Show that $x^3$ is open and $x^2$ is not.
2. Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous and open. Prove that $f$ is injective.
3. Prove that a continuous injective function on an interval is strictly monotone. Conclude that a continuous open $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a homeomorphism onto the open interval $f(\mathbb{R})$.

## Hint

Part 2: if $f(a)=f(b)$ with $a<b$, look at an extremum of $f$ on $[a,b]$.

Part 3: for $x<y$ and $a<b$, study $\varphi(t)=f\big(ty+(1-t)b\big)-f\big(tx+(1-t)a\big)$ on $[0,1]$.

## Solution

**Idea.** An open map cannot have a local extremum: near a local maximum value $M=f(c)$ the image of a small interval lies below $M$ and contains $M$, so it is not open. This forces strict monotonicity.

**1.** $x^3$ is a continuous strictly increasing bijection with continuous inverse, so it maps open intervals to open intervals, hence open sets (unions of intervals) to open sets. $x^2$ maps $(-1,1)$ to $[0,1)$, not open.

**2. Injectivity.** Suppose $f(a)=f(b)$ with $a<b$. By the extreme value theorem, $f$ attains a maximum $M$ and a minimum $m$ on $[a,b]$.
- If $M=m$, then $f$ is constant on $[a,b]$ and $f((a,b))$ is a single point, which is not open: contradiction.
- Otherwise one of $M,m$ differs from $f(a)=f(b)$, say $M>f(a)$ (the other case is symmetric). Then $M=f(c)$ for some $c\in(a,b)$, and $f((a,b))\subset(-\infty,M]$ contains $M$. A set contained in $(-\infty,M]$ and containing $M$ is not open (no interval around $M$ fits). Contradiction.

So $f$ is injective.

**3. Injective continuous $\Rightarrow$ strictly monotone.** Let $f$ be continuous and injective on an interval $I$, and fix $a<b$ in $I$; say $f(a)<f(b)$ (otherwise replace $f$ by $-f$). Take any $x<y$ in $I$ and define on $[0,1]$
$$\varphi(t)=f\big(ty+(1-t)b\big)-f\big(tx+(1-t)a\big).$$
Since $x<y$ and $a<b$, we have $tx+(1-t)a<ty+(1-t)b$ for every $t\in[0,1]$, so the two arguments are distinct and $\varphi(t)\ne0$ by injectivity. As $\varphi$ is continuous and never zero, it has constant sign (IVT). Since $\varphi(0)=f(b)-f(a)>0$, we get $\varphi(1)=f(y)-f(x)>0$. So $f$ is strictly increasing.

**Conclusion.** A continuous open map $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is injective (part 2), hence strictly monotone (part 3), so $f(\mathbb{R})$ is an open interval (an interval, and open because $f$ is open) and $f$ is a continuous bijection onto it whose inverse is continuous (monotone with interval image: the inverse has no jump).

**Common mistake.** Continuous and injective are not enough to be open on a *non-interval* domain, and continuity alone is not enough on an interval: $x^2$ is continuous but not open.

**Remark.** On $\mathbb{R}$ "open and continuous" is a very strong condition. In higher dimensions the situation is richer: the map $(x,y)\mapsto x$ from $\mathbb{R}^2$ to $\mathbb{R}$ is continuous, open, and very far from injective.

@@@ rt-ct-10-cauchy-sequences-and-uniform-continuity.md
---
title: Uniformly continuous maps and Cauchy sequences
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: l2
difficulty: 4
order: 10
tags: uniform continuity, Cauchy sequences, extension to the closure
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

1. Prove that a uniformly continuous function sends Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences.
2. Let $f:(0,1)\to\mathbb{R}$ send every Cauchy sequence to a Cauchy sequence. Prove that $f$ is uniformly continuous.
3. Deduce: a continuous $f:(0,1)\to\mathbb{R}$ is uniformly continuous iff $\lim_{x\to0^+}f(x)$ and $\lim_{x\to1^-}f(x)$ exist in $\mathbb{R}$.
4. Show that the converse of part 1 fails on $\mathbb{R}$.

## Hint

Part 2: if $f$ is not uniformly continuous, build two sequences $x_n,y_n$ with $|x_n-y_n|\to0$ but $|f(x_n)-f(y_n)|\ge\varepsilon$, then **interleave** them.

## Solution

**Idea.** Uniform continuity is exactly the property of mapping "sequences that come together" to sequences that come together. On a bounded domain every sequence has convergent subsequences, which lets us run the argument both ways.

**1.** Let $(x_n)$ be Cauchy, $\varepsilon>0$, and $\delta>0$ from uniform continuity. There is $N$ with $|x_n-x_m|<\delta$ for $n,m\ge N$, hence $|f(x_n)-f(x_m)|<\varepsilon$: $(f(x_n))$ is Cauchy.

**2.** Suppose $f$ is not uniformly continuous. Then there is $\varepsilon>0$ such that for every $n$ there exist $x_n,y_n\in(0,1)$ with $|x_n-y_n|<1/n$ and $|f(x_n)-f(y_n)|\ge\varepsilon$. The sequence $(x_n)$ is bounded, so a subsequence $x_{n_k}\to\ell\in[0,1]$, and then $y_{n_k}\to\ell$ too since $|x_{n_k}-y_{n_k}|<1/n_k$. The interleaved sequence
$$x_{n_1},y_{n_1},x_{n_2},y_{n_2},\ldots$$
converges to $\ell$ (it has the two sub-sequences converging to the same limit), hence is Cauchy as a sequence of real numbers (note: Cauchy-ness is a property of the sequence, not of the ambient space, so this sequence is Cauchy even if $\ell\in\{0,1\}\notin(0,1)$). Its image has consecutive differences $|f(x_{n_k})-f(y_{n_k})|\ge\varepsilon$, so it is not Cauchy. Contradiction.

**3.** ($\Leftarrow$) If both limits exist, $f$ extends to a continuous function on the compact $[0,1]$, which is uniformly continuous (Heine), hence so is its restriction. ($\Rightarrow$) Let $x_n\to0^+$. Then $(x_n)$ is Cauchy, so $(f(x_n))$ is Cauchy by part 1, hence converges in $\mathbb{R}$. Two sequences $x_n,x_n'\to0$ give limits of $f(x_n)$ and $f(x_n')$ that coincide (interleave them: the image of the interleaved sequence is Cauchy, so converges, so both subsequential limits agree). So $\lim_{x\to0^+}f(x)$ exists; the same at $1$.

**4. The converse fails on $\mathbb{R}$.** $f(x)=x^2$ is continuous, so it sends every Cauchy (= convergent) sequence to a convergent hence Cauchy sequence, but it is not uniformly continuous: $x_n=n$, $y_n=n+\frac1n$ give $|x_n-y_n|\to0$ and $|f(y_n)-f(x_n)|=2+\frac1{n^2}\ge2$.

**Common mistake.** On $\mathbb{R}$, Cauchy sequences converge, so *every continuous function* sends Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences. The criterion of part 2 is only informative on **incomplete** domains such as $(0,1)$. On unbounded domains the proof breaks because $(x_n)$ need not have a convergent subsequence.

**Remark.** The criterion generalises: a function on a totally bounded metric space $X$ is uniformly continuous iff it preserves Cauchy sequences, and then it extends to a continuous function on the completion of $X$. This is how real numbers, and many function spaces, are constructed as completions.

@@@ rt-ct-11-testing-uniform-continuity.md
---
title: Testing uniform continuity on examples
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 11
tags: uniform continuity, sequences criterion, counterexamples
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Decide whether each function is uniformly continuous on the given set, with proof.

1. $\sin x$ on $\mathbb{R}$.
2. $x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$, and on $[0,10]$.
3. $\sqrt x$ on $[0,\infty)$.
4. $\sin(x^2)$ on $\mathbb{R}$.
5. $x\sin x$ on $\mathbb{R}$.
6. $\dfrac1x$ on $(0,1)$ and on $[1,\infty)$.

## Hint

Sequence criterion: $f$ is **not** uniformly continuous iff there are $x_n,y_n$ with $|x_n-y_n|\to0$ but $|f(x_n)-f(y_n)|\not\to0$.

For $\sqrt x$ use $|\sqrt x-\sqrt y|\le\sqrt{|x-y|}$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Uniform continuity fails when the function becomes steeper and steeper somewhere (unbounded derivative at a finite point, or growing oscillations), and holds when the function is Lipschitz or Hölder or periodic-like.

**1. Yes.** $|\sin x-\sin y|\le|x-y|$ (mean value theorem, $|\cos|\le1$). Take $\delta=\varepsilon$.

**2. $x^2$.** Not on $\mathbb{R}$: $x_n=n$, $y_n=n+\frac1n$ give $|x_n-y_n|=\frac1n\to0$, $|y_n^2-x_n^2|=2+\frac1{n^2}\ge2$. Yes on $[0,10]$: $|x^2-y^2|=|x+y||x-y|\le20|x-y|$.

**3. Yes.** For $x\ge y\ge0$, $\sqrt x\le\sqrt y+\sqrt{x-y}$ (square both sides: $x\le y+(x-y)+2\sqrt{y(x-y)}$). So $|\sqrt x-\sqrt y|\le\sqrt{|x-y|}$ and $\delta=\varepsilon^2$ works.

**4. No.** Take $x_n=\sqrt{2\pi n}$ and $y_n=\sqrt{2\pi n+\pi/2}$. Then $\sin(x_n^2)=0$, $\sin(y_n^2)=1$, while
$$y_n-x_n=\frac{\pi/2}{x_n+y_n}\longrightarrow0.$$

**5. No.** Take $x_n=2\pi n$ and $y_n=2\pi n+\frac1n$. Then $x_n\sin x_n=0$ and $y_n\sin y_n=(2\pi n+\tfrac1n)\sin\tfrac1n\to2\pi$ (because $n\sin\frac1n\to1$), while $|x_n-y_n|=\frac1n\to0$.

**6. $\frac1x$.** Not on $(0,1)$: $x_n=\frac1n$, $y_n=\frac1{2n}$ gives $|x_n-y_n|=\frac1{2n}\to0$ but $|\frac1{x_n}-\frac1{y_n}|=n\to\infty$. Yes on $[1,\infty)$: $\left|\frac1x-\frac1y\right|=\frac{|x-y|}{xy}\le|x-y|$.

**Common mistake.** "Bounded derivative" is sufficient but not necessary: $\sqrt x$ has an unbounded derivative near $0$ yet is uniformly continuous. And "bounded function" does not help: $\sin(x^2)$ is bounded and not uniformly continuous.

**Remark.** A continuous function on a **compact** set is always uniformly continuous (Heine). All counterexamples above live on non-compact sets, where the function can "escape" to a bad region (infinity or an excluded endpoint).

@@@ rt-ct-12-lipschitz-functions.md
---
title: Lipschitz functions
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 12
tags: Lipschitz, uniform continuity, mean value theorem, Hölder
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

A function $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ is **$L$-Lipschitz** if $|f(x)-f(y)|\le L|x-y|$ for all $x,y\in A$.

1. Show that a Lipschitz function is uniformly continuous.
2. Show that a differentiable $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ with $|f'|\le L$ is $L$-Lipschitz.
3. Show that $\sqrt x$ is uniformly continuous on $[0,1]$ but not Lipschitz there. Is it Lipschitz on $[\delta,\infty)$ for $\delta>0$?
4. Show that $x\mapsto\operatorname{dist}(x,A)=\inf_{a\in A}|x-a|$ is $1$-Lipschitz for any non-empty $A\subset\mathbb{R}$.

## Hint

Part 4: for $a\in A$, $|x-a|\le|x-y|+|y-a|$; take the infimum over $a$.

## Solution

**Idea.** A Lipschitz function has *slopes of chords* bounded by $L$: it can never become steeper than $L$. This is the cleanest quantitative form of continuity.

**1.** Given $\varepsilon>0$ take $\delta=\varepsilon/L$ (if $L=0$ the function is constant). Then $|x-y|<\delta\Rightarrow|f(x)-f(y)|\le L|x-y|<\varepsilon$.

**2.** For $x<y$ the mean value theorem gives $c\in(x,y)$ with $f(y)-f(x)=f'(c)(y-x)$, hence $|f(y)-f(x)|\le L|y-x|$.

**3. $\sqrt x$.** On $[0,1]$, $|\sqrt x-\sqrt y|\le\sqrt{|x-y|}$, so it is uniformly continuous (also because $[0,1]$ is compact). It is not Lipschitz: with $y=0$,
$$\frac{|\sqrt x-\sqrt0|}{|x-0|}=\frac1{\sqrt x}\xrightarrow[x\to0^+]{}\infty.$$
On $[\delta,\infty)$ the derivative is $\frac1{2\sqrt x}\le\frac1{2\sqrt\delta}$, so $\sqrt x$ is $\frac1{2\sqrt\delta}$-Lipschitz there, by part 2.

**4.** Fix $x,y$ and $a\in A$. Then $\operatorname{dist}(x,A)\le|x-a|\le|x-y|+|y-a|$. Taking the infimum over $a\in A$: $\operatorname{dist}(x,A)\le|x-y|+\operatorname{dist}(y,A)$. Exchanging $x$ and $y$ gives $|\operatorname{dist}(x,A)-\operatorname{dist}(y,A)|\le|x-y|$.

**Common mistake.** A differentiable function with *unbounded* derivative can be uniformly continuous ($\sqrt x$ on $[0,1]$, whose derivative blows up at $0$ but which is $\frac12$-Hölder). Conversely, Lipschitz functions need not be differentiable: $|x|$ is $1$-Lipschitz.

**Remark.** The Hölder condition $|f(x)-f(y)|\le C|x-y|^\alpha$ with $0<\alpha\le1$ interpolates between "uniformly continuous" and "Lipschitz": $\sqrt x$ is Hölder with $\alpha=\frac12$ and not better.

@@@ rt-ct-13-banach-fixed-point-on-the-line.md
---
title: Contractions and the fixed point theorem on the line
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 13
tags: Banach fixed point theorem, contraction, completeness, iteration
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Let $F\subset\mathbb{R}$ be a non-empty closed set and $f:F\to F$ a **contraction**: $|f(x)-f(y)|\le k|x-y|$ for some $k<1$.

1. Prove that $f$ has a unique fixed point $x^*$, and that for any $x_0\in F$ the iterates $x_{n+1}=f(x_n)$ satisfy $|x_n-x^*|\le\dfrac{k^n}{1-k}|x_1-x_0|$.
2. Apply it to $f=\cos$ on $[0,1]$.
3. Show that the hypotheses cannot be weakened: (a) $F=(0,1]$ and $f(x)=x/2$; (b) $|f(x)-f(y)|<|x-y|$ for $x\ne y$ without a constant $k<1$, with $f(x)=x+\frac1{1+e^x}$ on $\mathbb{R}$.

## Hint

Show $(x_n)$ is Cauchy by comparing consecutive distances to a geometric series. Use that $F$ is closed to stay in $F$ when passing to the limit.

## Solution

**Idea.** Each application of $f$ shrinks all distances by the factor $k$. The orbit is therefore a Cauchy sequence, it converges because $\mathbb{R}$ is complete, and its limit is fixed by continuity.

**1. Convergence.** We have $|x_{n+1}-x_n|\le k|x_n-x_{n-1}|\le\dots\le k^n|x_1-x_0|$. For $m>n$,
$$|x_m-x_n|\le\sum_{j=n}^{m-1}k^j|x_1-x_0|\le\frac{k^n}{1-k}|x_1-x_0|\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0,$$
so $(x_n)$ is Cauchy and converges to some $x^*\in\mathbb{R}$. Since $x_n\in F$ and $F$ is closed, $x^*\in F$.

**Fixed point.** $f$ is continuous (Lipschitz), so $f(x^*)=\lim f(x_n)=\lim x_{n+1}=x^*$.

**Uniqueness.** If $f(x)=x$ and $f(y)=y$, then $|x-y|=|f(x)-f(y)|\le k|x-y|$ forces $|x-y|=0$.

**Error estimate.** Let $m\to\infty$ in the bound above.

**2. $\cos$ on $[0,1]$.** $\cos$ maps $[0,1]$ into $[\cos1,1]\subset[0,1]$ and $|\cos'|=|\sin|\le\sin1<1$ on $[0,1]$, so it is a contraction with $k=\sin1\approx0.84$. Hence $\cos x=x$ has a unique solution in $[0,1]$. Starting from $x_0=0.5$ the iterates converge to $x^*\approx0.7390851$ (after $60$ steps the error is below $10^{-10}$).

**3(a). Closedness is needed.** $f(x)=x/2$ maps $(0,1]$ into itself and is a contraction with $k=\frac12$, but its only fixed point in $\mathbb{R}$ is $0\notin(0,1]$. The limit of the orbit escapes from the set.

**3(b). A constant $k<1$ is needed.** $f(x)=x+\frac1{1+e^x}$ has $f'(x)=1-\frac{e^x}{(1+e^x)^2}\in\left[\frac34,1\right)$, so by the mean value theorem $|f(x)-f(y)|<|x-y|$ for $x\ne y$. But $f(x)=x$ would need $\frac1{1+e^x}=0$, impossible: no fixed point. Here $f'(x)\to1$ as $x\to\pm\infty$, so no uniform constant $k<1$ exists.

**Remark.** The theorem is valid in any complete metric space. It is the source of the existence and uniqueness theorem for ODEs (Picard–Lindelöf) and of the implicit function theorem. The error estimate says the convergence is at least geometric with ratio $k$, which makes the iteration practical.

@@@ rt-ct-14-fixed-points-of-continuous-self-maps.md
---
title: Fixed points of continuous maps of [0,1] and the necessity of the hypotheses
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 14
tags: fixed point, intermediate value theorem, counterexamples, horizontal chord
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

1. Show that every continuous $f:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ has a fixed point.
2. Show that continuity, the closedness of the interval, and its connectedness are all necessary, by giving counterexamples.
3. Let $g:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous with $g(0)=g(1)$. Show that there is $x\in[0,\frac12]$ with $g(x)=g\!\left(x+\frac12\right)$.

## Hint

Part 1: look at $h(x)=f(x)-x$ at the endpoints.

Part 3: apply the IVT to $h(x)=g(x+\frac12)-g(x)$ on $[0,\frac12]$ and compare $h(0)$ with $h(\frac12)$.

## Solution

**Idea.** A fixed point is a zero of $h(x)=f(x)-x$. The hypotheses $f(0)\ge0$ and $f(1)\le1$ say that $h$ is non-negative at the left end and non-positive at the right end: the IVT then does the job.

**1.** $h(0)=f(0)\ge0$ and $h(1)=f(1)-1\le0$. If either vanishes we are done; otherwise $h(0)>0>h(1)$ and the IVT gives $c\in(0,1)$ with $h(c)=0$, i.e. $f(c)=c$.

**2. Counterexamples.**
- *Continuity needed:* the step function $f(x)=\frac34$ for $x\le\frac12$ and $f(x)=\frac14$ for $x>\frac12$ maps $[0,1]$ into $[0,1]$ but is not continuous. A fixed point would need $x=\frac34>\frac12$ (impossible, since then $f(x)=\frac14$) or $x=\frac14\le\frac12$ (impossible, since then $f(x)=\frac34$). So $f$ has no fixed point.
- *Closedness needed:* $f(x)=x^2$ maps $(0,1)$ into itself, and $x^2=x$ only for $x\in\{0,1\}$.
- *Connectedness needed:* on $[0,\frac13]\cup[\frac23,1]$ the map $f(x)=x+\frac23$ on $[0,\frac13]$, $f(x)=x-\frac23$ on $[\frac23,1]$ is continuous and swaps the two pieces: no fixed point.
- *Boundedness needed:* $f(x)=x+1$ on $\mathbb{R}$.

**3. Horizontal chord.** Define $h(x)=g(x+\frac12)-g(x)$ on $[0,\frac12]$. Then
$$h(0)=g(\tfrac12)-g(0),\qquad h(\tfrac12)=g(1)-g(\tfrac12)=g(0)-g(\tfrac12)=-h(0).$$
So $h(0)$ and $h(\frac12)$ have opposite signs (or are both zero), and the IVT gives $x\in[0,\frac12]$ with $h(x)=0$.

**Consequence.** Over a closed course of length $1$ with continuous altitude $g$ returning to its starting value, there are two points at distance exactly $\frac12$ with the same altitude.

**Remark.** The same proof gives chords of length $\frac1n$ for every integer $n$ (use $h(x)=g(x+\frac1n)-g(x)$ and the sum $\sum_{k}h(\frac kn)=0$). It fails for lengths such as $\frac25$: there are continuous $g$ with $g(0)=g(1)$ and no horizontal chord of length $\frac25$ (the horizontal chord theorem of Paul Lévy).

@@@ rt-ct-15-semicontinuous-functions.md
---
title: Lower and upper semicontinuous functions
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: m1
difficulty: 4
order: 15
tags: semicontinuity, open sets, extreme value theorem, supremum
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

A function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is **lower semicontinuous (lsc)** at $x_0$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ with $f(x)>f(x_0)-\varepsilon$ for $|x-x_0|<\delta$. It is **upper semicontinuous (usc)** if $-f$ is lsc.

1. Prove: $f$ is lsc everywhere iff $\{f>a\}$ is open for every $a\in\mathbb{R}$.
2. Show that $f$ is continuous iff it is both lsc and usc.
3. Show that $\mathbf 1_U$ is lsc for $U$ open, and $\mathbf 1_C$ is usc for $C$ closed. Is $\lfloor x\rfloor$ lsc or usc?
4. Show that a supremum of any family of lsc functions (when finite) is lsc.
5. Show that an lsc function on a compact $K$ attains its minimum.

## Hint

Part 1: use $a=f(x_0)-\varepsilon$.

Part 5: take a minimising sequence, extract a convergent subsequence, and use lower semicontinuity at the limit.

## Solution

**Idea.** Lower semicontinuity allows the function to jump *up* at a point but not *down*: the value at the point is never larger than nearby values (up to $\varepsilon$). It is exactly the regularity needed for minimisation problems.

**1.** ($\Rightarrow$) Let $f(x_0)>a$ and $\varepsilon=f(x_0)-a>0$. For $|x-x_0|<\delta$, $f(x)>f(x_0)-\varepsilon=a$. So $\{f>a\}$ contains a neighbourhood of each of its points: it is open. ($\Leftarrow$) Given $x_0$, $\varepsilon$, the set $\{f>f(x_0)-\varepsilon\}$ is open and contains $x_0$, hence contains $(x_0-\delta,x_0+\delta)$.

**2.** Lsc plus usc at $x_0$ give $f(x_0)-\varepsilon<f(x)<f(x_0)+\varepsilon$ near $x_0$, which is continuity; the converse is immediate.

**3.** $\{\mathbf 1_U>a\}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ for $a<0$, $U$ for $0\le a<1$, $\emptyset$ for $a\ge1$: all open. So $\mathbf 1_U$ is lsc. For $C$ closed, $\mathbf 1_C=1-\mathbf 1_{\mathbb{R}\setminus C}$ is usc. The function $\lfloor x\rfloor$ is **usc** (it is right-continuous and jumps down to the left of each integer, so $f(x)<f(n)+\varepsilon$ nearby) but not lsc; $\lceil x\rceil$ is lsc.

**4.** If $f=\sup_if_i$ then $\{f>a\}=\bigcup_i\{f_i>a\}$, a union of open sets.

**5. Minimum.** Let $m=\inf_Kf\in[-\infty,\infty)$ and $x_n\in K$ with $f(x_n)\to m$. By compactness a subsequence $x_{n_k}\to x\in K$. Let $\varepsilon>0$. By lower semicontinuity at $x$, $f(x_{n_k})>f(x)-\varepsilon$ for large $k$, so $m=\lim f(x_{n_k})\ge f(x)-\varepsilon$. As $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, $m\ge f(x)$; in particular $m>-\infty$, and $m\le f(x)$ by definition of the infimum. So $f(x)=m$.

**Common mistake.** Do not confuse the direction: lsc functions attain **minima** on compact sets, usc functions attain **maxima**. An lsc function need not attain a maximum, and need not even be bounded above: $f(x)=\frac1x$ for $x>0$, $f(x)=0$ for $x\le0$ is lsc (it is continuous except at $0$, where $f(x)\ge0=f(0)$ near $0$) and is unbounded above on $[0,1]$.

**Remark.** The pointwise sup of continuous functions is lsc and, conversely, every lsc function is a sup of continuous functions (Baire). Lower semicontinuity is the natural hypothesis in the direct method of the calculus of variations.

@@@ rt-ct-16-discontinuities-of-monotone-functions.md
---
title: A monotone function has countably many discontinuities
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: l3
difficulty: 4
order: 16
tags: monotone functions, jump discontinuities, countability, rational numbers
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

1. Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be non-decreasing. Show that $f$ has one-sided limits at every point and that the set of discontinuity points of $f$ is at most countable.
2. Show that the countable set of discontinuities can be dense: construct a non-decreasing $f$ discontinuous exactly at the rational numbers.

## Hint

Part 1: at each discontinuity there is a non-empty interval $(f(x^-),f(x^+))$. Show these intervals are disjoint for distinct $x$ and each contains a rational.

Part 2: let $(q_n)$ enumerate $\mathbb{Q}$ and put $f(x)=\sum_{n:\,q_n\le x}2^{-n}$.

## Solution

**Idea.** A jump uses up a piece of the *range* of $f$. Disjoint pieces of $\mathbb{R}$ can be counted by choosing a rational in each.

**1. One-sided limits.** For $x\in\mathbb{R}$, the set $\{f(t):t<x\}$ is bounded above by $f(x)$, so $f(x^-)=\sup_{t<x}f(t)=\lim_{t\to x^-}f(t)$ exists, and $f(x^-)\le f(x)$. Similarly $f(x^+)=\inf_{t>x}f(t)\ge f(x)$. Hence
$$f(x^-)\le f(x)\le f(x^+).$$
$f$ is continuous at $x$ iff $f(x^-)=f(x^+)$.

**Discontinuities.** Let $D=\{x:f(x^-)<f(x^+)\}$ be the set of discontinuities. For $x\in D$, pick a rational $r_x\in(f(x^-),f(x^+))$. If $x<y$ are both in $D$, then for any $t$ with $x<t<y$ we have $f(x^+)\le f(t)\le f(y^-)$, so the intervals $(f(x^-),f(x^+))$ and $(f(y^-),f(y^+))$ are disjoint. Hence $x\mapsto r_x$ is injective $D\to\mathbb{Q}$, and $D$ is countable.

**2. A dense set of jumps.** Let $(q_n)_{n\ge1}$ enumerate $\mathbb{Q}$ and
$$f(x)=\sum_{n:\,q_n\le x}2^{-n}\in[0,1].$$
It is non-decreasing, because enlarging $x$ adds terms.

*Discontinuous at $q_m$.* For $x<q_m\le y$, $f(y)-f(x)\ge2^{-m}$ since the term $n=m$ is counted in $f(y)$ but not in $f(x)$. So $f(q_m^+)-f(q_m^-)\ge2^{-m}>0$.

*Continuous at irrational $x_0$.* Let $\varepsilon>0$ and choose $N$ with $2^{-N}<\varepsilon$. The finitely many $q_1,\dots,q_N$ are different from $x_0$, so there is $\delta>0$ with $(x_0-\delta,x_0+\delta)$ containing none of them. For $x_0-\delta<s<t<x_0+\delta$, the terms of index $n\le N$ cancel in $f(t)-f(s)$, and
$$0\le f(t)-f(s)\le\sum_{n>N}2^{-n}=2^{-N}<\varepsilon.$$
So $f$ is continuous at $x_0$.

**Remark.** This function is strictly increasing (every interval contains a rational, hence a jump), yet continuous at every irrational number. The set of discontinuities of a monotone function is countable but may be dense, and so cannot be understood just by looking at graphs.

@@@ rt-ct-17-the-set-of-continuity-points-is-a-g-delta.md
---
title: The set of continuity points is a G_delta
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: m1
difficulty: 4
order: 17
tags: oscillation, G-delta, open sets, continuity points
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

For $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}$, define the **oscillation** of $f$ at $x$:
$$\omega_f(x)=\inf_{\delta>0}\ \operatorname{diam}f\big((x-\delta,x+\delta)\big),\qquad\operatorname{diam}(S)=\sup_{s,t\in S}|s-t|\in[0,\infty].$$

1. Show that $f$ is continuous at $x$ iff $\omega_f(x)=0$.
2. Show that $\{x:\omega_f(x)<\varepsilon\}$ is open for each $\varepsilon>0$.
3. Deduce that the set $C_f$ of continuity points of $f$ is a $G_\delta$ (a countable intersection of open sets), and that the set of discontinuity points is an $F_\sigma$ (a countable union of closed sets).

## Hint

Part 2: if some interval $I$ around $x$ has $\operatorname{diam}f(I)<\varepsilon$, then every point $z\in I$ has a small interval around it inside $I$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Oscillation measures *how much $f$ fails to be continuous at $x$*: it is the size of the smallest window through which $f$ can be viewed near $x$. Being less than $\varepsilon$ is an "open" condition, because a good window at $x$ is also a good window for neighbouring points.

**1.** ($\Rightarrow$) Let $f$ be continuous at $x$ and $\varepsilon>0$. There is $\delta$ with $|f(y)-f(x)|<\varepsilon/2$ on $(x-\delta,x+\delta)$, so the diameter of the image is at most $\varepsilon$. Hence $\omega_f(x)\le\varepsilon$ for all $\varepsilon$, i.e. $\omega_f(x)=0$. ($\Leftarrow$) If $\omega_f(x)=0$, given $\varepsilon$ there is $\delta$ with $\operatorname{diam}f((x-\delta,x+\delta))<\varepsilon$, hence $|f(y)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ for $|y-x|<\delta$.

**2.** Suppose $\omega_f(x)<\varepsilon$. Then there is $\delta>0$ with $\operatorname{diam}f(I)<\varepsilon$ where $I=(x-\delta,x+\delta)$. Let $z\in I$. The interval $I$ is open, so there is $\eta>0$ with $(z-\eta,z+\eta)\subset I$, and then
$$\omega_f(z)\le\operatorname{diam}f\big((z-\eta,z+\eta)\big)\le\operatorname{diam}f(I)<\varepsilon.$$
So $I\subset\{\omega_f<\varepsilon\}$: the set is open.

**3.** By parts 1 and 2,
$$C_f=\{\omega_f=0\}=\bigcap_{n\ge1}\{\omega_f<1/n\}$$
is a countable intersection of open sets: a $G_\delta$. Its complement, the set of discontinuities, equals $\bigcup_n\{\omega_f\ge1/n\}$, a countable union of closed sets: an $F_\sigma$.

**Consequences.** (i) The set of discontinuities of a function is always an $F_\sigma$: for example, $\mathbb{Q}$ is an $F_\sigma$ (a countable union of points), so it can be the set of discontinuities of a function (see the next problem). (ii) A function can be continuous exactly on the irrationals. (iii) With Baire's theorem one shows that **no** function is continuous exactly on $\mathbb{Q}$, because $\mathbb{Q}$ is not a $G_\delta$.

**Remark.** Statement (iii) is a typical application of the Baire category theorem: if $\mathbb{Q}$ were a countable intersection of open sets, each of them would be dense and open, and so would $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{q\}$ for each rational $q$; the countable intersection of all these dense open sets would be empty, contradicting Baire.

@@@ rt-ct-18-computing-oscillations.md
---
title: Computing oscillations: the sign function, sin(1/x), the indicator of Q and Thomae
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: l3
difficulty: 3
order: 18
tags: oscillation, Thomae function, discontinuities, rational numbers
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Using the oscillation $\omega_f(x)=\inf_{\delta>0}\operatorname{diam}f((x-\delta,x+\delta))$, compute $\omega_f$ for:
1. $f(x)=\operatorname{sign}(x)$ (with $f(0)=0$).
2. $f(x)=\sin(1/x)$ for $x\ne0$, $f(0)=0$.
3. $f=\mathbf 1_{\mathbb{Q}}$.
4. **Thomae's function**: $f(0)=1$, $f(p/q)=1/q$ for $p/q$ in lowest terms ($q\ge1$), and $f(x)=0$ for $x$ irrational. Deduce that $f$ is continuous exactly at the irrational numbers.

## Hint

For each point, find the smallest interval containing all values taken near that point.

For Thomae, near $p/q$ every other rational has a denominator larger than any given bound, once the window is small.

## Solution

**Idea.** The oscillation is the "size of the jump" (or of the wiggling) at a point, measured as the spread of nearby values.

**1. Sign.** For $x\ne0$, $f$ is locally constant, so $\omega_f(x)=0$. At $0$, every window $(-\delta,\delta)$ contains the values $-1,0,1$, so the diameter is $2$ and $\omega_f(0)=2$.

**2. $\sin(1/x)$.** Away from $0$ the function is continuous, so $\omega_f=0$. At $0$, every window contains points where $\sin(1/x)=1$ (namely $x=\frac1{\pi/2+2k\pi}$ for large $k$) and where it equals $-1$, so the diameter is $2$: $\omega_f(0)=2$. The value $f(0)$ is irrelevant to the oscillation: no choice of $f(0)$ makes $f$ continuous.

**3. $\mathbf 1_{\mathbb{Q}}$.** Every window contains both rationals and irrationals, hence values $0$ and $1$: $\omega_f(x)=1$ for **every** $x$. So $f$ is continuous nowhere.

**4. Thomae.** *At an irrational $x_0$.* Let $\varepsilon>0$. Only finitely many rationals in $(x_0-1,x_0+1)$ have denominator $\le N=\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil$ (for each $q\le N$ there are at most $2q+1$ fractions $p/q$ there). So there is a window around $x_0$ avoiding all of them, and in the window $0\le f<\varepsilon$ (irrationals give $0$, rationals give $1/q\le\frac1{N+1}<\varepsilon$). Hence $\omega_f(x_0)\le\varepsilon$ for all $\varepsilon$: $\omega_f(x_0)=0$, i.e. $f$ is continuous at $x_0$.

*At a rational $p/q$.* The same finiteness argument shows that in a small enough window around $p/q$ every rational other than $p/q$ has denominator $>q$, so all values lie in $[0,1/q]$, and the window contains $f(p/q)=1/q$ and irrationals (value $0$). The diameter is exactly $1/q$, so $\omega_f(p/q)=1/q>0$. (For $x=0$ the value is $1$ and the same argument gives $\omega_f(0)=1$.)

**Conclusion.** $\omega_f(x)=0$ iff $x$ is irrational: Thomae's function is continuous exactly on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, and has a removable discontinuity at each rational (the limit is $0$).

**Remark.** The sets $\{\omega_f\ge1/n\}$ for Thomae's function are $\{p/q:q\le n\}$: closed and discrete, in accordance with the previous problem (the discontinuity set is an $F_\sigma$).

@@@ rt-ct-19-extending-a-continuous-function-from-a-closed-set.md
---
title: Extending a continuous function from a closed set (Tietze in dimension one)
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: m1
difficulty: 5
order: 19
tags: extension, closed sets, Tietze, open sets as unions of intervals
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Let $F\subset\mathbb{R}$ be non-empty and closed and $f:F\to\mathbb{R}$ continuous. Prove that $f$ extends to a continuous function $\tilde f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$. Show also that one may take $\inf f\le\tilde f\le\sup f$ whenever $f$ is bounded.

## Hint

The open set $\mathbb{R}\setminus F$ is a disjoint union of open intervals ("gaps"). Interpolate linearly on gaps with two endpoints in $F$, and use a constant on unbounded gaps.

## Solution

**Idea.** Fill each hole of $F$ by the simplest continuous function that matches the values at the two ends of the hole. The only delicate point is continuity at points of $F$ that are limits of infinitely many holes.

**Step 1: structure of the complement.** $U=\mathbb{R}\setminus F$ is open; it is the disjoint union of its connected components, which are open intervals $(a,b)$ with $-\infty\le a<b\le\infty$ whose finite endpoints belong to $F$ (an endpoint in $U$ would belong to a larger component).

**Step 2: definition.** Put $\tilde f=f$ on $F$ and on each component $(a,b)$ of $U$:
- if $a,b$ finite: $\tilde f(x)=f(a)+\dfrac{x-a}{b-a}\big(f(b)-f(a)\big)$ (linear interpolation);
- if $a=-\infty$, $b$ finite: $\tilde f(x)=f(b)$;
- if $b=+\infty$, $a$ finite: $\tilde f(x)=f(a)$;
- if $(a,b)=\mathbb{R}$ (that is $F=\emptyset$): excluded by assumption.

On every gap, $\tilde f$ is continuous (affine or constant), and its values lie between the values at the endpoints, hence between $\inf f$ and $\sup f$.

**Step 3: continuity at points of the interior of $U$.** Immediate, since $U$ is open and $\tilde f$ is continuous on each component.

**Step 4: continuity at $x_0\in F$.** Let $x_n\to x_0$. It suffices to show $\tilde f(x_n)\to f(x_0)$. We split $(x_n)$ into the terms in $F$ and those in $U$; by continuity of $f$ on $F$ the first group is fine. Consider the terms $x_n\in U$, lying in components $(a_n,b_n)$.

- *Infinitely many $x_n$ in the same component $(a,b)$.* Then $x_0\in[a,b]\cap F$. Since $x_0\notin(a,b)$ (it is in $F$), $x_0\in\{a,b\}$, say $x_0=a$; along this subsequence $\tilde f(x_n)\to\tilde f(a)=f(x_0)$ by continuity of the affine (or constant) extension on $[a,b)$.
- *Different components.* Since $x_0\in F$ is not in $(a_n,b_n)\ni x_n$, either $x_0\le a_n<x_n$ or $x_n<b_n\le x_0$. In the first case $|a_n-x_0|\le|x_n-x_0|$ so $a_n\to x_0$; in the second, $b_n\to x_0$. For the other endpoint: the components are pairwise disjoint open intervals all meeting the bounded set $[x_0-1,x_0+1]$ (for $n$ large), so they are contained in that bounded interval and are pairwise disjoint; consequently their total length is at most $2$. In particular the sum $\sum_n(b_n-a_n)$ over a subfamily of pairwise disjoint intervals is bounded, hence converges in $\mathbb{R}$, and therefore its terms tend to $0$: $b_n-a_n\to0$. So *both* endpoints tend to $x_0$ (for unbounded components the endpoint is the single finite one and the value is a constant $f(a_n)$ or $f(b_n)$). Then $\tilde f(x_n)$, a convex combination of $f(a_n)$ and $f(b_n)$, tends to $f(x_0)$, because $f$ is continuous on $F$ and $a_n,b_n\in F$ tend to $x_0$.

Hence $\tilde f$ is continuous at every $x_0\in F$.

**Common mistake.** Linear interpolation on each gap is not enough if one forgets the gaps that accumulate at a point of $F$ (for instance the Cantor set, with its gaps of lengths $\frac13,\frac19,\frac19,\dots$): continuity there uses that the lengths of the gaps tend to $0$, which follows from the finiteness of the total length of a family of pairwise disjoint intervals. Also, on an unbounded gap one cannot interpolate; the constant extension is needed.

**Remark.** Tietze's extension theorem states the same for every closed subset of a normal topological space. Its proof is much longer since gaps are no longer available. In dimension one, applied to the Cantor set $K$ and $f=$ the Cantor function, the extension described here is the usual picture of the Devil's staircase (constant on each gap).

@@@ rt-ct-20-periodic-continuous-functions.md
---
title: Continuous periodic functions are bounded and uniformly continuous
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 20
tags: periodic functions, uniform continuity, compactness, almost periodic
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous and $T$-periodic ($T>0$).

1. Show that $f$ is bounded and attains its maximum and minimum.
2. Show that $f$ is uniformly continuous.
3. Show that $g(x)=\sin x+\sin(\sqrt2x)$ is bounded and uniformly continuous but not periodic.

## Hint

Reduce everything to the compact interval $[0,2T]$ by translating by multiples of $T$.

For part 3: if $p$ were a period, expand $g(x+p)-g(x)$ and use that $\sin x,\cos x,\sin\sqrt2x,\cos\sqrt2x$ are linearly independent.

## Solution

**Idea.** A periodic function sees the same values over and over, so all its properties are decided on one period, which is compact.

**1.** On $[0,T]$ the continuous function $f$ attains its maximum $M$ and minimum $m$. Any $x\in\mathbb{R}$ can be written $x=x_0+kT$ with $x_0\in[0,T)$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, and $f(x)=f(x_0)\in[m,M]$. So $M$ and $m$ are global extrema.

**2.** By Heine's theorem $f$ is uniformly continuous on the compact $[0,2T]$: given $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta_0>0$ with $|f(s)-f(t)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $s,t\in[0,2T]$, $|s-t|<\delta_0$. Let $\delta=\min(\delta_0,T)$ and take any $x<y$ with $y-x<\delta$. Translate by a multiple of $T$ so that $x'=x-kT\in[0,T)$; then $y'=y-kT<x'+T<2T$, so both lie in $[0,2T]$ and $|y'-x'|<\delta_0$. Hence $|f(y)-f(x)|=|f(y')-f(x')|<\varepsilon$.

**3. Boundedness and uniform continuity of $g$.** $|g|\le2$ and $|g'(x)|=|\cos x+\sqrt2\cos\sqrt2x|\le1+\sqrt2$, so $g$ is $(1+\sqrt2)$-Lipschitz, hence uniformly continuous.

**$g$ is not periodic.** Suppose $g(x+p)=g(x)$ for all $x$ with $p>0$. Expanding with the addition formulas,
$$0\equiv(\cos p-1)\sin x+\sin p\cos x+(\cos\sqrt2p-1)\sin\sqrt2x+\sin\sqrt2p\cos\sqrt2x.$$
*Linear independence.* Suppose $A\sin x+B\cos x+C\sin\omega x+D\cos\omega x\equiv0$ with $\omega=\sqrt2$. Differentiating twice gives $-A\sin x-B\cos x-\omega^2(C\sin\omega x+D\cos\omega x)\equiv0$. Adding the first relation: $(1-\omega^2)(C\sin\omega x+D\cos\omega x)\equiv0$ hence $C\sin\omega x+D\cos\omega x\equiv0$; at $x=0$ this gives $D=0$, and then at $x=\pi/(2\omega)$ it gives $C=0$. Then $A\sin x+B\cos x\equiv0$ gives $A=B=0$ similarly.

So $\cos p=1$ and $\cos\sqrt2p=1$: $p=2\pi m$ and $\sqrt2p=2\pi n$ with $m,n$ positive integers, hence $\sqrt2=n/m\in\mathbb{Q}$: contradiction.

**Remark.** $g$ is a sum of two periodic functions with incommensurable periods: a typical **almost periodic** function. It shares with periodic functions the properties of part 1 (bounded) and part 2, but not periodicity. In fact $g$ comes arbitrarily close to its supremum $2$ without attaining it.

@@@ rt-ct-21-every-closed-set-is-a-zero-set.md
---
title: Every closed set is the zero set of a continuous function
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 21
tags: closed sets, distance function, Urysohn lemma, zero sets
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

1. Let $F\subset\mathbb{R}$ be closed and non-empty. Show that $d_F(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,F)$ is continuous and $\{d_F=0\}=F$. Deduce that every closed set is the zero set of a continuous function, and every open set is of the form $\{g>0\}$ with $g$ continuous.
2. Let $A,B$ be disjoint non-empty closed sets. Construct a continuous $h:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]$ with $h=0$ on $A$ and $h=1$ on $B$.
3. Is the statement of part 2 true for the disjoint sets $A=\{n:n\ge2\}$ and $B=\{n+\frac1n:n\ge2\}$ with a function that is **uniformly** continuous?

## Hint

Part 1: use that $d_F$ is $1$-Lipschitz. For $d_F(x)=0\Rightarrow x\in F$, use the definition of infimum and the closedness of $F$.

Part 2: try $h=\dfrac{d_A}{d_A+d_B}$.

## Solution

**Idea.** The distance to a closed set is a continuous function that vanishes exactly on that set: this translates "closed" into "zero set" and, with a quotient, separates disjoint closed sets.

**1. Continuity.** $d_F$ is $1$-Lipschitz (shown in the problem on Lipschitz functions), hence continuous.

**Zero set.** If $x\in F$ then $d_F(x)=0$. Conversely, if $d_F(x)=0$ there are $a_n\in F$ with $|x-a_n|\to0$, so $a_n\to x$, and $x\in F$ because $F$ is closed.

**Consequences.** $F=d_F^{-1}(\{0\})$. For an open set $U\ne\mathbb{R}$, $U\ne\emptyset$, the closed set $F=\mathbb{R}\setminus U$ gives $U=\{d_F>0\}$. (For $U=\emptyset$ take $g=0$ and for $U=\mathbb{R}$ take $g=1$; for $F=\emptyset$ use $f\equiv1$.)

**2.** Since $A,B$ are closed and disjoint, $d_A(x)+d_B(x)>0$ for every $x$: otherwise $d_A(x)=d_B(x)=0$, so $x\in A\cap B=\emptyset$. Thus
$$h(x)=\frac{d_A(x)}{d_A(x)+d_B(x)}$$
is continuous with values in $[0,1]$, $h=0$ exactly on $A$ and $h=1$ exactly on $B$.

**3. Uniform continuity can fail.** The sets $A=\{n:n\ge2\}$ and $B=\{n+\frac1n:n\ge2\}$ are closed and disjoint, yet $\operatorname{dist}(A,B)=0$ (take $n$ and $n+\frac1n$). If $h$ were uniformly continuous with $h=0$ on $A$ and $h=1$ on $B$, then $|h(n)-h(n+\frac1n)|=1$ for all $n$ would contradict $|n-(n+\frac1n)|\to0$. So no such uniformly continuous $h$ exists, although the continuous function of part 2 does.

**Common mistake.** Disjoint closed sets can be arbitrarily close (distance $0$); they are separated by a continuous function, not by a "gap". Only if one of them is **compact** is $\operatorname{dist}(A,B)>0$.

**Remark.** This is Urysohn's lemma in the case of $\mathbb{R}$. In a general metric space the same formula works verbatim; in general topological spaces one needs normality and a much more elaborate construction.

@@@ rt-ct-22-a-continuous-bijection-that-is-not-a-homeomorphism.md
---
title: A continuous bijection that is not a homeomorphism
category: topology/topology-of-r/r-continuity
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 22
tags: homeomorphism, continuous bijection, compactness, closed maps
date: 2026-11-12
---

## Statement

1. Let $D=[0,1)\cup[2,3]$ and $f:D\to[0,2]$, $f(x)=x$ on $[0,1)$, $f(x)=x-1$ on $[2,3]$. Show that $f$ is a continuous bijection whose inverse is not continuous.
2. Prove: a continuous bijection from a **compact** subset $K\subset\mathbb{R}$ onto a subset $Y\subset\mathbb{R}$ is a homeomorphism.
3. Prove: a continuous bijection from an **interval** onto an interval is a homeomorphism.

## Hint

Part 1: look at the inverse near the point $1$.

Part 2: show $f$ maps closed sets to closed sets, using compactness.

Part 3: a continuous injective function on an interval is strictly monotone.

## Solution

**Idea.** The inverse of a continuous bijection is continuous exactly when the map is *closed* (sends closed sets to closed sets). Compactness of the domain or the order structure of intervals guarantees this; a disconnected domain can break it.

**1.** $f$ is a bijection: $f([0,1))=[0,1)$ and $f([2,3])=[1,2]$, disjoint images covering $[0,2]$. It is continuous (on each piece it is a translation, and the two pieces are separated: a sequence in $D$ converging to a point of $D$ is eventually in the same piece).

*The inverse $g=f^{-1}:[0,2]\to D$ is discontinuous at $1$.* We have $g(1)=2$ since $f(2)=1$. But $g(1-\frac1n)=1-\frac1n\to1\ne2=g(1)$.
