---

## Statement

For $A\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ let $\sigma_1(A)\ge\dots\ge\sigma_n(A)\ge0$ be its singular values. Show that the map $\Sigma:A\mapsto(\sigma_1(A),\dots,\sigma_n(A))$ is continuous from $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ onto the closed cone $K=\{\sigma_1\ge\dots\ge\sigma_n\ge0\}$.

## Hint

Continuity is Weyl's inequality $|\sigma_k(A)-\sigma_k(B)|\le\|A-B\|$. For surjectivity use diagonal matrices.

## Solution

**Continuity.** By the Courant-Fischer min-max formula,
$$\sigma_k(A)=\max_{\dim V=k}\ \min_{x\in V,|x|=1}|Ax|.$$
If $|Ax|\le|Bx|+\|A-B\|$ for all unit $x$, then taking the $\min$ over $x\in V$ and the $\max$ over $V$ gives $\sigma_k(A)\le\sigma_k(B)+\|A-B\|$. Exchanging $A$ and $B$,
$$|\sigma_k(A)-\sigma_k(B)|\le\|A-B\|.$$
So each $\sigma_k$ is $1$-Lipschitz, hence $\Sigma$ is continuous.

**Image in $K$.** By definition $\sigma_1\ge\dots\ge\sigma_n\ge0$.

**Onto.** Given $(s_1\ge\dots\ge s_n\ge0)\in K$, the matrix $D=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\dots,s_n)$ has $D^TD=\operatorname{diag}(s_i^2)$, so its singular values are exactly $s_1,\dots,s_n$ in this order.

**Remark.** The fibres of $\Sigma$ are the orbits $\{U D V:U,V\in O(n)\}$ of the action of $O(n)\times O(n)$: two matrices have the same singular values iff they are orthogonally equivalent. So $K$ is the quotient $M_n(\mathbb{R})/(O(n)\times O(n))$.
@@@ mnspec-the-pseudo-inverse-is-discontinuous.md
---
title: The Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse is discontinuous
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: l2
difficulty: 2
tags: pseudo-inverse, discontinuity, rank, singular value decomposition
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

For $A=U\Sigma V^T$ (singular value decomposition) the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse is $A^+=V\Sigma^+U^T$, where $\Sigma^+$ inverts the nonzero diagonal entries and keeps the zeros. Show that $A\mapsto A^+$ is discontinuous at every matrix of rank $r<n$.

## Hint

Start with $A=0$ and $A_\varepsilon=\varepsilon e_1e_1^T$. For rank $r>0$, add a small multiple of a rank-one term built from singular vectors.

## Solution

**The case $A=0$.** $0^+=0$. Let $A_\varepsilon=\operatorname{diag}(\varepsilon,0,\dots,0)$ with $\varepsilon>0$. Then $A_\varepsilon\to0$ but $A_\varepsilon^+=\operatorname{diag}(1/\varepsilon,0,\dots,0)$ has norm $1/\varepsilon\to\infty$. So $A\mapsto A^+$ is not continuous at $0$ (it is not even bounded near $0$).

**General rank $r<n$.** Write $A=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_iu_iv_i^T$ with $\sigma_i>0$, where $(u_i)$ and $(v_i)$ are orthonormal families. Since $r<n$ we can complete the families and pick unit vectors $u_{r+1},v_{r+1}$ orthogonal to the previous ones. Put
$$A_\varepsilon=A+\varepsilon u_{r+1}v_{r+1}^T.$$
This is a singular value decomposition of $A_\varepsilon$ with $\sigma_{r+1}=\varepsilon>0$, so $\operatorname{rank}A_\varepsilon=r+1$ and
$$A_\varepsilon^+=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i^{-1}v_iu_i^T+\varepsilon^{-1}v_{r+1}u_{r+1}^T,\qquad\|A_\varepsilon^+\|=\max(\sigma_r^{-1},\varepsilon^{-1})\ \xrightarrow[\varepsilon\to0]{}\ \infty.$$
But $\|A_\varepsilon-A\|=\varepsilon\to0$ while $A^+$ is a fixed matrix. So $A^+$ is not the limit of $A_\varepsilon^+$.

**Remark.** The pseudo-inverse is continuous exactly on the set of matrices of *locally constant rank*, i.e. on each stratum $\{\operatorname{rank}=r\}$ and at the invertible matrices (where $A^+=A^{-1}$). This is why numerical rank decisions ("is this singular value zero?") are delicate.
@@@ mnspec-closest-matrix-of-rank-at-most-r-exists.md
---
title: Existence of a closest matrix of rank at most r
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: l2
difficulty: 2
tags: low rank approximation, compactness, coercivity
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $N$ be any norm on $M_n(\mathbb{R})$, $A\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ and $0\le r\le n$. Show that there exists $B_0$ with $\operatorname{rank}B_0\le r$ such that
$$N(A-B_0)=\min\{N(A-B):\operatorname{rank}B\le r\}.$$

## Hint

Show that $\mathcal{R}_r=\{\operatorname{rank}\le r\}$ is closed and restrict the minimisation to a compact subset.

## Solution

**Closedness of $\mathcal{R}_r$.** $\operatorname{rank}B\le r$ iff all minors of size $r+1$ vanish. Minors are polynomials in the entries, hence continuous, and $\mathcal{R}_r$ is an intersection of zero sets of continuous functions, so it is closed. (For $r=n$, $\mathcal{R}_r=M_n(\mathbb{R})$.)

**Reduction to a compact set.** $0\in\mathcal{R}_r$, so the minimum, if it exists, is at most $N(A)$. Consider
$$K=\mathcal{R}_r\cap\{B:N(B)\le2N(A)\}.$$
This is closed (closed $\cap$ closed ball) and bounded, so it is compact since $M_n(\mathbb{R})\cong\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$. If $B\in\mathcal{R}_r\setminus K$, then $N(B)>2N(A)$ and
$$N(A-B)\ge N(B)-N(A)>N(A)=N(A-0),$$
so such a $B$ is worse than $B=0\in K$.

**Existence.** $B\mapsto N(A-B)$ is continuous, so it attains its minimum on the nonempty compact set $K$, at some $B_0$. By the previous paragraph $B_0$ is a minimiser on all of $\mathcal{R}_r$.

**Remark.** Existence holds for every norm, but uniqueness may fail (for the operator norm there are many best rank-$r$ approximations when $\sigma_{r+1}=\sigma_{r+2}$ or even in general). For the Frobenius and operator norms the minimum is explicit: see the Eckart-Young problem. The statement is false for the *set of rank exactly $r$* matrices, which is not closed.
@@@ mnspec-the-numerical-range-of-a-real-matrix.md
---
title: The numerical range of a real matrix is an interval
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: l2
difficulty: 2
tags: Rayleigh quotient, connectedness, compactness, symmetric part
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ and $S=\frac{A+A^T}2$. Show that
$$\{x^TAx:\ x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ |x|=1\}=[\lambda_{\min}(S),\lambda_{\max}(S)].$$

## Hint

Show that $x^TAx=x^TSx$. Then use the Rayleigh principle for the endpoints, and connectedness of the unit sphere for the interior.

## Solution

**Step 1: only the symmetric part matters.** $x^TAx$ is a real number, so it equals its transpose $x^TA^Tx$. Hence $x^TAx=\frac12(x^TAx+x^TA^Tx)=x^TSx$.

**Step 2: the endpoints.** $S$ is symmetric; let $\lambda_1\le\dots\le\lambda_n$ be its eigenvalues with an orthonormal eigenbasis $v_1,\dots,v_n$. For a unit vector $x=\sum c_iv_i$ we have $\sum c_i^2=1$ and
$$x^TSx=\sum_i\lambda_ic_i^2\in[\lambda_1,\lambda_n],$$
with equality at $x=v_1$ and $x=v_n$. So $\min$ and $\max$ of $x^TSx$ on the sphere are $\lambda_{\min}$ and $\lambda_{\max}$.

**Step 3: no gaps.** The function $x\mapsto x^TSx$ is continuous. For $n\ge2$ the unit sphere $S^{n-1}$ is connected, so its image is a connected subset of $\mathbb{R}$, i.e. an interval, and it is compact. An interval containing $\lambda_{\min}$ and $\lambda_{\max}$ and contained in $[\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}]$ is the whole of $[\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}]$. (For $n=1$ the sphere is $\{\pm1\}$ and both sides equal $\{a\}$.)

**Explicit path.** For a direct proof, $x(t)=\cos t\,v_1+\sin t\,v_n$ gives $x(t)^TSx(t)=\lambda_1\cos^2t+\lambda_n\sin^2t$, which sweeps $[\lambda_1,\lambda_n]$ as $t\in[0,\pi/2]$.

**Remark.** For complex matrices the numerical range is a convex set in $\mathbb{C}$ (Toeplitz-Hausdorff theorem), not an interval. The real quadratic form only sees $S$, which is why a skew-symmetric $A$ has numerical range $\{0\}$.
@@@ mnspec-singular-matrices-are-a-null-set.md
---
title: Singular matrices have measure zero
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: l2
difficulty: 2
tags: Lebesgue measure, zero set of a polynomial, Fubini, determinant
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Show that $\{A\in M_n(\mathbb{R}):\det A=0\}$ has Lebesgue measure zero in $M_n(\mathbb{R})\cong\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$. Equivalently, $GL_n(\mathbb{R})$ has full measure.

## Hint

Prove first that the zero set of any nonzero polynomial in $k$ variables is Lebesgue-null, by induction on $k$ and Fubini's theorem. Then note that $\det$ is a nonzero polynomial.

## Solution

**Lemma.** If $p\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\dots,x_k]$ is not the zero polynomial, then $Z(p)=\{p=0\}$ has measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^k$.

*Proof by induction on $k$.* For $k=1$, a nonzero polynomial has finitely many roots. Let $k\ge2$ and write
$$p(x_1,\dots,x_k)=\sum_{j=0}^dq_j(x_1,\dots,x_{k-1})\,x_k^j,$$
with $q_d\not\equiv0$. By induction, $N=\{q_d=0\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{k-1}$ is null. For $x'=(x_1,\dots,x_{k-1})\notin N$, the polynomial $x_k\mapsto p(x',x_k)$ is nonzero, so its zero set in $\mathbb{R}$ is finite, hence null. By Fubini-Tonelli,
$$\lambda_k(Z(p))=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k-1}}\lambda_1\big(\{x_k:p(x',x_k)=0\}\big)\,dx'=0,$$
because the integrand vanishes for $x'\notin N$ and $N$ is null. $\square$

**Application.** $\det A$ is a polynomial of degree $n$ in the $n^2$ entries, and it is not the zero polynomial since $\det I=1$. By the lemma $\{\det=0\}$ is null.

**Remark.** The same proof shows that $\{\det=0\}$ is also nowhere dense: it is closed with empty interior (a null set cannot contain a ball). So a "random" matrix is almost surely invertible, and generic statements about invertible matrices extend to all matrices by continuity, a technique used throughout this topic.
@@@ mnspec-eigenvalues-are-only-holder-continuous.md
---
title: Eigenvalues are only Hölder continuous
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: l3
difficulty: 3
tags: eigenvalues, Hölder continuity, Jordan block, perturbation
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $n\ge2$, $J=J_n(0)$ the nilpotent Jordan block (ones on the superdiagonal), $E_{n1}$ the matrix unit with a single $1$ in position $(n,1)$, and $\varepsilon>0$. Compute the eigenvalues of $J+\varepsilon E_{n1}$ and deduce that the eigenvalues are not Lipschitz functions of the matrix.

## Hint

Compute the characteristic polynomial by expanding $\det(tI-M)$.

## Solution

**The matrix.** $M_\varepsilon=J+\varepsilon E_{n1}$ has $(M_\varepsilon)_{i,i+1}=1$ for $i<n$ and $(M_\varepsilon)_{n,1}=\varepsilon$, all other entries $0$. Equivalently $M_\varepsilon e_1=\varepsilon e_n$ and $M_\varepsilon e_{j}=e_{j-1}$ for $j\ge2$.

**Characteristic polynomial.** Let $x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ be an eigenvector for $\mu$: $M_\varepsilon x=\mu x$ reads $x_{i+1}=\mu x_i$ for $i<n$ and $\varepsilon x_1=\mu x_n$. Hence $x_k=\mu^{k-1}x_1$, $x_1\ne0$, and $\varepsilon x_1=\mu\cdot\mu^{n-1}x_1$, so $\mu^n=\varepsilon$. The $n$ numbers $\mu_k=\varepsilon^{1/n}e^{2\pi ik/n}$ are distinct, so
$$\chi_{M_\varepsilon}(t)=t^n-\varepsilon.$$

**Conclusion.** All eigenvalues of $M_\varepsilon$ have modulus $\varepsilon^{1/n}$, while those of $M_0=J$ are $0$. The perturbation has operator norm $\|M_\varepsilon-M_0\|=\varepsilon$, so
$$\max_k|\mu_k-0|=\varepsilon^{1/n}=\|M_\varepsilon-M_0\|^{1/n}\gg\|M_\varepsilon-M_0\|\qquad(\varepsilon\to0,\ n\ge2).$$
No inequality $|\mu-\mu'|\le C\|M-M'\|$ can hold near $J$.

**Example.** $n=2$, $\varepsilon=10^{-8}$: $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\10^{-8}&0\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $\pm10^{-4}$, four orders of magnitude larger than the perturbation.

**Remark.** The exponent $1/n$ is optimal in general (Bauer-Fike type bounds for non-diagonalisable matrices give Hölder $1/n$). For normal matrices the dependence is Lipschitz with constant $1$, as shown in the Bauer-Fike problem below.
@@@ mnspec-power-sums-determine-the-characteristic-polynomial.md
---
title: Power sums determine the characteristic polynomial
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: l3
difficulty: 3
tags: Newton identities, power sums, characteristic polynomial, continuity
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Show that $A\mapsto(\operatorname{tr}A,\operatorname{tr}A^2,\dots,\operatorname{tr}A^n)$ is continuous on $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ and that it determines the characteristic polynomial $\chi_A$.

## Hint

If $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ are the complex eigenvalues of $A$, then $\operatorname{tr}A^k=p_k(\lambda)=\sum_i\lambda_i^k$. Use Newton's identities.

## Solution

**Continuity.** The entries of $A^k$ are polynomials in the entries of $A$, and the trace is linear. So each $\operatorname{tr}A^k$ is a polynomial function of $A$, hence continuous.

**Link with the spectrum.** Over $\mathbb{C}$, triangularise $A=PTP^{-1}$ with diagonal $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ (with algebraic multiplicities). Then $A^k=PT^kP^{-1}$ and $T^k$ is triangular with diagonal $\lambda_i^k$, so
$$\operatorname{tr}A^k=\sum_i\lambda_i^k=:p_k.$$

**Newton's identities.** Write $\chi_A(t)=\prod_i(t-\lambda_i)=t^n-e_1t^{n-1}+e_2t^{n-2}-\dots+(-1)^ne_n$ where $e_k$ are the elementary symmetric polynomials of the $\lambda_i$. Newton's identities state that for $1\le k\le n$
$$ke_k=\sum_{j=1}^k(-1)^{j-1}e_{k-j}\,p_j,\qquad e_0=1.$$
Solving successively gives $e_1=p_1$, $e_2=\frac{p_1^2-p_2}2$, $e_3=\frac{p_1^3-3p_1p_2+2p_3}6$, and so on: each $e_k$ is a polynomial in $p_1,\dots,p_k$ with rational coefficients (dividing by $k$ is allowed in characteristic $0$).

**Conclusion.** The coefficients of $\chi_A$ are polynomials in $\operatorname{tr}A,\dots,\operatorname{tr}A^n$. Hence two matrices with the same first $n$ power traces have the same characteristic polynomial.

**Check.** $n=2$: $\chi_A(t)=t^2-(\operatorname{tr}A)t+\frac{(\operatorname{tr}A)^2-\operatorname{tr}A^2}2$, and indeed $\det A=\frac{(\operatorname{tr}A)^2-\operatorname{tr}(A^2)}2$.

**Remark.** The division by $k$ is essential: over a field of characteristic $p\le n$ the power sums do not determine the characteristic polynomial.
@@@ mnspec-the-spectral-mapping-theorem-for-polynomials.md
---
title: The spectral mapping theorem for polynomials
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: l3
difficulty: 3
tags: spectrum, triangularisation, polynomial of a matrix
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ with complex spectrum $\operatorname{spec}A$, and let $p$ be a polynomial. Show that $\operatorname{spec}\big(p(A)\big)=p\big(\operatorname{spec}A\big)$ (and in fact the eigenvalues of $p(A)$ with multiplicities are the $p(\lambda_i)$).

## Hint

Work over $\mathbb{C}$ and triangularise $A$.

## Solution

**Triangularisation (Schur).** Over $\mathbb{C}$ there is an invertible $P$ with $A=PTP^{-1}$, $T$ upper triangular with diagonal entries $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$, the eigenvalues of $A$ repeated according to multiplicity.

**Powers.** $A^k=PT^kP^{-1}$ for all $k\ge0$. A product of upper triangular matrices is upper triangular, with diagonal entries equal to the products of the diagonal entries; so $T^k$ is upper triangular with diagonal $(\lambda_i^k)$.

**Polynomials.** If $p(x)=\sum_kc_kx^k$, then $p(A)=\sum c_kPT^kP^{-1}=P\,p(T)\,P^{-1}$, and $p(T)=\sum c_kT^k$ is upper triangular with diagonal entries $\sum c_k\lambda_i^k=p(\lambda_i)$.

**Conclusion.** The characteristic polynomial of $p(A)$ is that of $p(T)$, namely $\prod_i(t-p(\lambda_i))$. Therefore the spectrum of $p(A)$ is $\{p(\lambda_1),\dots,p(\lambda_n)\}=p(\operatorname{spec}A)$.

**Example.** If $A$ is nilpotent, $\operatorname{spec}A=\{0\}$, so $A^2+I$ has spectrum $\{1\}$ and is invertible. If $A^2=A$ (projection), $\operatorname{spec}A\subset\{0,1\}$ because $p(x)=x^2-x$ gives $p(\operatorname{spec}A)=\operatorname{spec}(0)=\{0\}$.

**Remark.** The real spectrum is not enough: $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has no real eigenvalue but $p(x)=x^2+1$ gives $p(A)=0$. The theorem must be applied over $\mathbb{C}$.
@@@ mnspec-when-do-the-powers-of-a-matrix-converge-to-zero.md
---
title: A^k converges to 0 if and only if the spectral radius is less than 1
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: l3
difficulty: 3
tags: spectral radius, Jordan form, powers of a matrix
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ and $\rho(A)=\max\{|\lambda|:\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}A\}$ its spectral radius. Prove that $A^k\to0$ as $k\to\infty$ if and only if $\rho(A)<1$.

## Hint

($\Leftarrow$) Use the Jordan form and the entries $\binom kj\lambda^{k-j}$ of $J_m(\lambda)^k$. ($\Rightarrow$) Apply $A^k$ to a complex eigenvector.

## Solution

**($\Rightarrow$).** Suppose $\rho(A)\ge1$ and take an eigenvalue $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|\lambda|\ge1$ and an eigenvector $v\in\mathbb{C}^n$, $v\ne0$. Then $A^kv=\lambda^kv$ and $|A^kv|=|\lambda|^k|v|\ge|v|>0$ for all $k$. Hence $A^kv\not\to0$, so $A^k\not\to0$. Contrapositive: $A^k\to0\Rightarrow\rho(A)<1$.

**($\Leftarrow$).** Assume $\rho(A)<1$. Write $A=PJP^{-1}$ in Jordan form over $\mathbb{C}$; then $A^k=PJ^kP^{-1}$, and it suffices to show $J^k\to0$, i.e. $J_m(\lambda)^k\to0$ for each block with $|\lambda|<1$. Write $J_m(\lambda)=\lambda I+N$ with $N^m=0$ and $\lambda I$ commuting with $N$. By the binomial theorem
$$J_m(\lambda)^k=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\binom kj\lambda^{k-j}N^j.$$
For fixed $j$, $\binom kj\le k^j$, so
$$\left|\binom kj\lambda^{k-j}\right|\le k^j|\lambda|^{k-j}\xrightarrow[k\to\infty]{}0,$$
because geometric decay beats polynomial growth ($|\lambda|<1$; if $\lambda=0$ the term vanishes for $k>j$). A finite sum of terms tending to $0$ tends to $0$.

**Example.** $A=\begin{pmatrix}0.9&1\\0&0.9\end{pmatrix}$: $A^k=\begin{pmatrix}0.9^k&k\,0.9^{k-1}\\0&0.9^k\end{pmatrix}$. The off-diagonal entry first grows (it is $\approx1.7\times10^{...}$, maximal near $k=9$) but eventually tends to $0$.

**Remark.** The transient growth is the reason why $\rho(A)<1$ does not imply $\|A\|<1$ for a given norm. A norm with $\|A\|<1$ exists iff $\rho(A)<1$ (see Gelfand's formula below).
@@@ mnspec-the-set-where-the-powers-converge.md
---
title: The set of matrices whose powers converge is neither open nor closed
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: l3
difficulty: 3
tags: powers, convergence, open sets, closed sets
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $\mathcal{C}=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb{R}):\lim_{k\to\infty}A^k\text{ exists}\}$. Show that $\mathcal{C}$ is neither open nor closed.

## Hint

Use the diagonal matrices $\operatorname{diag}(x,0,\dots,0)$ and the behaviour of $x^k$ at $x=1$ and $x=-1$.

## Solution

**The family.** Let $D(x)=\operatorname{diag}(x,0,\dots,0)$. Then $D(x)^k=\operatorname{diag}(x^k,0,\dots,0)$, and $x^k$ converges iff $x\in(-1,1]$ (to $0$ for $|x|<1$, to $1$ for $x=1$; for $x=-1$ it oscillates, for $|x|>1$ it diverges). Thus
$$D(x)\in\mathcal{C}\iff x\in(-1,1].$$

**Not open.** $D(1)\in\mathcal{C}$, but $D(1+\varepsilon)\notin\mathcal{C}$ for every $\varepsilon>0$ and $D(1+\varepsilon)\to D(1)$. So $D(1)$ is not an interior point.

**Not closed.** $D(-1+\tfrac1j)\in\mathcal{C}$ for all $j\ge2$, and $D(-1+\tfrac1j)\to D(-1)$, but $D(-1)\notin\mathcal{C}$ since $(-1)^k$ has no limit. So $\mathcal{C}$ does not contain its limit points.

**Remark.** The interior of $\mathcal{C}$ is $\{\rho(A)<1\}$ (where $A^k\to0$) and its closure is the set of power-bounded matrices... more precisely, $\mathcal{C}$ is contained in $\{\rho\le1\}$ and contains $\{\rho<1\}$: the interesting matrices are on the boundary $\rho=1$, where convergence is governed by the Jordan structure of eigenvalue $1$ (semisimple) and the absence of other eigenvalues on the unit circle.
@@@ mnspec-power-bounded-matrices-do-not-form-a-closed-set.md
---
title: Power-bounded matrices do not form a closed set
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: l3
difficulty: 3
tags: power bounded, Jordan block, closed sets
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

A matrix $A$ is *power bounded* if $\sup_{k\ge0}\|A^k\|<\infty$. Show that the set $\mathcal{P}$ of power-bounded matrices of $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ ($n\ge2$) is not closed.

## Hint

Take a limit of matrices with spectral radius less than $1$ which is a Jordan block of size $2$ at the eigenvalue $1$.

## Solution

**The sequence.** For $0<\varepsilon<1$ let
$$A_\varepsilon=\begin{pmatrix}1-\varepsilon&1\\0&1-\varepsilon\end{pmatrix}\oplus0_{n-2}.$$
Its eigenvalues are $1-\varepsilon$ (and $0$), so $\rho(A_\varepsilon)<1$ and $A_\varepsilon^k\to0$ by the previous results. A convergent sequence is bounded, so $A_\varepsilon^k$ is bounded in $k$: $A_\varepsilon\in\mathcal{P}$.

**The limit.** As $\varepsilon\to0$, $A_\varepsilon\to A_0=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\oplus0$. By induction $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}^k=\begin{pmatrix}1&k\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, whose norm is at least $k$. Hence $\sup_k\|A_0^k\|=\infty$: $A_0\notin\mathcal{P}$.

**Conclusion.** $A_\varepsilon\in\mathcal{P}$, $A_\varepsilon\to A_0\notin\mathcal{P}$, so $\mathcal{P}$ is not closed.

**Remark.** What is true: $\mathcal{P}$ is contained in $\{\rho\le1\}$ and contains $\{\rho<1\}$; and the set $\{A:\|A^k\|\le1\ \forall k\}$ for a given norm is closed. A matrix is power bounded iff $\rho\le1$ and the eigenvalues of modulus $1$ are semisimple (no nontrivial Jordan block). The growth of $\|A_\varepsilon^k\|$ before decay is of order $\frac1{e\varepsilon}$, which blows up as $\varepsilon\to0$: power-boundedness holds but not *uniformly*.
@@@ mnspec-rank-one-matrices.md
---
title: The cone of rank-one matrices
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: l3
difficulty: 3
tags: rank one, closed cone, connectedness, minors
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $\mathcal{R}_1=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb{R}):\operatorname{rank}A\le1\}$.

1. Show that $\mathcal{R}_1=\{xy^T:x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\}$ and that it is closed and stable under multiplication by scalars.
2. Show that $\{\operatorname{rank}A=1\}$ is connected when $n\ge2$.

## Hint

For part 1, a rank-one matrix has one-dimensional column space. For part 2, the set is the image of the connected set $(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\})^2$ under a continuous map.

## Solution

**1. Description.** If $A=xy^T$ then every column is a multiple of $x$, so $\operatorname{rank}A\le1$. Conversely if $\operatorname{rank}A=1$, pick a nonzero column space generator $x$; each column of $A$ is $y_jx$ for a scalar $y_j$, so $A=xy^T$ (and $A=0=0\cdot0^T$ if the rank is $0$).

**Closedness.** $\operatorname{rank}A\le1$ iff all $2\times2$ minors $a_{ij}a_{kl}-a_{il}a_{kj}$ vanish. These are polynomials, so $\mathcal{R}_1$ is the common zero set of continuous functions and is closed. It is stable under $A\mapsto tA$.

(Alternative: a limit of $x_jy_j^T$ need not obviously be of this form if $x_j,y_j$ blow up; the minor characterisation avoids this issue.)

**2. Connectedness of rank exactly $1$.** The map $\Phi:(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\})^2\to M_n(\mathbb{R})$, $(x,y)\mapsto xy^T$ is continuous, and its image is exactly the rank-one matrices (by part 1, a nonzero $xy^T$ requires both $x,y\ne0$). For $n\ge2$, $\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}$ is path connected (it is homotopy equivalent to $S^{n-1}$, which is connected), hence so is the product, hence so is its continuous image.

**Remark.** For $n=1$, "rank exactly $1$" is $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$, which is disconnected. In general $\{\operatorname{rank}=r\}$ is connected for $1\le r\le n-1$ and splits into two components ($\det>0$ and $\det<0$) for $r=n$.
@@@ mnspec-semicontinuity-of-minimal-polynomial-degree-and-centraliser-dimension.md
---
title: Semicontinuity of the minimal polynomial degree and of the centraliser
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: l3
difficulty: 3
tags: lower semicontinuity, minimal polynomial, centraliser, rank
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

For $A\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ let $\mu_A$ be its minimal polynomial and $C(A)=\{X:AX=XA\}$ its centraliser. Show that $A\mapsto\deg\mu_A$ is lower semicontinuous and $A\mapsto\dim C(A)$ is upper semicontinuous.

## Hint

$\deg\mu_A\ge k$ iff $I,A,\dots,A^{k-1}$ are linearly independent. And $C(A)=\ker(\operatorname{ad}_A)$ with $\operatorname{ad}_A(X)=AX-XA$.

## Solution

**Degree of $\mu_A$.** The degree of $\mu_A$ is the smallest $d$ such that $A^d$ is a combination of $I,\dots,A^{d-1}$. So $\deg\mu_A\ge k$ iff $I,A,\dots,A^{k-1}$ are linearly independent, i.e. the $n^2\times k$ matrix $M_k(A)$ whose columns are the vectorised powers has rank $k$. This means that some $k\times k$ minor of $M_k(A)$ is nonzero. Each such minor is a polynomial in the entries of $A$, hence continuous, so
$$\{A:\deg\mu_A\ge k\}=\bigcup_{\text{minors}}\{m(A)\ne0\}$$
is open. A function $f$ with $\{f\ge k\}$ open for each $k$ is lower semicontinuous: $\liminf_{B\to A}f(B)\ge f(A)$.

**Centraliser.** The map $\operatorname{ad}_A:M_n\to M_n$, $X\mapsto AX-XA$, is linear in $X$ and its matrix (in the standard basis of $M_n$) depends linearly on $A$ (it is $I\otimes A-A^T\otimes I$ up to conventions). Rank is lower semicontinuous (same argument with minors: $\operatorname{rank}\ge r$ is open), so near $A$ we have $\operatorname{rank}\operatorname{ad}_B\ge\operatorname{rank}\operatorname{ad}_A$. By rank-nullity,
$$\dim C(B)=n^2-\operatorname{rank}\operatorname{ad}_B\le n^2-\operatorname{rank}\operatorname{ad}_A=\dim C(A).$$
So $\dim C$ is upper semicontinuous.

**Example.** $A=0$: $\deg\mu_A=1$ (minimal possible) and $\dim C(A)=n^2$ (maximal). Near $0$, nearby generic matrices have $\deg\mu=n$ and $\dim C=n$: degrees jump *up* and centraliser dimensions jump *down* off the special matrices.

**Remark.** Always $\dim C(A)\ge n$, with equality iff $A$ is *non-derogatory* ($\deg\mu_A=n$, i.e. $\mu_A=\chi_A$), which is an open dense condition.
@@@ mnspec-inertia-of-symmetric-matrices-is-semicontinuous.md
---
title: Semicontinuity of the inertia of symmetric matrices
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: l3
difficulty: 3
tags: inertia, symmetric matrices, Weyl, semicontinuity
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

On $\mathrm{Sym}_n(\mathbb{R})$ let $n_+(S)$ be the number of positive eigenvalues (with multiplicity) and $n_0(S)=\dim\ker S$ the nullity. Show that $n_+$ is lower semicontinuous and $n_0$ is upper semicontinuous.

## Hint

Order the eigenvalues $\lambda_1(S)\le\dots\le\lambda_n(S)$ and use that each $\lambda_k$ is a continuous (indeed $1$-Lipschitz) function of $S$.

## Solution

**Eigenvalues are Lipschitz.** For symmetric $S,S'$ Weyl's inequality gives $|\lambda_k(S)-\lambda_k(S')|\le\|S-S'\|$ for each $k$ (min-max formula for the Rayleigh quotient).

**$n_+$ is lower semicontinuous.** Let $m=n_+(S)$, so $\lambda_n(S),\dots,\lambda_{n-m+1}(S)>0$. Let $\delta=\lambda_{n-m+1}(S)>0$ be the smallest of them. If $\|S'-S\|<\delta$ then
$$\lambda_{n-m+1}(S')>\lambda_{n-m+1}(S)-\delta=0,$$
and so at least $m$ eigenvalues of $S'$ are positive: $n_+(S')\ge n_+(S)$ in a neighbourhood.

**$n_0$ is upper semicontinuous.** The nullity is $n-\operatorname{rank}S$, and the rank is lower semicontinuous (a nonzero minor stays nonzero nearby). Hence $n_0(S')=n-\operatorname{rank}S'\le n-\operatorname{rank}S=n_0(S)$ near $S$.

**Example.** $S=0$ has $n_+=0$, $n_0=n$. Nearby $S'=\varepsilon I$ has $n_+=n$ and $n_0=0$: the invariants can only jump up for $n_+$ and down for $n_0$ in a neighbourhood.

**Remark.** By symmetry $n_-$ is also lower semicontinuous, and $n_++n_-+n_0=n$. Near a given $S$ the signature can only change by turning zero eigenvalues into positive or negative ones; $n_+$ and $n_-$ never decrease locally. In particular, $\{n_+=n\}$ (positive definite matrices) is open.
@@@ mnspec-inversion-reverses-the-loewner-order.md
---
title: Inversion reverses the order of positive definite matrices
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: l3
difficulty: 3
tags: Loewner order, positive definite, inverse, square root
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Write $A\le B$ for symmetric matrices if $B-A$ is positive semidefinite. Show that $S\mapsto S^{-1}$ is an involutive homeomorphism of the cone $\mathrm{PD}$ of positive definite matrices onto itself, and that it reverses the order: $A\le B\Rightarrow B^{-1}\le A^{-1}$.

## Hint

Conjugate by $A^{-1/2}$ to reduce to the case $A=I$.

## Solution

**Homeomorphism.** If $S\in\mathrm{PD}$, its eigenvalues are positive, so $S^{-1}$ is symmetric with eigenvalues $1/\lambda_i>0$: $S^{-1}\in\mathrm{PD}$. The map is continuous on $GL_n$ (entries of $S^{-1}$ are $\operatorname{adj}(S)/\det S$, rational with nonvanishing denominator), it is its own inverse, hence a homeomorphism of $\mathrm{PD}$.

**Order reversal.** Let $0<A\le B$ and let $C=A^{-1/2}$ (symmetric, positive definite). Congruence preserves the order: $X\le Y\Rightarrow CXC\le CYC$, because $v^TC(Y-X)Cv=(Cv)^T(Y-X)(Cv)\ge0$. Thus
$$I=CAC\le CBC=:T.$$
So all eigenvalues of the PD matrix $T$ are $\ge1$, hence the eigenvalues of $T^{-1}$ are $\le1$, i.e. $T^{-1}\le I$. Now $T^{-1}=C^{-1}B^{-1}C^{-1}=A^{1/2}B^{-1}A^{1/2}$, so
$$A^{1/2}B^{-1}A^{1/2}\le I.$$
Conjugating by $A^{-1/2}$ again: $B^{-1}\le A^{-1}$.

**Example.** $A=I$, $B=\operatorname{diag}(1,4)$: $B^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(1,\frac14)\le I=A^{-1}$.

**Remark.** The map $S\mapsto S^{-1}$ reverses the order but $S\mapsto S^2$ does *not* preserve it (while $S\mapsto\sqrt S$ does, see the operator monotonicity problem). A function $f$ preserving the Loewner order is *operator monotone*; $-1/x$, $\ln x$, $x^{r}$ ($0\le r\le1$) are, and $x^2$ is not.
@@@ mnspec-matrices-with-positive-definite-symmetric-part.md
---
title: Matrices with positive definite symmetric part
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: l3
difficulty: 3
tags: positive definite, convex cone, eigenvalues, real part
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $\mathcal{K}=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb{R}):A+A^T\text{ is positive definite}\}$. Show that $\mathcal{K}$ is open and convex, and that every eigenvalue $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$ of every $A\in\mathcal{K}$ satisfies $\operatorname{Re}\lambda>0$.

## Hint

$\mathcal{K}$ is the preimage of the cone $\mathrm{PD}$ under a linear map. For the eigenvalues, compute $\operatorname{Re}(v^*Av)$ for a complex eigenvector $v$.

## Solution

**Openness and convexity.** The map $L:A\mapsto A+A^T$ is linear, hence continuous, and $\mathrm{PD}$ is open and convex (it is defined by $x^TSx>0$ for all $x\ne0$, a convex condition; openness by Sylvester's criterion or by compactness of the unit sphere). Therefore $\mathcal{K}=L^{-1}(\mathrm{PD})$ is open and convex.

**Eigenvalues.** Let $Av=\lambda v$ with $v\in\mathbb{C}^n\setminus\{0\}$. Write $S=\frac{A+A^T}2$, real symmetric, positive definite on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and also on $\mathbb{C}^n$: $v=x+iy$ gives $v^*Sv=x^TSx+y^TSy>0$ (the cross terms cancel because $S$ is symmetric). Since $A$ is real,
$$\overline{v^*Av}=v^TA^T\bar v=(\bar v)^*\ldots$$
more simply, $v^*A^Tv=\overline{v^*Av}$ because $A^T=A^*$ for real $A$. Hence
$$v^*Sv=\tfrac12\big(v^*Av+v^*A^*v\big)=\operatorname{Re}(v^*Av).$$
But $v^*Av=\lambda\,v^*v=\lambda|v|^2$, so
$$\operatorname{Re}\lambda\,|v|^2=v^*Sv>0\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{Re}\lambda>0.$$

**Example.** $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&5\\-5&1\end{pmatrix}$: $A+A^T=2I>0$ and the eigenvalues are $1\pm5i$, real part $1>0$.

**Remark.** The converse fails: $\begin{pmatrix}1&10\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has both eigenvalues $1$ but $A+A^T=\begin{pmatrix}2&10\\10&2\end{pmatrix}$ is indefinite (determinant $4-100<0$). Positivity of the symmetric part is a *uniform* (for all vectors) version of positivity of the spectrum, and it is related to Lyapunov stability with $P=I$.
@@@ mnspec-the-determinantal-hypersurface.md
---
title: Where is {det = 0} a manifold?
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: l3
difficulty: 3
tags: determinant, implicit function theorem, singular point, cone, local homology
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

1. Show that $\Sigma=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb{R}):\det A=0\}$ is a smooth hypersurface (a manifold of dimension $n^2-1$) near every $A$ of rank $n-1$.
2. For $n=2$, show that $\Sigma$ is not a topological manifold near $0$.

## Hint

The gradient of $\det$ at $A$ is the transpose of the adjugate matrix. For part 2, diagonalise the quadratic form $ad-bc$ and see $\Sigma$ as a cone over a torus.

## Solution

**1. Gradient.** Expanding $\det$ along row $i$: $\det A=\sum_ja_{ij}C_{ij}$ with the cofactor $C_{ij}$ independent of the entries of row $i$. So $\dfrac{\partial\det}{\partial a_{ij}}=C_{ij}$, i.e. $\nabla\det(A)=\operatorname{adj}(A)^T$ (the cofactor matrix).

If $\operatorname{rank}A=n-1$, then $\operatorname{adj}A\ne0$: indeed $A\operatorname{adj}A=0$ and at least one $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ minor of $A$ is nonzero (rank $n-1$), which is an entry of the cofactor matrix. So $0$ is a regular value of $\det$ near $A$ and by the implicit function theorem $\Sigma$ is a smooth hypersurface near $A$.

**2. The case $n=2$ at $0$.** With $s=a+d$, $u=a-d$, $v=b+c$, $w=b-c$ we have $a=\frac{s+u}2$, $d=\frac{s-u}2$ and
$$ad-bc=\frac{s^2-u^2}4-\frac{v^2-w^2}4=\frac{s^2+w^2-u^2-v^2}4.$$
So $\Sigma\cong\{(s,w,u,v)\in\mathbb{R}^4:s^2+w^2=u^2+v^2\}$, a quadratic cone. Its intersection with the sphere of radius $r$ is $\{s^2+w^2=u^2+v^2=r^2/2\}$, a product of two circles, a torus $T^2$. Hence $\Sigma\setminus\{0\}\cong T^2\times(0,\infty)$ and $\Sigma$ is the open cone over $T^2$.

*$\Sigma$ is not a manifold at $0$.* Suppose $0$ had a neighbourhood in $\Sigma$ homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^3$. Then the local homology $H_2(\Sigma,\Sigma\setminus\{0\})$ would equal $H_2(\mathbb{R}^3,\mathbb{R}^3\setminus0)\cong\tilde H_1(S^2)=0$. For a cone $\Sigma$ over a space $L$, however,
$$H_k(\Sigma,\Sigma\setminus0)\cong\tilde H_{k-1}(L),$$
which for $L=T^2$ and $k=2$ is $H_1(T^2)=\mathbb{Z}^2\ne0$. Contradiction. (Equivalently: the punctured neighbourhoods of $0$ retract onto a torus, which is not a $2$-sphere; a punctured $3$-ball would retract onto $S^2$.)

**Remark.** The singular locus of $\Sigma$ is exactly $\{\operatorname{rank}\le n-2\}$, of codimension $4$ in $M_n(\mathbb{R})$. The hypersurface is smooth elsewhere, so singularities of $\{\det=0\}$ are "rare" and invisible to a transversal curve.
@@@ mnspec-the-discriminant-of-a-2-by-2-matrix.md
---
title: The discriminant of a 2×2 matrix and a cone
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: l3
difficulty: 3
tags: discriminant, 2x2 matrices, convex cone, complex eigenvalues
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

For $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ put $u=a-d$, $v=b+c$, $w=b-c$. Show that
$$\operatorname{tr}(A)^2-4\det A=u^2+v^2-w^2,$$
and deduce that $\{A:\operatorname{tr}^2<4\det\}$ (matrices with non-real eigenvalues) has exactly two connected components, each of them convex.

## Hint

Expand $(a+d)^2-4(ad-bc)=(a-d)^2+4bc$ and write $4bc$ with $b+c$ and $b-c$.

## Solution

**The identity.**
$$\operatorname{tr}^2-4\det=(a+d)^2-4ad+4bc=(a-d)^2+4bc.$$
Since $(b+c)^2-(b-c)^2=4bc$,
$$\operatorname{tr}^2-4\det=u^2+(b+c)^2-(b-c)^2=u^2+v^2-w^2.$$

**Non-real spectrum.** The eigenvalues are real iff the discriminant $\operatorname{tr}^2-4\det\ge0$. So the matrices with non-real eigenvalues form
$$\mathcal{E}=\{u^2+v^2<w^2\}\subset\mathbb{R}^4$$
(coordinates $s=a+d,u,v,w$ are a linear change of coordinates, so topology and convexity are preserved). The variable $s$ is free.

**Two components.** The condition $u^2+v^2<w^2$ forces $w\ne0$, so $\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{E}_+\sqcup\mathcal{E}_-$ with $\mathcal{E}_\pm=\{\pm w>\sqrt{u^2+v^2}\}$, both open and disjoint.

**Convexity of each piece.** $\mathcal{E}_+=\mathbb{R}_s\times\{(u,v,w):w>\sqrt{u^2+v^2}\}$. The function $(u,v)\mapsto\sqrt{u^2+v^2}$ is a norm, hence convex, so its epigraph (strict) $\{w>\sqrt{u^2+v^2}\}$ is convex. A product with $\mathbb{R}$ is convex. Same for $\mathcal{E}_-$. Convex sets are connected, so there are exactly two components.

**Example.** The rotation $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has $b=-1,c=1$, $w=-2$, $u=v=0$: it lies in $\mathcal{E}_-$; its transpose (rotation by $-90^\circ$) lies in $\mathcal{E}_+$. Orientation of the rotation decides the component.

**Remark.** The sign of $w=b-c$ is the "angular velocity" of the linear flow $\dot x=Ax$ when the eigenvalues are complex: the two components are counter-clockwise and clockwise spiral behaviours. They cannot be connected without passing through matrices with real eigenvalues.
@@@ mnspec-the-bauer-fike-theorem.md
---
title: The Bauer-Fike theorem
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: Bauer-Fike, perturbation of eigenvalues, condition number, diagonalisable
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $A=VDV^{-1}\in M_n(\mathbb{C})$ with $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\dots,d_n)$ and let $\kappa(V)=\|V\|\,\|V^{-1}\|$ (operator $2$-norm). Show that every eigenvalue $\mu$ of $A+E$ satisfies
$$\min_i|\mu-d_i|\le\kappa(V)\,\|E\|.$$

## Hint

If $\mu$ is not an eigenvalue of $A$, write $(A+E-\mu)x=0$ in the basis $V$ and isolate $y=V^{-1}x$.

## Solution

**Trivial case.** If $\mu\in\{d_i\}$ the left side is $0$ and there is nothing to prove. Assume $\mu\notin\{d_i\}$, so $D-\mu I$ is invertible.

**Reformulation.** Let $x\ne0$ with $(A+E)x=\mu x$. Then $(A-\mu I)x=-Ex$. Substituting $A=VDV^{-1}$ and $y=V^{-1}x\ne0$:
$$V(D-\mu I)V^{-1}x=-Ex\ \Longrightarrow\ (D-\mu I)y=-V^{-1}EVy.$$

**Inverting $D-\mu$.**
$$y=-(D-\mu I)^{-1}V^{-1}EV\,y.$$
Take norms and use submultiplicativity:
$$|y|\le\|(D-\mu I)^{-1}\|\,\|V^{-1}\|\,\|E\|\,\|V\|\,|y|.$$

**Conclusion.** Dividing by $|y|>0$ gives $1\le\|(D-\mu I)^{-1}\|\,\kappa(V)\,\|E\|$. For a diagonal matrix, $\|(D-\mu I)^{-1}\|=\max_i\frac1{|d_i-\mu|}=\frac1{\min_i|d_i-\mu|}$. Therefore
$$\min_i|d_i-\mu|\le\kappa(V)\|E\|.$$

**Example.** $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1+\delta\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvectors with $\kappa(V)\approx2/\delta$ (nearly parallel eigenvectors), so a perturbation of size $\eta$ can move the eigenvalues by about $\sqrt{\eta}$ when $\delta\approx\sqrt\eta$: the bound is quantitatively sharp as $A$ approaches a Jordan block.

**Remark.** The theorem quantifies how ill-conditioned the eigenvalues of a nearly non-diagonalisable matrix are, and recovers the Hölder phenomenon of the Jordan block ($\kappa\to\infty$).
@@@ mnspec-eigenvalues-of-normal-matrices-are-well-conditioned.md
---
title: Eigenvalues of normal matrices move by at most the size of the perturbation
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: normal matrices, Bauer-Fike, Weyl, unitary diagonalisation
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb{C})$ be normal ($AA^*=A^*A$), for instance real symmetric. Show that for every $E$, every eigenvalue $\mu$ of $A+E$ is within distance $\|E\|$ of some eigenvalue of $A$. For real symmetric $A,E$ show the sharper statement that the sorted eigenvalues satisfy $|\lambda_k(A+E)-\lambda_k(A)|\le\|E\|$.

## Hint

Normal matrices are unitarily diagonalisable, so the condition number of the eigenvector matrix is $1$.

## Solution

**First statement.** By the spectral theorem for normal matrices, $A=UDU^*$ with $U$ unitary and $D$ diagonal. Then $\|U\|=\|U^{-1}\|=1$, so $\kappa(U)=1$. Bauer-Fike gives
$$\min_i|\mu-d_i|\le\kappa(U)\|E\|=\|E\|.$$

**Symmetric case, sorted eigenvalues (Weyl).** For real symmetric $A$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\le\dots\le\lambda_n$, the Courant-Fischer formula says
$$\lambda_k(A)=\min_{\dim V=k}\ \max_{x\in V,|x|=1}x^TAx.$$
For a unit $x$, $x^T(A+E)x\le x^TAx+\|E\|$, hence $\lambda_k(A+E)\le\lambda_k(A)+\|E\|$. Applying this to the pair $(A+E,-E)$ gives $\lambda_k(A)\le\lambda_k(A+E)+\|E\|$. So
$$|\lambda_k(A+E)-\lambda_k(A)|\le\|E\|.$$

**Example.** $A=\operatorname{diag}(1,3)$ and $E=\begin{pmatrix}0&\varepsilon\\\varepsilon&0\end{pmatrix}$ with $\|E\|=\varepsilon$: the eigenvalues of $A+E$ are $2\pm\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}$, which differ from $1,3$ by $\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}-1\le\varepsilon^2/2<\varepsilon$.

**Remark.** The contrast with the nilpotent Jordan block (change $\varepsilon^{1/n}$ for a perturbation of size $\varepsilon$) shows that non-normality is exactly what makes eigenvalues sensitive. This also explains why symmetric eigenproblems are numerically much easier than general ones.
@@@ mnspec-gelfand-s-spectral-radius-formula.md
---
title: Gelfand's spectral radius formula
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: spectral radius, Gelfand formula, norms, powers
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $\|\cdot\|$ be any submultiplicative norm on $M_n(\mathbb{C})$ (or $M_n(\mathbb{R})$). Prove that
$$\rho(A)=\lim_{k\to\infty}\|A^k\|^{1/k}.$$

## Hint

Lower bound: $\rho(A)^k=\rho(A^k)\le\|A^k\|$ by the spectral mapping theorem. Upper bound: apply "$B^k\to0$ if $\rho(B)<1$" to $B=A/(\rho(A)+\varepsilon)$.

## Solution

**Step 1: $\rho(A)\le\|A^k\|^{1/k}$ for every $k$.** If $Av=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$ ($v$ complex) and $|\lambda|=\rho(A)$, then $A^kv=\lambda^kv$, so $\rho(A)^k=\rho(A^k)$ (spectral mapping with $p(x)=x^k$). For a *submultiplicative matrix norm induced by a vector norm*, $\|A^k\|\ge\rho(A^k)$ since $|A^kv|=|\lambda|^k|v|$ gives $\|A^k\|\ge|\lambda|^k$. For a general submultiplicative norm that is not induced by a vector norm, use the equivalence of norms: $\|\cdot\|\ge c\,\|\cdot\|_{op}$ for some $c>0$, so $\|A^k\|^{1/k}\ge c^{1/k}\rho(A)$, and $c^{1/k}\to1$. Either way,
$$\liminf_{k}\|A^k\|^{1/k}\ge\rho(A).$$

**Step 2: $\limsup\le\rho(A)$.** Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and set $B=A/(\rho(A)+\varepsilon)$. Then $\rho(B)=\frac{\rho(A)}{\rho(A)+\varepsilon}<1$, so $B^k\to0$ (previous problem), hence $\|B^k\|\le1$ for all large $k$. Equivalently
$$\|A^k\|\le(\rho(A)+\varepsilon)^k\quad\text{for large }k,\qquad\text{so}\qquad\|A^k\|^{1/k}\le\rho(A)+\varepsilon.$$
Hence $\limsup\|A^k\|^{1/k}\le\rho(A)+\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.

**Conclusion.** $\liminf\ge\rho(A)\ge\limsup-\varepsilon$ for all $\varepsilon$; the limit exists and equals $\rho(A)$.

**Example.** $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ has $\rho=0$ and $A^2=0$: $\|A^k\|^{1/k}=0$ for $k\ge2$. For $A=\begin{pmatrix}0.9&1\\0&0.9\end{pmatrix}$, $\|A^{50}\|^{1/50}\approx0.9\cdot1.0\!\ldots$ approaches $0.9$ slowly.

**Remark.** As a corollary, $\rho(A)=\inf_{\|\cdot\|}\|A\|$ over all operator norms: for each $\varepsilon$ there is a norm with $\|A\|<\rho(A)+\varepsilon$. This is the topological meaning of the spectral radius.
@@@ mnspec-monotonicity-of-the-spectral-radius-for-nonnegative-matrices.md
---
title: The spectral radius is monotone on nonnegative matrices
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: spectral radius, nonnegative matrices, Gelfand formula, monotonicity
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

If $A,B\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ satisfy $0\le A\le B$ entrywise, show that $\rho(A)\le\rho(B)$.

## Hint

Use Gelfand's formula with the norm $\|M\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_j|m_{ij}|$ (maximum absolute row sum).

## Solution

**Entrywise inequality for powers.** We prove $0\le A^k\le B^k$ entrywise by induction. For $k=1$ it is the hypothesis. If $0\le A^k\le B^k$, then
$$(A^{k+1})_{ij}=\sum_l(A^k)_{il}A_{lj}\le\sum_l(B^k)_{il}B_{lj}=(B^{k+1})_{ij},$$
because all terms are nonnegative and each factor is dominated.

**The norm.** For a matrix with nonnegative entries, $\|M\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_jM_{ij}$ is nondecreasing in the entries. Hence
$$\|A^k\|_\infty\le\|B^k\|_\infty\quad\text{for all }k.$$

**Gelfand.** Taking $k$-th roots and letting $k\to\infty$ (Gelfand's formula for the submultiplicative norm $\|\cdot\|_\infty$):
$$\rho(A)=\lim_k\|A^k\|_\infty^{1/k}\le\lim_k\|B^k\|_\infty^{1/k}=\rho(B).$$

**Example.** $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\le B=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$: $\rho(A)=0\le\rho(B)=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$.

**Remark.** Nonnegativity is essential: for $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&-3\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\le B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ (entrywise) there is no problem, but with $A=\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}\le B=I$ we get $\rho(A)=2>\rho(B)=1$. This monotonicity is a first step of the Perron-Frobenius theory.
@@@ mnspec-existence-of-a-stationary-distribution.md
---
title: A stochastic matrix has a stationary distribution
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: stochastic matrices, compactness, Cesàro averages, Markov chains
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $P\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ be row-stochastic ($P_{ij}\ge0$, $\sum_jP_{ij}=1$). Show that there is a probability row vector $\pi$ (that is $\pi_i\ge0$, $\sum\pi_i=1$) with $\pi P=\pi$.

## Hint

Apply $P$ repeatedly to a probability vector, average, and use compactness of the simplex.

## Solution

**The simplex is invariant.** Let $\Delta=\{\pi\in\mathbb{R}^n:\pi_i\ge0,\sum\pi_i=1\}$, a compact convex set. If $\pi\in\Delta$ then $\pi P\ge0$ and $\sum_j(\pi P)_j=\sum_i\pi_i\sum_jP_{ij}=1$, so $\pi P\in\Delta$.

**Cesàro averages.** Let $\pi_0=(\frac1n,\dots,\frac1n)$ and
$$m_N=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\pi_0P^k\in\Delta$$
(an average of points of the convex set $\Delta$). Then
$$m_NP-m_N=\frac1N\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{N}\pi_0P^k-\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\pi_0P^k\Big)=\frac{\pi_0P^N-\pi_0}N.$$
Since $\pi_0P^N,\pi_0\in\Delta$ have $1$-norm $1$, $\|m_NP-m_N\|_1\le\frac2N\to0$.

**Compactness.** $\Delta$ is compact, so a subsequence $m_{N_j}$ converges to some $\pi\in\Delta$. By continuity of $x\mapsto xP-x$,
$$\pi P-\pi=\lim_j(m_{N_j}P-m_{N_j})=0.$$

**Example.** $P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$: $P^k$ does not converge, but the averages $m_N\to(\frac12,\frac12)$, which is stationary.

**Remark.** This is the Markov-Kakutani / Brouwer-type argument. The vector $\pi$ is generally not unique (e.g. $P=I$) and $\pi_0P^k$ need not converge, which is why Cesàro averaging is needed; under the positivity assumption of the next problem, uniqueness and convergence hold.
@@@ mnspec-dobrushin-s-contraction-argument.md
---
title: Dobrushin's contraction for positive stochastic matrices
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: stochastic matrices, Dobrushin, oscillation, convergence of powers
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $P$ be a row-stochastic $n\times n$ matrix with all entries $P_{ij}\ge\delta>0$. Show that $P^k$ converges, as $k\to\infty$, to a matrix $\mathbf{1}\pi^T$ whose rows are all equal to the same probability vector $\pi$, and that the convergence is geometric with ratio at most $1-n\delta$.

## Hint

For a vector $x$ let $\operatorname{osc}(x)=\max_ix_i-\min_ix_i$. Show $\operatorname{osc}(Px)\le(1-n\delta)\operatorname{osc}(x)$.

## Solution

**Step 1: rows are close.** Let $p,q$ be two rows of $P$, probability vectors with all entries $\ge\delta$. The vector $d=p-q$ has zero sum, so $\sum_id_i^+=\sum_id_i^-=\frac12\|d\|_1$, where $d^\pm$ are the positive/negative parts. Moreover
$$\sum_id_i^+=\sum_i(p_i-q_i)^+=1-\sum_i\min(p_i,q_i)\le1-n\delta.$$

**Step 2: oscillation contracts.** For $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, $(Px)_r-(Px)_s=d\cdot x$ with $d=p_r-p_s$. Because $\sum d_i=0$,
$$d\cdot x=\sum d_i^+x_i-\sum d_i^-x_i\le\Big(\sum d_i^+\Big)\max x-\Big(\sum d_i^-\Big)\min x=\Big(\sum d_i^+\Big)\operatorname{osc}(x).$$
Hence $\operatorname{osc}(Px)\le(1-n\delta)\operatorname{osc}(x)$, and by induction $\operatorname{osc}(P^kx)\le(1-n\delta)^k\operatorname{osc}(x)$.

**Step 3: $P^kx$ converges to a constant.** Since $P$ is stochastic, each coordinate of $Px$ is an average of the coordinates of $x$: $\max P^kx$ is nonincreasing, $\min P^kx$ is nondecreasing, and both converge; as the oscillation tends to $0$, they converge to the same limit $c(x)$. So $P^kx\to c(x)\mathbf{1}$, with $|P^kx-c(x)\mathbf{1}|_\infty\le(1-n\delta)^k\operatorname{osc}(x)$.

**Step 4: the limit matrix.** $c$ is linear in $x$ (a limit of linear maps), so $c(x)=\pi\cdot x$ for $\pi_i=c(e_i)$. Taking $x=e_i$ with $c(e_i)\ge0$ (the entries of $P^k$ are $\ge0$) and $x=\mathbf{1}$ with $c(\mathbf{1})=1$ shows that $\pi_i\ge0$ and $\sum\pi_i=1$. Therefore $P^kx\to\mathbf{1}\pi^Tx$ for each $x$, i.e. $P^k\to\mathbf{1}\pi^T$.

**Example.** $P=\begin{pmatrix}0.9&0.1\\0.2&0.8\end{pmatrix}$ has $\delta=0.1$ and ratio $\le0.8$ (the actual second eigenvalue is $0.7$); $\pi=(\frac23,\frac13)$.

**Remark.** The constant $1-n\delta$ is the Dobrushin ergodicity coefficient. Also $\pi P=\pi$ follows from $\mathbf{1}\pi^TP=\lim P^{k+1}=\mathbf{1}\pi^T$, and $\pi$ is unique, so the Markov chain forgets its initial state exponentially fast.
@@@ mnspec-a-trace-zero-matrix-has-a-zero-diagonal-in-some-basis.md
---
title: A traceless matrix has a zero diagonal in some orthonormal basis
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: trace, numerical range, orthonormal basis, induction
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ with $\operatorname{tr}A=0$. Prove that there is an orthonormal basis $(f_1,\dots,f_n)$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $f_i^TAf_i=0$ for all $i$; that is, $Q^TAQ$ has zero diagonal for some orthogonal $Q$.

## Hint

Show first that there is a unit vector $x$ with $x^TAx=0$ (the numerical range contains the mean of the diagonal). Then induct on the compression of $A$ to $x^\perp$.

## Solution

**Step 1: a unit vector with $x^TAx=0$.** Let $S=\frac{A+A^T}2$; $\operatorname{tr}S=\operatorname{tr}A=0$. Its eigenvalues $\lambda_1\le\dots\le\lambda_n$ have sum $0$, so $\lambda_1\le0\le\lambda_n$. By the numerical range theorem (previous problem, $n\ge2$) $\{x^TAx:|x|=1\}=[\lambda_1,\lambda_n]\ni0$. So there is a unit $x_1$ with $x_1^TAx_1=0$. (For $n=1$, $A=(0)$ and any unit vector works.)

**Step 2: induction.** Extend $x_1$ to an orthonormal basis and let $W=x_1^\perp$ (dimension $n-1$), with an orthonormal basis forming the columns of an $n\times(n-1)$ matrix $B$. The compression $A'=B^TAB\in M_{n-1}(\mathbb{R})$ has
$$\operatorname{tr}A'=\operatorname{tr}A-x_1^TAx_1=0-0=0,$$
since the trace in the orthonormal basis $(x_1,\text{columns of }B)$ is the sum of the diagonal entries $x_1^TAx_1+\operatorname{tr}A'$.

By the induction hypothesis there is an orthonormal basis $(g_2,\dots,g_n)$ of $W$ in which $A'$ has zero diagonal, i.e. $g_i^TAg_i=0$ (for $g_i\in W$, $g_i^TA g_i$ is exactly the corresponding diagonal entry of the compression).

**Conclusion.** $(x_1,g_2,\dots,g_n)$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with all $f_i^TAf_i=0$.

**Example.** $A=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$: $x=\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,1)$ gives $x^TAx=0$, and $\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1)$ also; in this basis $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

**Remark.** Conversely a matrix with zero diagonal in an orthonormal basis has trace zero, so $\operatorname{tr}A=0$ iff $A$ is orthogonally similar to a zero-diagonal matrix. The same statement holds with "similar" in place of "orthogonally similar" (trivially, with a basis that is not orthonormal) and it is the matrix version of: a trace-zero matrix is a sum of commutators (Albert-Muckenhoupt).
@@@ mnspec-sylvester-s-criterion.md
---
title: Sylvester's criterion and the openness of the positive cone
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: Sylvester criterion, positive definite, LDL decomposition, leading minors
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $S\in\mathrm{Sym}_n(\mathbb{R})$ and let $\Delta_k=\det(S_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le k}$ be its leading principal minors. Prove that $S$ is positive definite iff $\Delta_1>0,\dots,\Delta_n>0$. Deduce that $\mathrm{PD}$ is open in $\mathrm{Sym}_n$.

## Hint

($\Rightarrow$) Leading blocks are positive definite. ($\Leftarrow$) Gaussian elimination without pivoting gives $S=LDL^T$ with $d_k=\Delta_k/\Delta_{k-1}$.

## Solution

**($\Rightarrow$).** If $S>0$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^k\setminus0$, extend $x$ by zeros to $\tilde x\in\mathbb{R}^n$: $x^TS_kx=\tilde x^TS\tilde x>0$. So each leading block $S_k$ is positive definite, its eigenvalues are positive and $\Delta_k=\det S_k>0$.

**($\Leftarrow$).** Assume all $\Delta_k>0$. We do Gaussian elimination without row exchanges. The first pivot is $\Delta_1>0$. After eliminating the first column, the lower right block is the Schur complement and is again symmetric; inductively the $k$-th pivot is $d_k=\Delta_k/\Delta_{k-1}$ (with $\Delta_0=1$), since the determinant of the leading $k\times k$ block is the product of the first $k$ pivots and elimination does not change leading minors. All pivots are $>0$, so the elimination never breaks down, and we obtain
$$S=LDL^T,\qquad L\text{ unit lower triangular},\ D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\dots,d_n).$$
Therefore for $x\ne0$, with $y=L^Tx\ne0$ ($L$ is invertible),
$$x^TSx=y^TDy=\sum_kd_ky_k^2>0.$$

**Openness.** The functions $\Delta_k:\mathrm{Sym}_n\to\mathbb{R}$ are polynomials, so continuous, and
$$\mathrm{PD}=\bigcap_{k=1}^n\Delta_k^{-1}\big((0,\infty)\big)$$
is open.

**Example.** $S=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$: $\Delta_1=2$, $\Delta_2=3$, so $S>0$ and $S=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-\frac12&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&\frac32\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&-\frac12\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.

**Remark.** The criterion needs *leading* minors: $S=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ has $\Delta_1=0$ and $S_{22}=-1<0$. For positive *semi*definiteness one needs *all* principal minors $\ge0$, not only the leading ones: $\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ has leading minors $0,0$ yet is not semidefinite.
@@@ mnspec-lyapunov-s-criterion-for-stability.md
---
title: Lyapunov's criterion for Hurwitz matrices
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: Hurwitz, Lyapunov equation, stability, positive definite
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

A real matrix $A$ is *Hurwitz* if all its eigenvalues have negative real part. Show that $A$ is Hurwitz iff there exists a symmetric positive definite $P$ with $A^TP+PA<0$ (negative definite).

## Hint

($\Leftarrow$) Evaluate the quadratic form on a complex eigenvector. ($\Rightarrow$) Take $P=\int_0^\infty e^{A^Tt}e^{At}\,dt$.

## Solution

**($\Leftarrow$).** Let $Av=\lambda v$, $v\in\mathbb{C}^n\setminus\{0\}$. Since $A$ is real, $v^*A^T=(Av)^*=\bar\lambda v^*$. Therefore
$$v^*(A^TP+PA)v=\bar\lambda\,v^*Pv+\lambda\,v^*Pv=2\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ v^*Pv.$$
The left side is $<0$ (a negative definite real symmetric matrix is negative definite on $\mathbb{C}^n$ too), and $v^*Pv>0$. Hence $\operatorname{Re}\lambda<0$.

**($\Rightarrow$).** Suppose $A$ is Hurwitz. Then there are $C,c>0$ with $\|e^{At}\|\le Ce^{-ct}$ for $t\ge0$ (Jordan form: entries of $e^{At}$ are $t^je^{\lambda t}$ with $\operatorname{Re}\lambda<0$). So the integral
$$P=\int_0^\infty e^{A^Tt}e^{At}\,dt$$
converges absolutely (integrand $\le C^2e^{-2ct}$). It is symmetric, and for $x\ne0$,
$$x^TPx=\int_0^\infty|e^{At}x|^2dt>0,$$
because $e^{At}$ is invertible so $e^{At}x\ne0$ for all $t$ and the integrand is continuous and positive. So $P>0$. Moreover
$$A^TP+PA=\int_0^\infty\frac{d}{dt}\Big(e^{A^Tt}e^{At}\Big)dt=\lim_{T\to\infty}e^{A^TT}e^{AT}-I=-I,$$
which is negative definite.

**Example.** $A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&10\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ is Hurwitz but $A^T+A$ is indefinite: $P=I$ does not work, yet a suitable $P=\begin{pmatrix}1&5\\5&51\end{pmatrix}$-like matrix does. The Lyapunov function $V(x)=x^TPx$ decreases along the flow $\dot x=Ax$.

**Remark.** In topological terms, the set of Hurwitz matrices is open (eigenvalues are continuous), and it is the union over $P>0$ of the open convex cones $\{A:A^TP+PA<0\}$; each cone is convex but the union is not (the set of Hurwitz matrices is *not* convex).
@@@ mnspec-the-eckart-young-theorem.md
---
title: The Eckart-Young theorem in the operator norm
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: Eckart-Young, low rank approximation, singular values, dimension counting
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ have singular values $\sigma_1\ge\dots\ge\sigma_n$ and let $0\le r<n$. Show that
$$\min\{\|A-B\|:\operatorname{rank}B\le r\}=\sigma_{r+1}(A)$$
for the operator norm.

## Hint

Upper bound by truncating the singular value decomposition. Lower bound: $\ker B$ has dimension $\ge n-r$, so it meets $\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_{r+1})$ nontrivially.

## Solution

**Setup.** Take a singular value decomposition $A=\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_iu_iv_i^T$ with orthonormal families $(u_i)$, $(v_i)$.

**Upper bound.** Let $B_0=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_iu_iv_i^T$, which has rank $\le r$. Then $A-B_0=\sum_{i>r}\sigma_iu_iv_i^T$, whose singular values are $\sigma_{r+1},\dots,\sigma_n$ so $\|A-B_0\|=\sigma_{r+1}$.

**Lower bound.** Let $\operatorname{rank}B\le r$. Then $\dim\ker B\ge n-r$. Let $V=\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_{r+1})$, of dimension $r+1$. Since $(n-r)+(r+1)=n+1>n$, the subspaces $\ker B$ and $V$ intersect in a nonzero subspace; pick a unit vector $x$ in the intersection. Because $Bx=0$,
$$\|A-B\|\ge|(A-B)x|=|Ax|.$$
Writing $x=\sum_{i\le r+1}c_iv_i$ with $\sum c_i^2=1$, orthonormality of $(u_i)$ gives
$$|Ax|^2=\sum_{i\le r+1}\sigma_i^2c_i^2\ge\sigma_{r+1}^2\sum c_i^2=\sigma_{r+1}^2.$$
Thus $\|A-B\|\ge\sigma_{r+1}$ for every $B$ of rank $\le r$.

**Conclusion.** The minimum is attained at $B_0$ and equals $\sigma_{r+1}$.

**Corollary (distance to singular matrices).** For $r=n-1$: the operator-norm distance from an invertible $A$ to the set $\{\det=0\}$ is $\sigma_n(A)=1/\|A^{-1}\|$.

**Example.** $A=\operatorname{diag}(3,2,1)$, $r=1$: the best rank-one approximation is $\operatorname{diag}(3,0,0)$ at distance $2=\sigma_2$.

**Remark.** The same truncation $B_0$ is optimal for the Frobenius norm, with error $\sqrt{\sigma_{r+1}^2+\dots+\sigma_n^2}$ (Eckart-Young-Mirsky); the proof is different.
@@@ mnspec-the-square-root-is-operator-monotone.md
---
title: The square root is operator monotone
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: m1
difficulty: 5
tags: Loewner order, operator monotone, square root, positive semidefinite
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $A,B$ be symmetric matrices with $0\le A\le B$ (Loewner order: $B-A$ is positive semidefinite). Show that $\sqrt A\le\sqrt B$, where $\sqrt{\cdot}$ is the positive semidefinite square root.

## Hint

First treat positive definite $A,B$. Put $X=\sqrt B-\sqrt A$ and check the identity $B-A=\sqrt B\,X+X\sqrt A$. Evaluate $v^T(B-A)v$ on an eigenvector $v$ of $X$.

## Solution

**Step 1: positive definite case.** Assume $0<A\le B$ and let $X=\sqrt B-\sqrt A$, a symmetric matrix. We have the algebraic identity
$$\sqrt B\,X+X\sqrt A=B-\sqrt B\sqrt A+\sqrt B\sqrt A-A=B-A.$$
Suppose $X$ had a negative eigenvalue $\lambda<0$ with eigenvector $v\ne0$. Since $X$ is symmetric, $v^TX=\lambda v^T$ and $Xv=\lambda v$. Then
$$v^T(B-A)v=v^T\sqrt B\,Xv+v^TX\sqrt A\,v=\lambda\,v^T\sqrt B\,v+\lambda\,v^T\sqrt A\,v=\lambda\big(v^T\sqrt Bv+v^T\sqrt Av\big)<0,$$
because $\sqrt A$ and $\sqrt B$ are positive definite so the bracket is positive, while $\lambda<0$. This contradicts $B-A\ge0$. So all eigenvalues of $X$ are $\ge0$, i.e. $\sqrt A\le\sqrt B$.

**Step 2: general case.** If $0\le A\le B$, then for each $\varepsilon>0$, $0<A+\varepsilon I\le B+\varepsilon I$, so by Step 1
$$\sqrt{A+\varepsilon I}\le\sqrt{B+\varepsilon I}.$$
The square root is continuous on the cone of positive semidefinite matrices, and the set $\{(X,Y):X\le Y\}$ is closed. Letting $\varepsilon\to0$ gives $\sqrt A\le\sqrt B$.

**Example.** The analogous statement for squares is false: $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\le B=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ but $A^2=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}\not\le B^2=\begin{pmatrix}5&3\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$, since $B^2-A^2=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $-1<0$.

**Remark.** More generally $t\mapsto t^r$ is operator monotone for $0\le r\le1$ (L\"owner-Heinz inequality) and not for $r>1$. This result is one of the first examples where order on matrices behaves differently from order on numbers.
@@@ mnspec-conjugacy-classes-in-the-plane-of-trace-and-determinant.md
---
title: The fibres of (trace, determinant) on 2×2 matrices
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: conjugacy classes, 2x2 matrices, hyperboloid, trace, determinant
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Consider $F=(\operatorname{tr},\det):M_2(\mathbb{R})\to\mathbb{R}^2$. For $s,\delta\in\mathbb{R}$ describe the fibre $F^{-1}(s,\delta)$ geometrically and its decomposition into conjugacy classes (under $GL_2(\mathbb{R})$).

## Hint

Use the coordinates $s=a+d$, $u=a-d$, $v=b+c$, $w=b-c$, in which $\operatorname{tr}^2-4\det=u^2+v^2-w^2$.

## Solution

**The fibre.** Fix $s=\operatorname{tr}$ and $\delta=\det$, and put $\Delta=s^2-4\delta$. In the coordinates $(u,v,w)\in\mathbb{R}^3$ the fibre is the quadric
$$Q_\Delta=\{u^2+v^2-w^2=\Delta\}.$$

**Case $\Delta>0$ (two distinct real eigenvalues).** $Q_\Delta$ is a one-sheeted hyperboloid, connected. All such matrices are diagonalisable with the same eigenvalues $\frac{s\pm\sqrt\Delta}2$, hence all conjugate: the fibre is a single conjugacy class.

**Case $\Delta<0$ (complex conjugate eigenvalues).** $w^2=u^2+v^2+|\Delta|$: a two-sheeted hyperboloid, with two components $w>0$ and $w<0$. Over $\mathbb{R}$, all matrices with the same non-real eigenvalues are similar (rational canonical form), so the fibre is one $GL_2(\mathbb{R})$-orbit. It is disconnected: conjugation by $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ (determinant $-1$) sends $(b,c)\mapsto(-b,-c)$, hence $w\mapsto-w$, swapping the two sheets. Under the connected subgroup $GL_2^+(\mathbb{R})$ each sheet is an orbit.

**Case $\Delta=0$ (double eigenvalue $\frac s2$).** $u^2+v^2=w^2$: a double cone. The apex $u=v=w=0$ is the scalar matrix $\frac s2I$, a one-point conjugacy class. The rest, the cone minus the apex (two nappes, $w>0$ and $w<0$), consists of the matrices $\frac s2I+N$ with $N\ne0$ nilpotent. All nonzero nilpotent $2\times2$ matrices are similar to $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, so this is a single $GL_2(\mathbb{R})$-orbit (again with two components, swapped by $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$).

**Summary.** Each fibre with $\Delta\ne0$ is one conjugacy class, and the fibre with $\Delta=0$ consists of two: the scalar matrix and the non-diagonalisable matrices.

**Check.** $\Delta=0$, $s=2$, $\delta=1$: $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has $u=0$, $v=1$, $w=1$: on the cone. The identity $I$ has $u=v=w=0$: the apex.

**Remark.** The orbit space $M_2(\mathbb{R})/GL_2(\mathbb{R})$ is *not* the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ of $(s,\delta)$: the quotient is non-Hausdorff along the parabola $\Delta=0$ (the apex and the cone minus apex cannot be separated), while the map $(\operatorname{tr},\det)$ identifies them.
@@@ mnspec-the-space-of-matrices-with-real-distinct-eigenvalues-in-dimension-two.md
---
title: Matrices with two distinct real eigenvalues retract onto a circle
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-rank-spectrum
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: homotopy equivalence, deformation retraction, 2x2 matrices, discriminant
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Show that $\mathcal{U}=\{A\in M_2(\mathbb{R}):\operatorname{tr}(A)^2>4\det A\}$ (two distinct real eigenvalues) is homotopy equivalent to a circle.

## Hint

In the coordinates $(s,u,v,w)$ with $\operatorname{tr}^2-4\det=u^2+v^2-w^2$, push $w$ to $0$ and forget $s$.

## Solution

**Description.** With $s=a+d$, $u=a-d$, $v=b+c$, $w=b-c$ (an invertible linear change of coordinates),
$$\mathcal{U}=\{(s,u,v,w):u^2+v^2>w^2\}=\mathbb{R}_s\times\mathcal{V},\qquad\mathcal{V}=\{(u,v,w):w^2<u^2+v^2\}.$$

**Deformation retraction of $\mathcal{V}$.** Define $H:\mathcal{V}\times[0,1]\to\mathcal{V}$,
$$H\big((u,v,w),t\big)=(u,v,(1-t)w).$$
It stays in $\mathcal{V}$: $\big((1-t)w\big)^2\le w^2<u^2+v^2$. Also $H_0=\mathrm{id}$, $H_1(u,v,w)=(u,v,0)$, and $H_t$ fixes the points $\mathcal{V}\cap\{w=0\}=\{(u,v,0):(u,v)\ne0\}$. So $\mathcal{V}$ deformation retracts onto
$$\{(u,v,0):(u,v)\ne(0,0)\}\cong\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}.$$

**Further retraction.** $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}$ deformation retracts onto the unit circle by $(u,v)\mapsto\frac{(u,v)}{|(u,v)|^{t}}$-type radial homotopy. Hence $\mathcal{V}\simeq S^1$.

**The factor $\mathbb{R}_s$.** It is contractible, so $\mathcal{U}=\mathbb{R}\times\mathcal{V}\simeq\mathcal{V}\simeq S^1$.

**Interpretation.** A point on the circle is the pair $(u,v)/|(u,v)|$, the direction of the "eigenspace configuration": the matrix $\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)$ conjugated by a rotation of angle $\theta$ gives $(u,v)=(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)(\cos2\theta,\sin2\theta)/2\cdot$-type, and a rotation by $\pi$ returns to the same matrix ($\theta\mapsto\theta+\pi$ gives $2\theta\mapsto2\theta+2\pi$) while $\theta\mapsto\theta+\frac\pi2$ swaps the eigenvalues, going halfway around the circle.

**Remark.** The fundamental group of $\mathcal{U}$ is $\mathbb{Z}$. By contrast the set $\{\operatorname{tr}^2<4\det\}$ has two contractible components (previous discriminant problem), so the "real" region is topologically richer than the "complex" one.

@@@ mnexp-convergence-of-the-matrix-exponential.md
---
title: Convergence of the matrix exponential and its first bounds
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-exp-log
level: l2
difficulty: 1
tags: matrix exponential, absolute convergence, submultiplicative norm
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Throughout, $\|\cdot\|$ is the operator norm on $M_n(\mathbb{R})$, so $\|AB\|\le\|A\|\,\|B\|$ and $\|I\|=1$.

Show that for every $A\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ the series $e^A=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{A^k}{k!}$ converges absolutely, and that
$$\|e^A\|\le e^{\|A\|},\qquad\|e^A-I\|\le e^{\|A\|}-1.$$
Deduce that $\exp:M_n(\mathbb{R})\to M_n(\mathbb{R})$ is continuous.

## Hint

By submultiplicativity, $\|A^k\|\le\|A\|^k$. Compare with the scalar exponential series.

## Solution

**Idea.** The series of norms is dominated by the scalar series $\sum\|A\|^k/k!$, which converges.

**Absolute convergence.** Submultiplicativity gives $\|A^k\|\le\|A\|^k$ by induction on $k$ (with $A^0=I$ and $\|I\|=1$ for the operator norm). Hence
$$\sum_{k\ge0}\left\|\frac{A^k}{k!}\right\|\le\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\|A\|^k}{k!}=e^{\|A\|}<\infty.$$
Since $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ is complete (it is $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$), an absolutely convergent series converges, so $e^A$ is well defined.

**The two bounds.** By the triangle inequality for series,
$$\|e^A\|\le\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\|A\|^k}{k!}=e^{\|A\|},$$
and, removing the term $k=0$ (which is $I$),
$$\|e^A-I\|=\Big\|\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{A^k}{k!}\Big\|\le\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\|A\|^k}{k!}=e^{\|A\|}-1.$$

**Continuity.** On the ball $\{\|A\|\le R\}$ the $k$-th term is bounded by $R^k/k!$, and $\sum R^k/k!<\infty$. By the Weierstrass M-test the series converges uniformly on this ball. Each partial sum $\sum_{k\le N}A^k/k!$ is a polynomial in the entries, hence continuous, and a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous. So $\exp$ is continuous on every ball, hence on $M_n(\mathbb{R})$.

**Remark.** (For the Frobenius norm $\|I\|=\sqrt n$, and the first bound would need the factor $\sqrt n$; the second bound is unchanged.) The bound $\|e^A-I\|\le e^{\|A\|}-1$ shows that $e^A$ is close to $I$ when $A$ is small: this is the starting point of the local study of $\exp$ and $\log$ near $I$.
@@@ mnexp-exponential-of-a-sum-commuting-and-not.md
---
title: The exponential of a sum: commuting and non-commuting matrices
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-exp-log
level: l2
difficulty: 1
tags: matrix exponential, commutation, counterexample
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

1. Show that if $AB=BA$ then $e^{A+B}=e^Ae^B$.
2. Show that this fails in general, using $A=E_{12}$ and $B=E_{21}$ (the matrix units of $M_2(\mathbb{R})$).

## Hint

For part 1, the binomial theorem holds for commuting matrices; then use the Cauchy product of two absolutely convergent series. For part 2, compute $e^{E_{12}}$ and $e^{E_{21}}$ by hand: both squares are $0$.

## Solution

**1. Commuting case.** Since $AB=BA$, the binomial theorem gives
$$\frac{(A+B)^m}{m!}=\sum_{i+j=m}\frac{A^i}{i!}\cdot\frac{B^j}{j!}.$$
Summing over $m$ gives the Cauchy product of the series for $e^A$ and $e^B$. Both converge absolutely (problem on convergence of $\exp$), so the Cauchy product converges to the product of the sums:
$$e^{A+B}=\sum_m\sum_{i+j=m}\frac{A^i}{i!}\frac{B^j}{j!}=e^Ae^B.$$

**2. A counterexample.** Let $A=E_{12}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=E_{21}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Then $A^2=B^2=0$, so
$$e^A=I+A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad e^B=I+B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
Multiplying,
$$e^Ae^B=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad e^Be^A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}.$$
These are different. Now $A+B$ is the symmetric matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $(A+B)^2=I$, so
$$e^{A+B}=\cosh1\,I+\sinh1\,(A+B)=\begin{pmatrix}\cosh1&\sinh1\\\sinh1&\cosh1\end{pmatrix}\approx\begin{pmatrix}1.543&1.175\\1.175&1.543\end{pmatrix},$$
which equals neither $e^Ae^B$ nor $e^Be^A$.

**Remark.** Since $e^Ae^B\ne e^Be^A$, the identity $e^{A+B}=e^Ae^B$ cannot hold when $A$ and $B$ do not commute: the left side is symmetric in $A,B$ but the right sides are not. The correct replacement is the Lie product formula (see below).
@@@ mnexp-the-derivative-of-the-exponential-of-ta.md
---
title: The derivative of the matrix exponential and the one-parameter group property
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-exp-log
level: l2
difficulty: 2
tags: matrix exponential, derivative, homomorphism
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$. Show that $t\mapsto e^{tA}$ is differentiable with $\frac d{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}$, and that it is a continuous group homomorphism $(\mathbb{R},+)\to GL_n(\mathbb{R})$.

## Hint

A power series in $t$ can be differentiated termwise inside its disc of convergence. For the homomorphism property, use the commuting case $e^{X+Y}=e^Xe^Y$.

## Solution

**Termwise differentiation.** We have $e^{tA}=\sum_k\frac{t^k}{k!}A^k$, a power series in the real variable $t$ with matrix coefficients. Its entries are real power series in $t$ with infinite radius of convergence (each entry is bounded by $\|A\|^k|t|^k/k!$ times a constant). A power series may be differentiated termwise on its interval of convergence, so
$$\frac d{dt}e^{tA}=\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{kt^{k-1}}{k!}A^k=A\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{t^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}A^{k-1}=Ae^{tA}.$$
(The matrix $A$ can be pulled out on the left or on the right: $Ae^{tA}=e^{tA}A$.)

**Homomorphism.** For $s,t\in\mathbb{R}$ the matrices $sA$ and $tA$ commute, so
$$e^{(s+t)A}=e^{sA}e^{tA}.$$
In particular $e^{tA}e^{-tA}=e^{0}=I$, so $e^{tA}$ is invertible with inverse $e^{-tA}$: the map takes values in $GL_n(\mathbb{R})$.

**Continuity.** It is differentiable, hence continuous (or: composition of the continuous maps $t\mapsto tA$ and $\exp$).

**Remark.** The matrix function $\Phi(t)=e^{tA}$ is the unique solution of the linear differential equation $\Phi'=A\Phi$, $\Phi(0)=I$: if $\Psi$ is another one, $\frac d{dt}\bigl(e^{-tA}\Psi(t)\bigr)=-Ae^{-tA}\Psi+e^{-tA}A\Psi=0$, so $e^{-tA}\Psi$ is constant $=I$. This uniqueness is used in the classification of one-parameter subgroups below.
@@@ mnexp-the-exponential-is-not-injective.md
---
title: The exponential is not injective: rotations as exponentials
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-exp-log
level: l2
difficulty: 2
tags: matrix exponential, rotation, kernel
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Let $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Show that $e^{\theta J}=R_\theta=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$ for all real $\theta$. Deduce that $e^{2\pi J}=I$ and that $\exp:M_2(\mathbb{R})\to GL_2(\mathbb{R})$ is not injective.

## Hint

Compute the powers of $J$: $J^2=-I$.

## Solution

**Powers of $J$.** $J^2=-I$, hence $J^3=-J$, $J^4=I$, and in general $J^{2k}=(-1)^kI$, $J^{2k+1}=(-1)^kJ$.

**Splitting the series.** Separating even and odd terms,
$$e^{\theta J}=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\theta^{2k}}{(2k)!}J^{2k}+\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\theta^{2k+1}}{(2k+1)!}J^{2k+1}=\Bigl(\sum_k\frac{(-1)^k\theta^{2k}}{(2k)!}\Bigr)I+\Bigl(\sum_k\frac{(-1)^k\theta^{2k+1}}{(2k+1)!}\Bigr)J.$$
The two scalar series are $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$, so
$$e^{\theta J}=\cos\theta\,I+\sin\theta\,J=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}=R_\theta.$$
(Rearranging the series into even and odd parts is allowed by absolute convergence.)

**Non-injectivity.** $e^{2\pi J}=R_{2\pi}=I=e^{0}$ but $2\pi J\ne0$. More generally $e^{(\theta+2\pi k)J}=e^{\theta J}$ for all integers $k$.

**Remark.** This is the matrix version of $e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$: the subalgebra $\{aI+bJ\}$ of $M_2(\mathbb{R})$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{C}$, with $J\leftrightarrow i$. Non-injectivity of $\exp$ on the real matrices is the same phenomenon as the multivaluedness of the complex logarithm.
@@@ mnexp-determinant-of-an-exponential.md
---
title: The determinant of an exponential: det exp(A) = exp(tr A)
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-exp-log
level: l3
difficulty: 3
tags: matrix exponential, determinant, trace, triangularisation
date: 2026-11-06
---

## Statement

Prove that for every $A\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$, $\det e^A=e^{\operatorname{tr}A}$. Deduce that $e^A\in GL_n^+(\mathbb{R})$ for every real matrix $A$.

## Hint

Over $\mathbb{C}$, every matrix is similar to an upper triangular matrix. Check how $\exp$ behaves under conjugation and on triangular matrices.

## Solution

**Idea.** Reduce to triangular matrices, where both sides can be computed on the diagonal.

**Step 1: conjugation.** For invertible $P$ and any $X$, $(PXP^{-1})^k=PX^kP^{-1}$, so
$$e^{PXP^{-1}}=Pe^XP^{-1}.$$
(Termwise, and $X\mapsto PXP^{-1}$ is linear and continuous.)

**Step 2: triangularisation.** Over $\mathbb{C}$ (Schur or Jordan form) there are an invertible $P\in GL_n(\mathbb{C})$ and an upper triangular $T$ with $A=PTP^{-1}$. The same series definition works in $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, and the identity of step 1 still holds. Hence $e^A=Pe^TP^{-1}$.

**Step 3: triangular matrices.** Let $T$ be upper triangular with diagonal entries $t_{11},\dots,t_{nn}$. Powers of $T$ are upper triangular and the diagonal of $T^k$ is $(t_{11}^k,\dots,t_{nn}^k)$. So $e^T$ is upper triangular with diagonal entries $\sum_kt_{ii}^k/k!=e^{t_{ii}}$.

**Step 4: conclusion.** The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries, so
$$\det e^A=\det(Pe^TP^{-1})=\det e^T=\prod_ie^{t_{ii}}=e^{\sum t_{ii}}=e^{\operatorname{tr}T}=e^{\operatorname{tr}A},$$
because the trace is invariant under conjugation.

**Consequence.** For real $A$, $e^A$ is real and $\det e^A=e^{\operatorname{tr}A}>0$. Hence $\exp(M_n(\mathbb{R}))\subset GL_n^+(\mathbb{R})$ and in particular $\exp(\mathfrak{sl}_n)\subset SL_n$.

**Check.** For $A=\theta J$ we have $\operatorname{tr}A=0$ and $\det R_\theta=1$. For $A=\operatorname{diag}(a,b)$, $\det e^A=e^{a+b}$.

**Remark.** An alternative proof: $f(t)=\det e^{tA}$ satisfies $f'(t)=\operatorname{tr}(A)f(t)$ (Jacobi's formula), so $f(t)=e^{t\operatorname{tr}A}$.
@@@ mnexp-the-exponential-of-skew-symmetric-matrices-is-onto-so-n.md
---
title: The exponential maps skew-symmetric matrices onto SO(n)
category: topology/topology-of-mnr/mn-exp-log
level: l3
difficulty: 3
tags: orthogonal group, skew-symmetric, normal form, connectedness
date: 2026-11-06
