For the triangle inequality $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$ it is enough to treat the case $x\ne z$, where the left side equals $1$. For (4), use $\varepsilon=\tfrac12$ in the definition of a Cauchy sequence.

## Solution

**Idea.** Distances only take the values $0$ and $1$, so "close" means "equal".

**1. Metric.** Positivity, symmetry and $d(x,y)=0\iff x=y$ are immediate. Triangle inequality: if $x=z$ the left side is $0$ and there is nothing to prove. If $x\ne z$ then $d(x,z)=1$, and $y$ cannot be equal to both $x$ and $z$; so at least one of $d(x,y),d(y,z)$ equals $1$, and the right side is at least $1$.

**2. Balls.** If $0<r\le1$ then $B(x,r)=\{y: d(x,y)<r\}=\{x\}$, because $d(x,y)=1\ge r$ for $y\ne x$. If $r>1$ then $B(x,r)=X$.

**3. Open and closed sets.** Let $A\subset X$. For $a\in A$ the ball $B(a,1)=\{a\}$ lies in $A$, so $A$ is open. The complement $X\setminus A$ is also a subset, hence open, so $A$ is closed.

**4. Sequences.** If $x_n\to\ell$, apply the definition with $\varepsilon=\tfrac12$: for $n\ge N$, $d(x_n,\ell)<\tfrac12$, i.e. $x_n=\ell$. So convergent sequences are exactly the sequences that are eventually constant. If $(x_n)$ is Cauchy, taking $\varepsilon=\tfrac12$ gives $N$ with $d(x_n,x_m)<\tfrac12$, i.e. $x_n=x_m$, for all $n,m\ge N$: the sequence is eventually constant. So every Cauchy sequence converges: $(X,d)$ is complete.

**Remark.** Every set carries this metric, so every set is a metric space. It is the extreme example where all subsets are open: a convergent sequence does not "approach" its limit, it reaches it. Compact subsets are exactly the finite ones (an open cover by singletons has a finite subcover only for finite sets).

@@@ mt-bs-002-uniform-and-integral-metrics-on-continuous-functions.md
---
title: Two metrics on $C([0,1])$
category: metric/mt-basics
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 2
tags: metric space, sup metric, integral metric, comparison of metrics
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

On $E=C([0,1],\mathbb{R})$ put
$$d_\infty(f,g)=\max_{t\in[0,1]}|f(t)-g(t)|,\qquad d_1(f,g)=\int_0^1|f(t)-g(t)|\,dt.$$

1. Prove that $d_\infty$ and $d_1$ are metrics on $E$.
2. Show that $d_1\le d_\infty$.
3. Show that there is no constant $C$ with $d_\infty\le C\,d_1$.
4. Deduce that a sequence converging for $d_\infty$ converges for $d_1$, but not conversely.

## Hint

For the definiteness of $d_1$ you need continuity: a continuous non-negative function with zero integral is zero. For (3), look at $f_n(t)=t^n$ and $g=0$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Uniform distance looks at the worst point, the integral distance looks at the average; a function can be large on a tiny set without having a large average.

**1. Metrics.** Symmetry and the triangle inequality follow from $|f-h|\le|f-g|+|g-h|$ pointwise: for the max, take the max of both sides and use $\max(a+b)\le\max a+\max b$; for $d_1$, integrate. Definiteness: $d_\infty(f,g)=0$ forces $f=g$ everywhere. If $d_1(f,g)=0$, the function $\varphi=|f-g|$ is continuous, non-negative, with $\int_0^1\varphi=0$. If $\varphi(t_0)>0$, then $\varphi>\varphi(t_0)/2$ on an interval around $t_0$ of positive length $\eta$ inside $[0,1]$, giving $\int\varphi\ge\eta\varphi(t_0)/2>0$, a contradiction. So $\varphi\equiv0$.

**2. Comparison.** $|f(t)-g(t)|\le d_\infty(f,g)$ for all $t$; integrating over $[0,1]$ gives $d_1(f,g)\le d_\infty(f,g)$.

**3. No reverse inequality.** Let $f_n(t)=t^n$ and $g=0$. Then $d_\infty(f_n,g)=1$ while $d_1(f_n,g)=\int_0^1t^n\,dt=\tfrac1{n+1}$. An inequality $1\le C/(n+1)$ for all $n$ is impossible.

**4. Convergence.** If $d_\infty(f_n,f)\to0$ then $d_1(f_n,f)\le d_\infty(f_n,f)\to0$. Conversely $f_n(t)=t^n$ satisfies $d_1(f_n,0)\to0$ but $d_\infty(f_n,0)=1$, so $f_n\not\to0$ uniformly.

**Remark.** The two metrics define different topologies on $E$: every $d_\infty$-open set is $d_1$-open? No, the converse inclusion is the one that holds: $d_1$-open sets are $d_\infty$-open (by $d_1\le d_\infty$) but not conversely. Also $(E,d_\infty)$ is complete while $(E,d_1)$ is not, which is why integral metrics usually lead to the larger space $L^1$.

@@@ mt-bs-003-the-french-railway-metric.md
---
title: The French railway metric on the plane
category: metric/mt-basics
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 3
tags: metric space, balls, SNCF metric, counterexamples
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Let $|\cdot|$ be the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb{R}^2$. For $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^2$ define
$$d(x,y)=\begin{cases}|x-y|&\text{if } x,y \text{ and } 0 \text{ lie on a common line},\\ |x|+|y|&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
(Every train goes through Paris, placed at the origin.)

1. Prove that $d$ is a metric.
2. Describe the open ball $B(a,r)$ for $a\ne0$, separately for $r\le|a|$ and $r>|a|$.
3. Show that the sequence $x_n=(1,\tfrac1n)$ does not converge to $(1,0)$ for $d$.

## Hint

Always $|x-y|\le d(x,y)\le|x|+|y|$. For the triangle inequality $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$ distinguish whether $x,z,0$ are collinear.

## Solution

**Idea.** To go from $x$ to $z$ you stay on your line if $z$ is on it, and otherwise you must pass through the origin.

**1. Metric.** Symmetry and $d(x,y)=0\iff x=y$ are clear (if $x\ne y$ then $d\ge|x-y|>0$). We prove $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. Write "$x\sim z$" when $x,z,0$ are collinear.

*Case A: $x\sim z$.* Then $d(x,z)=|x-z|$. Whatever $d(x,y)$ and $d(y,z)$ are, $d(x,y)\ge|x-y|$ and $d(y,z)\ge|y-z|$, so the Euclidean triangle inequality gives $d(x,z)=|x-z|\le|x-y|+|y-z|\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$.

*Case B: $x\not\sim z$.* Then $d(x,z)=|x|+|z|$ and both $x,z\ne0$. If $y=0$, then $d(x,0)+d(0,z)=|x|+|z|$: equality. If $y\ne0$, then $y$ cannot be collinear with $0$ and both $x$ and $z$ (otherwise $x,z$ would lie on the line $\mathbb{R}y$). Say $y\not\sim x$ (the other case is symmetric). Then $d(x,y)=|x|+|y|$ and $d(y,z)\ge|y-z|\ge\big||z|-|y|\big|$, so
$$d(x,y)+d(y,z)\ge|x|+|y|+\big||z|-|y|\big|\ge|x|+|z|=d(x,z).$$

**2. Balls.** Let $a\ne0$ and $L=\mathbb{R}a$. A point $y\notin L$ satisfies $d(a,y)=|a|+|y|$; a point $y\in L$ satisfies $d(a,y)=|a-y|$.

- If $r\le|a|$: for $y\notin L$, $d(a,y)\ge|a|\ge r$, so $y\notin B(a,r)$. Hence $B(a,r)=\{y\in L:|y-a|<r\}$, an open Euclidean segment of length $2r$ centred at $a$ which does not contain $0$.
- If $r>|a|$: $B(a,r)=\{y\in L:|y-a|<r\}\ \cup\ \{y\notin L: |y|<r-|a|\}$, a segment of $L$ (now containing $0$) together with the Euclidean disc of radius $r-|a|$ around the origin (minus $L$, but those points of $L$ are already in the segment).

**3. Non-convergence.** Put $a=(1,0)$, $x_n=(1,\tfrac1n)$. For every $n$, $x_n\notin\mathbb{R}a$, so $d(x_n,a)=|x_n|+|a|\ge2$. The sequence does not tend to $a$, although it does in the Euclidean sense.

**Remark.** For $d$, a point $a\ne0$ has arbitrarily small neighbourhoods contained in its own ray-line, so convergence to $a$ forces the sequence to lie eventually on that line. Convergence to $0$, however, coincides with Euclidean convergence: $B(0,r)$ is the Euclidean disc. The topology is therefore different from the Euclidean one, although the two metrics agree on each line through $0$.

@@@ mt-bs-004-the-arctan-metric-on-the-real-line.md
---
title: The arctan metric on $\mathbb{R}$
category: metric/mt-basics
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 4
tags: metric space, equivalent metrics, completeness, bounded metric
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

For $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$ let $\delta(x,y)=|\arctan x-\arctan y|$.

1. Prove that $\delta$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}$, and that it is bounded.
2. Describe the balls $B_\delta(0,r)$.
3. Show that $\delta$ and the usual metric $|x-y|$ define the same open sets.
4. Show that $(\mathbb{R},\delta)$ is not complete, whereas $(\mathbb{R},|\cdot|)$ is.

## Hint

A metric transported by an injective map is a metric: $\delta(x,y)=|\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)|$ with $\varphi=\arctan$ injective. For (3), use continuity of $\arctan$ and of $\tan$ on $(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2)$.

## Solution

**Idea.** $\arctan$ squeezes the line into the bounded interval $(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2)$ without changing the topology, but the squeezing changes which sequences are Cauchy.

**1. Metric.** Symmetry and the triangle inequality come from those of $|\cdot|$. Also $\delta(x,y)=0\Rightarrow\arctan x=\arctan y\Rightarrow x=y$ since $\arctan$ is injective. Boundedness: $\delta(x,y)<\pi$.

**2. Balls.** Since $\arctan$ is an increasing bijection $\mathbb{R}\to(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2)$: if $r\le\tfrac\pi2$, $B_\delta(0,r)=\{x:|\arctan x|<r\}=(-\tan r,\tan r)$ for $r<\tfrac\pi2$, and it equals $\mathbb{R}$ for $r\ge\tfrac\pi2$. Hence for $r\ge\tfrac\pi2$ the ball is the whole line, although we may use the value $r=\tfrac\pi2$ without trouble.

**3. Same topology.** Let $a\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\varepsilon>0$.

- By continuity of $\arctan$ at $a$ there is $\eta>0$ with $|x-a|<\eta\Rightarrow\delta(x,a)<\varepsilon$.
- By continuity of $\tan$ at $\arctan a\in(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2)$ there is $\eta'>0$ such that $|\theta-\arctan a|<\eta'$ and $\theta\in(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2)$ give $|\tan\theta-a|<\varepsilon$. Taking $\theta=\arctan x$: $\delta(x,a)<\eta'\Rightarrow|x-a|<\varepsilon$.

So every $|\cdot|$-ball around $a$ contains a $\delta$-ball around $a$ and vice versa. Hence a set is open for one metric iff it is open for the other.

**4. Completeness.** Let $x_n=n$. Since $\arctan n\to\tfrac\pi2$, the sequence $(\arctan n)$ is Cauchy in $\mathbb{R}$, i.e. $(x_n)$ is $\delta$-Cauchy. If $x_n\to\ell$ for $\delta$, then $\arctan n\to\arctan\ell<\tfrac\pi2$, contradicting $\arctan n\to\tfrac\pi2$. So $(\mathbb{R},\delta)$ is not complete. Of course $(\mathbb{R},|\cdot|)$ is complete.

**Remark.** Completeness is *not* a topological property: two metrics with the same open sets can differ on it. Completeness is preserved by uniformly equivalent metrics, which $\delta$ and $|\cdot|$ are not.

@@@ mt-bs-005-truncating-and-compressing-a-metric.md
---
title: Truncated and compressed metrics
category: metric/mt-basics
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 5
tags: metric space, bounded metric, equivalent metrics, open sets
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space. Define
$$e(x,y)=\min(1,d(x,y)),\qquad d'(x,y)=\frac{d(x,y)}{1+d(x,y)}.$$

1. Prove that $e$ and $d'$ are metrics on $X$, both bounded by $1$.
2. Show that $d$, $e$, $d'$ define the same open sets.
3. Show that a sequence is Cauchy for $d$ iff it is Cauchy for $e$ iff it is Cauchy for $d'$.

## Hint

For $e$: if $d(x,z)\ge1$ show $e(x,y)+e(y,z)\ge1$. For $d'$ use $\frac{a}{1+a}\le\frac{b+c}{1+b+c}$ when $a\le b+c$. For (2), small balls coincide up to a change of radius.

## Solution

**Idea.** Both new metrics are the same as $d$ at small scale; they only change what happens at distances of order $1$ or more.

**1. Metrics.** Definiteness and symmetry are clear.

*Triangle inequality for $e$.* Let $x,y,z\in X$. If $e(x,y)=1$ or $e(y,z)=1$, then $e(x,y)+e(y,z)\ge1\ge e(x,z)$. Otherwise $d(x,y)<1$ and $d(y,z)<1$, so $e(x,y)+e(y,z)=d(x,y)+d(y,z)\ge d(x,z)\ge e(x,z)$.

*Triangle inequality for $d'$.* If $a=d(x,z)$, $b=d(x,y)$, $c=d(y,z)$ then $a\le b+c$. Since $t\mapsto\frac t{1+t}$ is increasing,
$$d'(x,z)\le\frac{b+c}{1+b+c}=\frac b{1+b+c}+\frac c{1+b+c}\le\frac b{1+b}+\frac c{1+c}=d'(x,y)+d'(y,z).$$
Both are bounded by $1$.

**2. Open sets.** For $0<r<1$:
$$B_e(x,r)=B_d(x,r),\qquad B_{d'}(x,r)=B_d\!\left(x,\tfrac r{1-r}\right),$$
because $\frac t{1+t}<r\iff t<\frac r{1-r}$. So every ball of small radius for one metric is a ball for another, with a different radius. If $U$ is $d$-open and $x\in U$, with $B_d(x,\rho)\subset U$, then $B_e(x,\min(\rho,\tfrac12))\subset U$ and $B_{d'}(x,\tfrac\rho{1+\rho})\subset U$. Conversely, a $d'$-ball $B_{d'}(x,r)$ with $r<1$ is a $d$-ball. Hence the three metrics have the same open sets.

**3. Cauchy sequences.** Given $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, $e(x,y)<\varepsilon\iff d(x,y)<\varepsilon$ and $d'(x,y)<\varepsilon\iff d(x,y)<\frac\varepsilon{1-\varepsilon}$. Since "for all $\varepsilon>0$" can be restricted to small $\varepsilon$, the Cauchy conditions are equivalent.

**Remark.** Every metric is thus equivalent to a bounded one, so boundedness is not a topological property. The metric $e$ also shows that completeness is retained by this change; compare with the arctan metric, where completeness is lost.

@@@ mt-bs-006-composing-a-metric-with-a-subadditive-function.md
---
title: Composing a metric with a subadditive function
category: metric/mt-basics
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 6
tags: metric space, subadditive, concave functions, constructing metrics
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Let $f:[0,+\infty)\to[0,+\infty)$ be non-decreasing, with $f(0)=0$, $f(t)>0$ for $t>0$ and subadditive: $f(s+t)\le f(s)+f(t)$.

1. Show that if $d$ is a metric on $X$, then $f\circ d$ is a metric on $X$.
2. Show that a concave function $f$ with $f(0)=0$ (and $f>0$ on $(0,\infty)$) is subadditive; deduce that $\sqrt d$, $d^\alpha$ for $0<\alpha\le1$ and $\ln(1+d)$ are metrics.
3. Show that $f(t)=t^2$ is not suitable: $|x-y|^2$ is not a metric on $\mathbb{R}$.

## Hint

For (1), use monotonicity then subadditivity. For (2), write $s=\frac s{s+t}(s+t)+\frac t{s+t}\cdot0$.

## Solution

**Idea.** The triangle inequality for $f\circ d$ is $f(d(x,z))\le f(d(x,y))+f(d(y,z))$. Monotonicity transports $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$ through $f$, and subadditivity splits the sum.

**1.** Definiteness: $f(d(x,y))=0\iff d(x,y)=0\iff x=y$, using $f(t)>0$ for $t>0$ and $f(0)=0$. Symmetry is clear. Triangle:
$$f(d(x,z))\le f\big(d(x,y)+d(y,z)\big)\le f(d(x,y))+f(d(y,z)).$$

**2. Concave implies subadditive.** Let $s,t>0$. By concavity and $f(0)=0$,
$$f(s)=f\Big(\tfrac s{s+t}(s+t)+\tfrac t{s+t}\cdot0\Big)\ge\tfrac s{s+t}f(s+t),\qquad f(t)\ge\tfrac t{s+t}f(s+t).$$
Adding gives $f(s)+f(t)\ge f(s+t)$ (the case $s=0$ or $t=0$ is trivial). A concave function with $f(0)=0$ and $f>0$ on $(0,\infty)$ is automatically non-decreasing (concave and positive on $(0,\infty)$ with $f(0)=0$ cannot decrease: if $f(a)>f(b)$ with $a<b$, concavity would force $f$ to become negative further on). Hence $\sqrt t$, $t^\alpha$ ($0<\alpha\le1$) and $\ln(1+t)$ (all concave, vanishing at $0$, positive and increasing) are admissible, and give metrics $\sqrt d$, $d^\alpha$, $\ln(1+d)$. Also $\min(1,t)$ and $\frac t{1+t}$ are admissible.

**3. Failure for $t^2$.** On $\mathbb{R}$ with $x=0,y=1,z=2$: $|x-z|^2=4>1+1=|x-y|^2+|y-z|^2$. The function $t^2$ is not subadditive: $(1+1)^2=4>2$.

**Remark.** The snowflake metrics $d^\alpha$, $0<\alpha<1$, define the same topology as $d$ but are not Lipschitz equivalent to it; for $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $\alpha<1$ they give a space where balls are "fatter" than expected (this is the beginning of fractal dimension).

@@@ mt-bs-007-ultrametric-spaces-isosceles-triangles-and-balls.md
---
title: Ultrametric spaces
category: metric/mt-basics
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 7
tags: ultrametric, balls, isosceles triangles, Cauchy sequences
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

A metric $d$ on $X$ is an **ultrametric** if $d(x,z)\le\max\big(d(x,y),d(y,z)\big)$ for all $x,y,z$.

1. Prove: if $d(x,y)\ne d(y,z)$ then $d(x,z)=\max(d(x,y),d(y,z))$. Deduce that every triangle is isosceles, with the two largest sides equal.
2. Prove: if $y\in B(x,r)$ then $B(y,r)=B(x,r)$ (every point of a ball is a centre).
3. Prove that two open balls are either disjoint or nested.
4. Prove that every open ball is also closed.
5. Prove that $(x_n)$ is Cauchy iff $d(x_n,x_{n+1})\to0$.

## Hint

For (1) say $d(x,y)<d(y,z)$ and apply the ultrametric inequality twice. For (4) show that the complement is open, using (2). For (5) show $d(x_n,x_m)\le\max_{n\le k<m}d(x_k,x_{k+1})$ by induction.

## Solution

**Idea.** In an ultrametric all the geometry of the Euclidean plane is replaced by "the longest side wins", which makes balls behave like clopen blocks.

**1.** Suppose $d(x,y)<d(y,z)$. Then $d(x,z)\le\max(d(x,y),d(y,z))=d(y,z)$. Also $d(y,z)\le\max(d(y,x),d(x,z))$. Since $d(y,x)<d(y,z)$, the maximum must be $d(x,z)$, and $d(y,z)\le d(x,z)$. Hence $d(x,z)=d(y,z)=\max$. In a triangle the three sides cannot be pairwise distinct, and if two are different the two largest are equal.

**2.** Let $y\in B(x,r)$. If $z\in B(y,r)$ then $d(x,z)\le\max(d(x,y),d(y,z))<r$, so $z\in B(x,r)$. By symmetry ($x\in B(y,r)$ since $d(y,x)<r$) the reverse inclusion holds.

**3.** Suppose $B(a,r)\cap B(b,s)\ne\emptyset$, containing $y$. By (2), $B(a,r)=B(y,r)$ and $B(b,s)=B(y,s)$, and two balls with the same centre are nested.

**4.** Let $y\notin B(x,r)$. We claim $B(y,r)\cap B(x,r)=\emptyset$. If $z$ belonged to both, (2) would give $B(x,r)=B(z,r)=B(y,r)\ni y$, a contradiction. So the complement is open and the ball is closed.

**5.** ($\Rightarrow$) is clear. ($\Leftarrow$) By induction, for $n<m$: $d(x_n,x_m)\le\max(d(x_n,x_{m-1}),d(x_{m-1},x_m))\le\max_{n\le k<m}d(x_k,x_{k+1})$. Given $\varepsilon$, choose $N$ with $d(x_k,x_{k+1})<\varepsilon$ for $k\ge N$; then $d(x_n,x_m)<\varepsilon$ for $m>n\ge N$.

**Remark.** Statement (5) is false in $\mathbb{R}$: $x_n=\sum_{k\le n}\frac1k$ has $|x_{n+1}-x_n|\to0$ but diverges. In an ultrametric world the condition "terms tend to $0$" alone ensures convergence of series, in complete spaces such as the $p$-adic numbers.

@@@ mt-bs-008-the-2-adic-distance-on-the-integers.md
---
title: The 2-adic distance on the integers
category: metric/mt-basics
level: m1
difficulty: 3
order: 8
tags: ultrametric, 2-adic, convergence, geometric series
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

For $n\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$ let $v(n)$ be the exponent of $2$ in $n$ (so $v(12)=2$). Define 
$$ d(m,n)=2^{-v(m-n)} \, \text{if } m\ne n \, \text{ and} \, d(m,m)=0. $$

1. Prove that $d$ is an ultrametric on $\mathbb{Z}$.
2. Describe the ball $B(0,2^{-k})$ for $k\ge0$.
3. Show that $2^k\to0$ and $n!\to0$ for $d$.
4. Show that $s_k=1+2+4+\dots+2^k$ converges to $-1$ for $d$. In what sense is 
$$ 1+2+4+\dots=-1 $$ 
true?

## Hint

Use $v(a+b)\ge\min(v(a),v(b))$ (when $a,b,a+b\ne0$). For (2), $d(n,0)<2^{-k}\iff v(n)>k$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Here two integers are close when their difference is divisible by a high power of $2$.

**1.** Definiteness and symmetry hold ($v(-n)=v(n)$). For distinct $m,n,p$ we have $m-p=(m-n)+(n-p)$. Write $a=m-n=2^{i}a'$ and $b=n-p=2^{j}b'$ with $a',b'$ odd, $i\le j$: then $a+b=2^i(a'+2^{j-i}b')$, so $2^i\mid m-p$, i.e. $v(m-p)\ge\min(v(m-n),v(n-p))$. (If $m-p=0$ the inequality is trivial.) Hence $d(m,p)\le\max(d(m,n),d(n,p))$. If two of the points coincide the inequality is also trivial.

**2.** $d(n,0)<2^{-k}\iff2^{-v(n)}<2^{-k}\iff v(n)>k\iff2^{k+1}\mid n$. So $B(0,2^{-k})=2^{k+1}\mathbb{Z}$. By the ultrametric property these balls are also closed subgroups.

**3.** $d(2^k,0)=2^{-k}\to0$. For $n\ge1$, $v(n!)\ge\lfloor n/2\rfloor\to\infty$, so $d(n!,0)\le2^{-\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\to0$.

**4.** $s_k=2^{k+1}-1$, hence $s_k-(-1)=2^{k+1}$ and $d(s_k,-1)=2^{-(k+1)}\to0$. So the geometric series $\sum2^k$ converges to $-1$ in this metric. This agrees with the formula $\frac1{1-2}=-1$, which has no meaning in $\mathbb{R}$ but is perfectly meaningful 2-adically.

**Remark.** By Problem 7(5), a series $\sum a_k$ in this ultrametric converges as soon as $d(a_k,0)\to0$, in a complete extension of $\mathbb{Z}$ (the 2-adic integers $\mathbb{Z}_2$). The space $(\mathbb{Z},d)$ itself is not complete: for instance the partial sums of $\sum 2^{k^2}$... they have no integer limit.

@@@ mt-bs-009-balls-and-diameters.md
---
title: Diameter of balls and of closures
category: metric/mt-basics
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 9
tags: diameter, bounded sets, balls, closure
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

In a metric space $(X,d)$ the diameter of a non-empty set $A$ is $\operatorname{diam}A=\sup\{d(x,y):x,y\in A\}\in[0,+\infty]$; $A$ is *bounded* if its diameter is finite.

1. Show that $\operatorname{diam}B(a,r)\le2r$, and give examples where the inequality is strict and where it is an equality which is not attained.
2. Show that $A$ is bounded iff $A$ is contained in some ball.
3. Show that $\operatorname{diam}A=\operatorname{diam}\overline A$.
4. Show that a finite union of bounded sets is bounded.

## Hint

For (3), take sequences in $A$ converging to two points of the closure and use the triangle inequality twice. For (4), the distance between a point of $A$ and a point of $B$ is at most $\operatorname{diam}A+d(a_0,b_0)+\operatorname{diam}B$.

## Solution

**Idea.** The triangle inequality lets us pass from a point of the ball to its centre and back.

**1.** For $x,y\in B(a,r)$: $d(x,y)\le d(x,a)+d(a,y)<2r$. So $\operatorname{diam}B(a,r)\le2r$. Strict case: in the discrete metric, $B(a,1)=\{a\}$ has diameter $0<2$. Non-attained case: in $\mathbb{R}$, $B(0,1)=(-1,1)$ has diameter $2$, but no pair $x,y$ in the ball has $|x-y|=2$.

**2.** If $A\subset B(a,r)$, $A$ is bounded by (1). Conversely, if $\operatorname{diam}A=D<\infty$ and $a\in A$ (assume $A\ne\emptyset$), then for all $x\in A$, $d(a,x)\le D<D+1$, so $A\subset B(a,D+1)$.

**3.** Since $A\subset\overline A$, $\operatorname{diam}A\le\operatorname{diam}\overline A$. Conversely let $x,y\in\overline A$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $x',y'\in A$ with $d(x,x')<\varepsilon$ and $d(y,y')<\varepsilon$. Then
$$d(x,y)\le d(x,x')+d(x',y')+d(y',y)<2\varepsilon+\operatorname{diam}A.$$
Letting $\varepsilon\to0$ and taking the sup over $x,y$ gives $\operatorname{diam}\overline A\le\operatorname{diam}A$.

**4.** Let $A,B$ be bounded, non-empty, fix $a_0\in A$, $b_0\in B$. For $a\in A,b\in B$: $d(a,b)\le d(a,a_0)+d(a_0,b_0)+d(b_0,b)\le\operatorname{diam}A+d(a_0,b_0)+\operatorname{diam}B$. Hence $\operatorname{diam}(A\cup B)\le\max(\operatorname{diam}A,\operatorname{diam}B,\operatorname{diam}A+d(a_0,b_0)+\operatorname{diam}B)<\infty$. Induction gives finite unions.

**Remark.** Boundedness depends on the metric, not on the topology: $\mathbb{R}$ is unbounded for $|\cdot|$ and bounded for $\min(1,|x-y|)$. In a normed space with Euclidean norm one has $\operatorname{diam}B(a,r)=2r$ exactly.

@@@ mt-bs-010-two-metrics-with-the-same-open-sets.md
---
title: Same open sets, different Cauchy sequences
category: metric/mt-basics
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 10
tags: equivalent metrics, uniform equivalence, Cauchy sequences, Lipschitz equivalence
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

On $X=(0,+\infty)$ consider $d_1(x,y)=|x-y|$ and $d_2(x,y)=\left|\frac1x-\frac1y\right|$.

1. Show that $d_2$ is a metric and that $d_1,d_2$ define the same open sets.
2. Show that there are no constants $c,C>0$ with $c\,d_1\le d_2\le C\,d_1$.
3. Give a sequence which is $d_1$-Cauchy but not $d_2$-Cauchy, and one which is $d_2$-Cauchy but not $d_1$-Cauchy.
4. Is $(X,d_1)$ complete? Is $(X,d_2)$?

## Hint

$d_2$ comes from the injective map $x\mapsto1/x$. For (2) compare at points $\frac1n$ and $\frac2n$, and at points $n$ and $n+1$.

## Solution

**Idea.** The map $x\mapsto1/x$ is a homeomorphism of $(0,\infty)$ which stretches the neighbourhood of $0$ and compresses the neighbourhood of infinity.

**1.** $d_2(x,y)=|\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)|$ with $\varphi(x)=1/x$ injective, so $d_2$ is a metric. Both $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}=\varphi$ are continuous on $(0,\infty)$. As in the arctan problem, continuity of $\varphi$ at $a$ gives, for each $\varepsilon$, a $\delta$ with $|x-a|<\delta\Rightarrow d_2(x,a)<\varepsilon$, and continuity of $\varphi^{-1}=\varphi$ gives the converse. So the open sets coincide.

**2.** $d_2(x,y)=\frac{|x-y|}{xy}$. With $x=\frac1n,y=\frac2n$: $d_2/d_1=n^2/2$ is unbounded, so no $C$. With $x=n,y=n+1$: $d_2/d_1=\frac1{n(n+1)}\to0$, so no $c>0$.

**3.** $x_n=\frac1n$: $d_1(x_n,x_m)\to0$, so it is $d_1$-Cauchy. But $d_2(x_n,x_m)=|n-m|\ge1$, not Cauchy. $y_n=n$: $d_2(y_n,y_m)=|\frac1n-\frac1m|\to0$, $d_2$-Cauchy; $d_1(y_n,y_m)=|n-m|$, not $d_1$-Cauchy.

**4.** Neither is complete. The $d_1$-Cauchy sequence $\frac1n$ has no limit in $(0,\infty)$ (the only candidate is $0$). The $d_2$-Cauchy sequence $n$ has no limit either: a limit $\ell$ would satisfy $\frac1n\to\frac1\ell>0$.

**Remark.** The failure of (2) shows that these metrics are topologically equivalent but not uniformly equivalent. In fact the metric completion differs: adding the point $0$ completes $d_1$, adding a point "at infinity" completes $d_2$.

@@@ mt-bs-011-product-metrics.md
---
title: Metrics on a product of two metric spaces
category: metric/mt-basics
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 11
tags: product metric, equivalent metrics, convergence, balls
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces. On $X\times Y$ put, for $p=(x,y)$, $p'=(x',y')$,
$$d_\infty(p,p')=\max(d_X(x,x'),d_Y(y,y')),\quad d_1(p,p')=d_X(x,x')+d_Y(y,y'),$$
$$d_2(p,p')=\sqrt{d_X(x,x')^2+d_Y(y,y')^2}.$$

1. Prove that $d_\infty,d_1,d_2$ are metrics.
2. Prove $d_\infty\le d_2\le d_1\le2d_\infty$.
3. Describe the $d_\infty$-ball $B((x,y),r)$ and deduce that a product of open sets is open.
4. Show that $(x_n,y_n)\to(x,y)$ iff $x_n\to x$ and $y_n\to y$.

## Hint

The triangle inequality for $d_2$ comes from the Euclidean triangle inequality in $\mathbb{R}^2$ applied to the vectors of distances $(d_X(x,x'),d_Y(y,y'))$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Each $d$ is the Euclidean-type norm of the vector of coordinate distances; the three norms on $\mathbb{R}^2$ are equivalent.

**1.** Definiteness and symmetry are clear. For the triangle inequality, put $u=(d_X(x,x''),d_Y(y,y''))$, $v=(d_X(x,x'),d_Y(y,y'))$, $w=(d_X(x',x''),d_Y(y',y''))$. By the triangle inequalities in $X$ and $Y$, $0\le u\le v+w$ coordinatewise. Each norm $N\in\{\|\cdot\|_\infty,\|\cdot\|_1,\|\cdot\|_2\}$ is monotone on vectors with non-negative entries, so $N(u)\le N(v+w)\le N(v)+N(w)$, which is the triangle inequality for $d_\infty,d_1,d_2$.

**2.** With $a,b\ge0$: $\max(a,b)\le\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\le a+b\le2\max(a,b)$ (the middle one by squaring: $a^2+b^2\le a^2+2ab+b^2$).

**3.** $B_\infty((x,y),r)=B_X(x,r)\times B_Y(y,r)$. If $U\subset X$ and $V\subset Y$ are open and $(x,y)\in U\times V$, pick $r_1,r_2$ with $B(x,r_1)\subset U$, $B(y,r_2)\subset V$ and $r=\min(r_1,r_2)$: then $B_\infty((x,y),r)\subset U\times V$. So $U\times V$ is open for $d_\infty$, hence for $d_1,d_2$ by (2).

**4.** By (2), the three metrics have the same convergent sequences. For $d_\infty$: $d_\infty\big((x_n,y_n),(x,y)\big)\to0$ iff both $d_X(x_n,x)\to0$ and $d_Y(y_n,y)\to0$.

**Remark.** In particular $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the Euclidean metric is the product of two copies of $\mathbb{R}$, and a product of complete spaces is complete.

@@@ mt-bs-012-a-metric-on-the-space-of-all-real-sequences.md
---
title: A metric on the space of all real sequences
category: metric/mt-basics
level: m1
difficulty: 3
order: 12
tags: infinite product, metric space, coordinatewise convergence, bounded metric
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Let $E=\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$ be the set of all real sequences $x=(x_n)_{n\ge1}$ and define
$$d(x,y)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^{-n}\min\big(1,|x_n-y_n|\big).$$

1. Prove that $d$ is well defined and is a metric, with $d\le1$.
2. Prove that $x^{(k)}\to x$ for $d$ iff $x^{(k)}_n\to x_n$ for every $n$ (coordinatewise convergence).
3. Is $(E,d)$ equivalent to a norm-induced metric $\|x-y\|_\infty$? (The sup norm is not finite on $E$.) Show that the sequence $e_k=(0,\dots,0,1,0,\dots)$ does not converge to $0$ for the sup-distance of $\ell^\infty$ but does converge to $0$ for $d$.

## Hint

For (2, $\Leftarrow$): choose $N$ with $2^{-N}<\varepsilon/2$ so that the tail of the series is small, then use the finite number of coordinates $n\le N$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Weights $2^{-n}$ make the first coordinates count much more than the later ones, and truncating by $\min(1,\cdot)$ keeps the series bounded.

**1.** Each term is between $0$ and $2^{-n}$, so the series converges with $d\le\sum2^{-n}=1$. Symmetry is clear. $d(x,y)=0$ forces all $\min(1,|x_n-y_n|)=0$, so $x=y$. Triangle: by Problem 5, $e_n(s,t)=\min(1,|s-t|)$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}$, so $e_n(x_n,z_n)\le e_n(x_n,y_n)+e_n(y_n,z_n)$. Multiply by $2^{-n}$ and sum.

**2.** ($\Rightarrow$) For each $n$: $2^{-n}\min(1,|x^{(k)}_n-x_n|)\le d(x^{(k)},x)\to0$, so $\min(1,|x^{(k)}_n-x_n|)\to0$, hence $|x^{(k)}_n-x_n|\to0$.

($\Leftarrow$) Let $\varepsilon>0$ and $N$ with $2^{-N}<\varepsilon/2$. Then
$$d(x^{(k)},x)\le\sum_{n\le N}2^{-n}\min(1,|x^{(k)}_n-x_n|)+\sum_{n>N}2^{-n}.$$
The second sum is $2^{-N}<\varepsilon/2$. The first is a finite sum of terms tending to $0$, so it is $<\varepsilon/2$ for $k$ large. Hence $d(x^{(k)},x)<\varepsilon$.

**3.** The vector $e_k$ has $\sup|e_k-0|=1$ for all $k$, so it does not tend to $0$ in $\ell^\infty$. But $e_k$ has coordinatewise limit $0$ (the coordinate $n$ vanishes as soon as $k>n$), so $e_k\to0$ for $d$; directly, $d(e_k,0)=2^{-k}$.

**Remark.** This metric defines the topology of coordinatewise (product) convergence. It makes $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$ a complete metric space and shows that a countable product of metric spaces is metrizable.

@@@ mt-bs-013-subspaces-and-relative-open-sets.md
---
title: Open sets of a subspace
category: metric/mt-basics
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 13
tags: subspace, relative topology, open sets, discrete subsets
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and $A\subset X$, with the restricted metric.

1. Show that the ball of $A$ is $B_A(a,r)=B_X(a,r)\cap A$.
2. Prove: $U\subset A$ is open in $A$ iff $U=V\cap A$ for some open $V\subset X$.
3. Application. Is $[0,1)$ open in $[0,1]$? In $\mathbb{R}$? Is $\{0\}\cup\{\frac1n:n\ge1\}$ discrete as a subspace of $\mathbb{R}$? Is $\{\frac1n:n\ge1\}$?
4. Show that if $A$ is open in $X$, then $U\subset A$ is open in $A$ iff it is open in $X$.

## Hint

For (2, $\Rightarrow$) take $V=\bigcup_{a\in U}B_X(a,r_a)$ where $B_A(a,r_a)\subset U$.

## Solution

**Idea.** An open set of the subspace is the trace of an open set of the ambient space.

**1.** For $a\in A$: $B_A(a,r)=\{y\in A:d(a,y)<r\}=B_X(a,r)\cap A$.

**2.** ($\Leftarrow$) Let $U=V\cap A$ with $V$ open, and $a\in U$. There is $r$ with $B_X(a,r)\subset V$, so $B_A(a,r)=B_X(a,r)\cap A\subset V\cap A=U$.

($\Rightarrow$) Let $U$ be open in $A$. For $a\in U$ choose $r_a$ with $B_A(a,r_a)\subset U$, and set $V=\bigcup_{a\in U}B_X(a,r_a)$, open in $X$. Then $V\cap A=\bigcup_a(B_X(a,r_a)\cap A)=\bigcup_aB_A(a,r_a)\subset U$, and $U\subset V\cap A$ since $a\in B_X(a,r_a)$. So $U=V\cap A$.

**3.** $[0,1)=(-1,1)\cap[0,1]$ is open in $[0,1]$. It is not open in $\mathbb{R}$ (no ball around $0$ is contained in it). The set $S=\{\frac1n\}$ is discrete: $\{\frac1n\}=S\cap(\frac1{n+1},\frac1{n-1})$ (with the convention $\frac10=\infty$) is open in $S$, since the interval contains no other point of $S$. The set $\{0\}\cup S$ is not discrete: any interval around $0$ contains points $\frac1n$, so $\{0\}$ is not open.

**4.** If $U$ is open in $X$ then $U=U\cap A$ is open in $A$. Conversely, if $U=V\cap A$ with $V$ open and $A$ open, then $U$ is an intersection of two open sets of $X$, hence open.

**Remark.** "Open" is only meaningful relative to a space. $[0,1)$ is open in $[0,1]$ and not in $\mathbb{R}$; the same holds for $\{0\}$ and $\mathbb{Z}$ in $\mathbb{Z}\subset\mathbb{R}$: every singleton $\{n\}=(n-\tfrac12,n+\tfrac12)\cap\mathbb{Z}$ is open in $\mathbb{Z}$, which makes $\mathbb{Z}$ a discrete subspace.

@@@ mt-bs-014-the-distance-to-a-set.md
---
title: The distance function to a set
category: metric/mt-basics
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 14
tags: distance to a set, Lipschitz, closure, separation of closed sets
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and $A\subset X$ non-empty. Put $d(x,A)=\inf_{a\in A}d(x,a)$.

1. Show that $|d(x,A)-d(y,A)|\le d(x,y)$ for all $x,y$. Conclude that $x\mapsto d(x,A)$ is continuous.
2. Show that $d(x,A)=0\iff x\in\overline A$. Deduce that if $A$ is closed, $A=\{x:d(x,A)=0\}$.
3. Let $A,B$ be non-empty disjoint closed sets. Prove that $f(x)=\frac{d(x,A)}{d(x,A)+d(x,B)}$ is well defined and continuous, $f=0$ on $A$ and $f=1$ on $B$. Deduce that $A,B$ have disjoint open neighbourhoods.
4. Show by an example that $d(A,B)=\inf\{d(a,b)\}$ may vanish for disjoint closed sets.

## Hint

(1) For all $a\in A$: $d(x,A)\le d(x,a)\le d(x,y)+d(y,a)$; then take the inf over $a$. (2) Use sequences in $A$ whose distance to $x$ tends to $d(x,A)$.

## Solution

**Idea.** $d(\cdot,A)$ is a continuous function which detects $A$; it turns topological questions into questions about real-valued functions.

**1.** For $a\in A$: $d(x,A)\le d(x,a)\le d(x,y)+d(y,a)$. Taking the infimum over $a\in A$ gives $d(x,A)\le d(x,y)+d(y,A)$. By symmetry, $|d(x,A)-d(y,A)|\le d(x,y)$: the function is $1$-Lipschitz, hence continuous.

**2.** If $x\in\overline A$ there are $a_n\in A$ with $a_n\to x$ so $d(x,A)\le d(x,a_n)\to0$. Conversely if $d(x,A)=0$, for each $n$ there is $a_n\in A$ with $d(x,a_n)<\frac1n$, so $a_n\to x$ and $x\in\overline A$. If $A$ is closed, $\overline A=A$.

**3.** If $d(x,A)+d(x,B)=0$ then $x\in A\cap B$ by (2), impossible since $A\cap B=\emptyset$. So the denominator never vanishes and $f$ is continuous as a quotient of continuous functions. On $A$, $d(x,A)=0$ so $f=0$; on $B$, $d(x,B)=0$ so $f=1$. The sets $\{f<\frac12\}\supset A$ and $\{f>\frac12\}\supset B$ are open (preimages of open sets) and disjoint.

**4.** In $\mathbb{R}^2$ let $A=\{(x,0)\}$ and $B=\{(x,\frac1x):x>0\}$. Both are closed and disjoint, but $d(A,B)=0$ since $d((x,0),(x,\frac1x))=\frac1x\to0$. (In a compact space such a pair has positive distance.)

**Remark.** The result in (3) says that metric spaces are *normal*. The same function gives, for a closed set $A$, a continuous function whose zero set is exactly $A$.

@@@ mt-bs-015-isometries-of-the-real-line.md
---
title: Isometries of the real line
category: metric/mt-basics
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 15
tags: isometry, real line, rigidity
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

A map $f:X\to Y$ between metric spaces is an **isometry** if $d_Y(f(x),f(y))=d_X(x,y)$ for all $x,y$.

1. Show that an isometry is injective and continuous, and that the composition of isometries is an isometry.
2. Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be an isometry for $|\cdot|$. Prove that $f(x)=x+b$ or $f(x)=-x+b$ for some $b\in\mathbb{R}$. In particular $f$ is onto.
3. Show that the map $x\mapsto(x,0)$ from $\mathbb{R}$ to $(\mathbb{R}^2,\|\cdot\|_\infty)$ is an isometry which is not onto.

## Hint

Subtract $f(0)$ and reduce to the case $f(0)=0$, $f(1)=1$. Then $f(x)$ must be at distance $|x|$ from $0$ and $|x-1|$ from $1$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Knowing the images of the two points $0$ and $1$ determines the image of every point.

**1.** If $f(x)=f(y)$ then $d(x,y)=d(f(x),f(y))=0$, so $x=y$. Isometries are $1$-Lipschitz, hence continuous. Composition: $d(g(f(x)),g(f(y)))=d(f(x),f(y))=d(x,y)$.

**2.** Put $g(x)=f(x)-f(0)$, an isometry with $g(0)=0$. Then $|g(x)|=|x|$ for all $x$; so $g(1)=\pm1$. Let $\varepsilon=g(1)\in\{\pm1\}$ and $h=\varepsilon g$: $h$ is an isometry with $h(0)=0,h(1)=1$. For $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $|h(x)|=|x|$ gives $h(x)=\pm x$, and $|h(x)-1|=|x-1|$. If $h(x)=-x$, then $|x+1|=|x-1|$, which forces $x=0$ and $h(0)=0=x$ anyway. So $h(x)=x$ for all $x$. Hence $g(x)=\varepsilon x$ and $f(x)=\varepsilon x+f(0)$.

**3.** $\|(x,0)-(y,0)\|_\infty=|x-y|$: isometry. The point $(0,1)$ is not in the image.

**Remark.** The isometry group of $\mathbb{R}$ is thus generated by translations and the reflection $x\mapsto-x$. In general an isometry need not be onto (3), but a surjective isometry of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with Euclidean metric is always an affine map (next problem).

@@@ mt-bs-016-euclidean-isometries-are-affine.md
---
title: Isometries of Euclidean space are affine
category: metric/mt-basics
level: m1
difficulty: 4
order: 16
tags: isometry, Euclidean space, inner product, polarization
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfy $\|f(x)-f(y)\|=\|x-y\|$ for all $x,y$ (Euclidean norm), and $f(0)=0$.

1. Show that $\|f(x)\|=\|x\|$ and $\langle f(x),f(y)\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$ for all $x,y$.
2. Show that $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ and $f(\lambda x)=\lambda f(x)$. Conclude that $f$ is linear and orthogonal.
3. Deduce that every isometry of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is of the form $x\mapsto Ux+b$ with $U$ orthogonal.

## Hint

To prove $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$, show that $\|f(x+y)-f(x)-f(y)\|^2=0$ by expanding the square and using (1) to replace every inner product of images by the inner product of the originals.

## Solution

**Idea.** The Euclidean distance determines the inner product (polarization), and a map preserving the inner product is automatically linear.

**1.** Taking $y=0$: $\|f(x)\|=\|f(x)-f(0)\|=\|x\|$. Now expand
$$\|f(x)-f(y)\|^2=\|f(x)\|^2-2\langle f(x),f(y)\rangle+\|f(y)\|^2=\|x\|^2-2\langle f(x),f(y)\rangle+\|y\|^2.$$
Comparing with $\|x-y\|^2=\|x\|^2-2\langle x,y\rangle+\|y\|^2$ gives $\langle f(x),f(y)\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$.

**2.** Let $w=f(x+y)-f(x)-f(y)$. Expand $\|w\|^2$ as a sum of squared norms and inner products of $f(x+y),f(x),f(y)$; by (1) each term equals the corresponding term with $f$ removed, so
$$\|w\|^2=\|(x+y)-x-y\|^2=0.$$
Likewise $\|f(\lambda x)-\lambda f(x)\|^2=\|\lambda x-\lambda x\|^2=0$, computed in the same way. So $f$ is linear and preserves the inner product, i.e. its matrix $U$ satisfies $U^TU=I$.

**3.** For a general isometry $g$, put $f(x)=g(x)-g(0)$, which is an isometry fixing $0$. By (2), $f=U$ is orthogonal and $g(x)=Ux+g(0)$.

**Remark.** The finite-dimensional hypothesis is not needed in this proof, but the surjectivity is: on a general normed space an isometry fixing $0$ is linear only under surjectivity (Mazur-Ulam), and Problem 15(3) shows non-surjective isometries exist in other norms. For a strictly convex norm such as the Euclidean norm, no surjectivity is needed.

@@@ mt-bs-017-the-symmetric-difference-metric.md
---
title: The symmetric difference metric on finite sets
category: metric/mt-basics
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 17
tags: metric space, finite sets, Hamming distance, l1 embedding
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Let $\mathcal F$ be the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, and put $d(A,B)=|A\,\Delta\,B|$, where $A\Delta B=(A\setminus B)\cup(B\setminus A)$.

1. Prove that $d$ is a metric on $\mathcal F$.
2. Describe the balls of radius $r\le1$, and deduce that $(\mathcal F,d)$ is a discrete space.
3. Show that the ball $B(\emptyset,k)$ is infinite for $k\ge2$, so $(\mathcal F,d)$ is not compact on bounded sets.
4. Show that $A\mapsto\mathbf 1_A$ is an isometry from $\mathcal F$ to $\ell^1(\mathbb{N})$ with its usual distance $\sum_n|u_n-v_n|$.

## Hint

For the triangle inequality, prove the inclusion $A\Delta C\subset(A\Delta B)\cup(B\Delta C)$: a point in exactly one of $A,C$ is not in exactly the same status relative to $B$.

## Solution

**Idea.** The distance between two finite sets counts the number of elements on which they differ.

**1.** Symmetry is clear, and $d(A,B)=0\iff A\Delta B=\emptyset\iff A=B$. For the triangle inequality, take $x\in A\Delta C$, say $x\in A$, $x\notin C$. If $x\in B$ then $x\in B\setminus C\subset B\Delta C$; if $x\notin B$ then $x\in A\setminus B\subset A\Delta B$. The case $x\in C\setminus A$ is symmetric. So $A\Delta C\subset(A\Delta B)\cup(B\Delta C)$, and taking cardinals, $|A\Delta C|\le|A\Delta B|+|B\Delta C|$.

**2.** The distance is an integer, so for $r\le1$, $B(A,r)=\{B:|A\Delta B|<r\}=\{A\}$ (for $r\le1$ we need $|A\Delta B|=0$). Hence each singleton is open, and every subset is open: $\mathcal F$ is discrete.

**3.** The sets $\{n\}$ for $n\in\mathbb{N}$ satisfy $d(\emptyset,\{n\})=1<2$, so $B(\emptyset,2)$ contains infinitely many points; being discrete and infinite, it is not compact (the cover by singletons has no finite subcover). So a closed bounded set can be non-compact in a metric space.

**4.** $\sum_n|\mathbf 1_A(n)-\mathbf 1_B(n)|=|\{n:\mathbf 1_A(n)\ne\mathbf 1_B(n)\}|=|A\Delta B|$.

**Remark.** The same formula $d(A,B)=|A\Delta B|$ is the Hamming distance on binary words of fixed length; it is a basic example of a metric not coming from a norm on a real vector space, although it embeds isometrically in $\ell^1$.
@@@ mt-tp-001-the-discrete-metric.md
---
title: The discrete metric
category: metric/mt-topology
level: l2
difficulty: 1
order: 18
tags: discrete metric, open sets, closed sets, balls, convergence
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

On an arbitrary set $X$ define $d(x,y)=0$ if $x=y$ and $d(x,y)=1$ if $x\ne y$.

1. Check that $d$ is a metric.
2. Describe the open balls $B(x,r)=\{y:d(x,y)<r\}$ for every $r>0$.
3. Show that every subset of $X$ is both open and closed.
4. Describe the convergent sequences and the Cauchy sequences of $(X,d)$. Is $(X,d)$ complete?

## Hint

The metric takes only two values, so a ball is either very small or everything. For (4) take $\varepsilon=\tfrac12$ in the definitions.

## Solution

**Idea.** Since distances are $0$ or $1$, radii below $1$ isolate points and radii above $1$ see the whole space.

**1. Metric.** Positivity and symmetry are clear, and $d(x,y)=0$ iff $x=y$. For the triangle inequality $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$: if $x=z$ the left side is $0$. If $x\ne z$ the left side is $1$, and $y$ cannot be equal to both $x$ and $z$, so at least one term on the right equals $1$.

**2. Balls.** If $0<r\le1$ then $B(x,r)=\{x\}$ (a point $y\ne x$ has $d(x,y)=1\ge r$). If $r>1$ then $B(x,r)=X$.

**3. Open and closed.** Let $A\subset X$ and $a\in A$. Then $B(a,1)=\{a\}\subset A$, so $A$ is open. The complement $X\setminus A$ is also a subset, hence open, so $A$ is closed.

**4. Sequences.** If $x_n\to x$, take $\varepsilon=\tfrac12$: for $n\ge N$, $d(x_n,x)<\tfrac12$ forces $x_n=x$. So convergent sequences are exactly the eventually constant ones. If $(x_n)$ is Cauchy, take $\varepsilon=\tfrac12$: there is $N$ with $d(x_n,x_m)<\tfrac12$, hence $x_n=x_m$, for $n,m\ge N$; the sequence is eventually constant, hence convergent. So $(X,d)$ is complete.

**Remark.** The discrete metric is the standard source of counterexamples: a ball of radius $1$ is a single point while the closed ball $\{d\le1\}$ is all of $X$ (see the problem on closed balls), and a set which is open and closed need not be $\emptyset$ or $X$ (the space is totally disconnected).

@@@ mt-tp-002-distance-to-a-set.md
---
title: The distance to a set is 1-Lipschitz
category: metric/mt-topology
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 19
tags: distance to a set, closure, Lipschitz, separation of closed sets
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and $\emptyset\ne A\subset X$. Define $d(x,A)=\inf_{a\in A}d(x,a)$.

1. Prove that $|d(x,A)-d(y,A)|\le d(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in X$. In particular $x\mapsto d(x,A)$ is continuous.
2. Prove that $\overline{A}=\{x: d(x,A)=0\}$. Deduce that $A$ is closed iff $A=\{x:d(x,A)=0\}$.
3. Let $A,B$ be disjoint non-empty closed sets. Show that there exist disjoint open sets $U\supset A$ and $V\supset B$.

## Hint

For (1) use the triangle inequality inside the infimum, then swap $x$ and $y$. For (3) compare the two functions $d(\cdot,A)$ and $d(\cdot,B)$.

## Solution

**Idea.** The function $d(\cdot,A)$ measures how far we are from $A$; it is continuous, so its sign-sets are open.

**1.** For every $a\in A$, $d(x,A)\le d(x,a)\le d(x,y)+d(y,a)$. Taking the infimum over $a$ gives $d(x,A)\le d(x,y)+d(y,A)$. Exchanging the roles of $x,y$ gives $d(y,A)\le d(x,y)+d(x,A)$. Together, $|d(x,A)-d(y,A)|\le d(x,y)$.

**2.** If $x\in\overline{A}$, then for each $\varepsilon>0$ the ball $B(x,\varepsilon)$ meets $A$, so $d(x,A)<\varepsilon$; hence $d(x,A)=0$. Conversely if $d(x,A)=0$, for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is $a\in A$ with $d(x,a)<\varepsilon$, so every ball around $x$ meets $A$, i.e. $x\in\overline{A}$. Since $A$ is closed iff $A=\overline{A}$, the second claim follows.

**3.** Put $f(x)=d(x,A)-d(x,B)$, continuous by (1). Let $U=\{f<0\}$ and $V=\{f>0\}$: they are open and disjoint. If $a\in A$ then $d(a,A)=0$ and, because $B$ is closed and $a\notin B$, part (2) gives $d(a,B)>0$. So $f(a)<0$ and $A\subset U$. Symmetrically $B\subset V$.

**Remark.** Part (3) says that a metric space is *normal*; in general topological spaces this separation is an extra assumption. The same function gives Urysohn's function $d(x,A)/(d(x,A)+d(x,B))$, which is $0$ on $A$ and $1$ on $B$.

@@@ mt-tp-003-open-balls-closed-balls-and-closures.md
---
title: Closure of an open ball versus the closed ball
category: metric/mt-topology
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 20
tags: closed ball, closure, normed space, counterexamples
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

In a metric space $(X,d)$ let $B(x,r)=\{d(x,\cdot)<r\}$ and $B_f(x,r)=\{y:d(x,y)\le r\}$.

1. Prove that $B_f(x,r)$ is closed and that $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset B_f(x,r)$.
2. Prove that equality holds in a normed vector space $(E,\|\cdot\|)$ with $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ for every $r>0$.
3. Give two examples of metric spaces where $\overline{B(x,r)}\ne B_f(x,r)$.

## Hint

(1) The function $d(x,\cdot)$ is continuous. (2) Move a point of the sphere slightly towards the centre. (3) Try the discrete metric, and a subset of $\mathbb{R}$ with a gap.

## Solution

**Idea.** Closed balls are closed, but the closure of an open ball only sees points that can be approached from inside; in a vector space the segment to the centre always gives such an approach.

**1.** The map $y\mapsto d(x,y)$ is continuous (it is 1-Lipschitz), and $B_f(x,r)$ is the preimage of the closed set $[0,r]$, hence closed. It contains $B(x,r)$, so it contains the closure.

**2.** Let $y\in E$ with $\|y-x\|=r$ (points with $\|y-x\|<r$ are already in $B(x,r)$). Put $y_n=x+\left(1-\tfrac1n\right)(y-x)$. Then $\|y_n-x\|=\left(1-\tfrac1n\right)r<r$, so $y_n\in B(x,r)$, and $\|y_n-y\|=\tfrac rn\to0$. Hence $y\in\overline{B(x,r)}$.

**3. Examples.**
(a) Discrete metric, $r=1$: $B(x,1)=\{x\}$ is closed, so $\overline{B(x,1)}=\{x\}$, while $B_f(x,1)=X$. They differ as soon as $X$ has two points.
(b) $X=[0,1]\cup\{2\}\subset\mathbb{R}$ with the usual distance, centre $0$, $r=2$: $B(0,2)=[0,1]$ is closed in $X$, so its closure is $[0,1]$, while $B_f(0,2)=[0,1]\cup\{2\}$.

**Remark.** The proof of (2) uses the existence of intermediate points on a segment; in the examples of (3) the space has "gaps" so no such approach exists. In $\mathbb{R}^n$ this is why the closed unit ball is the closure of the open one.

@@@ mt-tp-004-closure-interior-and-boundary.md
---
title: Closure, interior and boundary in a metric space
category: metric/mt-topology
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 21
tags: closure, interior, boundary, sequences
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Let $A,B$ be subsets of a metric space $X$. The boundary is $\partial A=\overline{A}\setminus\operatorname{int}A$.

1. Show that $x\in\overline{A}$ iff there is a sequence $(a_n)$ in $A$ with $a_n\to x$.
2. Show that $\operatorname{int}A=X\setminus\overline{X\setminus A}$ and $\partial A=\overline{A}\cap\overline{X\setminus A}$. Deduce that $\partial A$ is closed.
3. Show that $\partial(A\cup B)\subset\partial A\cup\partial B$, and give an example in $\mathbb{R}$ where the inclusion is strict.

## Hint

(1) Use the balls $B(x,1/n)$. (2) $x\notin\operatorname{int}A$ means that every ball around $x$ meets $X\setminus A$. (3) You may use $\overline{A\cup B}=\overline{A}\cup\overline{B}$.

## Solution

**Idea.** All three notions are expressed by "every ball around $x$ meets ...". Taking complements swaps interior and closure.

**1.** If $x\in\overline{A}$, each ball $B(x,1/n)$ meets $A$; pick $a_n\in A$ in it, so $d(a_n,x)<1/n\to0$. Conversely if $a_n\to x$ with $a_n\in A$, every ball around $x$ contains $a_n$ for $n$ large, hence meets $A$.

**2.** $x\in\operatorname{int}A$ iff some ball $B(x,r)\subset A$ iff some ball around $x$ does not meet $X\setminus A$ iff $x\notin\overline{X\setminus A}$. This is the first formula. Then
$$\partial A=\overline{A}\setminus\operatorname{int}A=\overline{A}\cap\left(X\setminus\operatorname{int}A\right)=\overline{A}\cap\overline{X\setminus A},$$
an intersection of two closed sets, hence closed.

**3.** First $\overline{A\cup B}=\overline{A}\cup\overline{B}$: the inclusion $\supset$ is clear by monotonicity; if $x\in\overline{A\cup B}$, a sequence in $A\cup B$ converging to $x$ has infinitely many terms in $A$ or in $B$, giving a subsequence in $A$ or in $B$ converging to $x$. Now let $x\in\partial(A\cup B)$. By (2), $x\in\overline{A\cup B}$ and $x\in\overline{X\setminus(A\cup B)}$. The latter set is $\overline{(X\setminus A)\cap(X\setminus B)}\subset\overline{X\setminus A}\cap\overline{X\setminus B}$. If $x\in\overline{A}$ then $x\in\overline{A}\cap\overline{X\setminus A}=\partial A$; otherwise $x\in\overline{B}$ and then $x\in\partial B$.

*Strict example.* $A=[0,1)$, $B=[1,2]$ in $\mathbb{R}$: $\partial A=\{0,1\}$, $\partial B=\{1,2\}$, but $A\cup B=[0,2]$ has boundary $\{0,2\}$.

**Remark.** For the boundary of a sum, intersection or product of sets, always start from $\partial A=\overline{A}\cap\overline{X\setminus A}$.

@@@ mt-tp-005-open-sets-of-a-subspace.md
---
title: Open sets of a subspace
category: metric/mt-topology
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 22
tags: subspace, relative topology, open sets, closed sets
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and $Y\subset X$ with the induced metric.

1. Show that $V\subset Y$ is open in $Y$ iff $V=U\cap Y$ for some open $U\subset X$, and closed in $Y$ iff $V=F\cap Y$ with $F$ closed in $X$.
2. Show that if $Y$ is open in $X$, a subset of $Y$ is open in $Y$ iff it is open in $X$.
3. For $X=\mathbb{R}$ give: (a) a set open in $Y=[0,1]$ but not in $\mathbb{R}$; (b) a set open and closed in $Y=\mathbb{Q}$, neither empty nor $\mathbb{Q}$; (c) the topology of $Y=\mathbb{Z}$.

## Hint

The ball of $Y$ around $y$ is $B_X(y,r)\cap Y$. For (3b) cut $\mathbb{Q}$ at an irrational number.

## Solution

**Idea.** Intersecting with $Y$ transports every statement about $X$ down to $Y$.

**1.** Balls in $Y$ are $B_Y(y,r)=B_X(y,r)\cap Y$. If $V=U\cap Y$ with $U$ open and $y\in V$, choose $r$ with $B_X(y,r)\subset U$; then $B_Y(y,r)\subset V$, so $V$ is open in $Y$. Conversely, if $V$ is open in $Y$, for each $y\in V$ pick $r_y$ with $B_Y(y,r_y)\subset V$ and put $U=\bigcup_{y\in V}B_X(y,r_y)$, which is open with $U\cap Y=V$. For closed sets take complements in $Y$: $Y\setminus V=U\cap Y$ gives $V=(X\setminus U)\cap Y$, and conversely.

**2.** If $V\subset Y$ is open in $X$, then $V=V\cap Y$ is open in $Y$. Conversely if $V=U\cap Y$ with $U,Y$ open in $X$, then $V$ is open in $X$.

**3.** (a) $[0,\tfrac12)=(-1,\tfrac12)\cap[0,1]$ is open in $[0,1]$ but not in $\mathbb{R}$ (it contains $0$ without a neighbourhood).
(b) Let $V=\{q\in\mathbb{Q}:q<\sqrt2\}=(-\infty,\sqrt2)\cap\mathbb{Q}$. It is open in $\mathbb{Q}$. Its complement in $\mathbb{Q}$ is $(\sqrt2,\infty)\cap\mathbb{Q}$, also open, so $V$ is closed too. Both are non-empty. (So $\mathbb{Q}$ is not connected.)
(c) $B_{\mathbb{Z}}(n,\tfrac12)=\{n\}$, so every singleton, hence every subset, is open: $\mathbb{Z}$ has the discrete topology although it is not open in $\mathbb{R}$.

**Remark.** "Open" and "closed" are never absolute notions: they always refer to an ambient space. The hypothesis "$Y$ open in $X$" in (2) cannot be dropped, by (3a).

@@@ mt-tp-006-density-of-piecewise-linear-functions.md
---
title: Piecewise linear functions are dense in C[0,1]
category: metric/mt-topology
level: m1
difficulty: 3
order: 23
tags: dense set, uniform norm, C[0,1], separability, uniform continuity
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Equip $C[0,1]$ with $\|f\|_\infty=\max_{[0,1]}|f|$.

1. Show that the set $P$ of continuous piecewise linear functions (affine on each interval of some finite subdivision) is dense in $C[0,1]$.
2. Deduce that $C[0,1]$ is separable, i.e. contains a countable dense subset.

## Hint

A continuous function on $[0,1]$ is uniformly continuous. Interpolate $f$ linearly at the points $k/n$. For (2) approximate the nodal values by rational numbers.

## Solution

**Idea.** Uniform continuity makes $f$ nearly constant on a short interval, so a polygonal line through some of its values stays uniformly close.

**1.** Let $f\in C[0,1]$ and $\varepsilon>0$. By the Heine-Cantor theorem there is $\delta>0$ with $|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $|x-y|\le\delta$. Choose $n$ with $1/n\le\delta$ and let $g$ be the polygonal function with $g(k/n)=f(k/n)$ for $k=0,\dots,n$, affine in between. On $[a,b]=[k/n,(k+1)/n]$ write $x=(1-t)a+tb$, $t\in[0,1]$; then $g(x)=(1-t)f(a)+tf(b)$ and
$$f(x)-g(x)=(1-t)(f(x)-f(a))+t(f(x)-f(b)).$$
Both $|x-a|$ and $|x-b|$ are at most $1/n\le\delta$, so $|f(x)-g(x)|<(1-t)\varepsilon+t\varepsilon=\varepsilon$. Hence $\|f-g\|_\infty\le\varepsilon$ with $g\in P$.

**2.** Let $P_{\mathbb{Q}}$ be the set of polygonal functions with nodes at the points $k/n$ ($n\ge1$) and rational nodal values. It is countable (a countable union over $n$ of copies of $\mathbb{Q}^{n+1}$). Given $g\in P$ with nodes at $k/n$ and $\varepsilon>0$, replace each nodal value $g(k/n)$ by a rational $r_k$ with $|r_k-g(k/n)|<\varepsilon$, and let $h$ be the polygonal function through the points $(k/n,r_k)$. On each subinterval $g-h$ is affine, so its maximum modulus is attained at an endpoint and is $<\varepsilon$. So $\|g-h\|_\infty<\varepsilon$. A polygonal function with several different subdivisions is refined to a common one, so every element of $P$ is approximated this way. Hence $P_{\mathbb{Q}}$ is dense in $P$, which is dense in $C[0,1]$.

**Remark.** The Weierstrass theorem gives another countable dense set (polynomials with rational coefficients). Contrast with $\ell^\infty$ (next problem), which is not separable.

@@@ mt-tp-007-l-infinity-is-not-separable.md
---
title: The space of bounded sequences is not separable
category: metric/mt-topology
level: m1
difficulty: 3
order: 24
tags: separability, l-infinity, dense set, disjoint balls
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Let $\ell^\infty$ be the space of bounded real sequences with $\|x\|_\infty=\sup_n|x_n|$.

1. For $S\subset\mathbb{N}$ let $1_S$ be its indicator sequence. Compute $\|1_S-1_T\|_\infty$ for $S\ne T$.
2. Show that the balls $B(1_S,\tfrac12)$, $S\subset\mathbb{N}$, are pairwise disjoint.
3. Deduce that $\ell^\infty$ has no countable dense subset.

## Hint

If $S\ne T$ some integer lies in exactly one of them. A dense set must meet every non-empty open set, in particular each of these balls.

## Solution

**Idea.** There are uncountably many points that are pairwise far apart; a countable set cannot be close to all of them.

**1.** If $S\ne T$ pick $n$ in one of the sets but not the other: $|1_S(n)-1_T(n)|=1$. All other coordinates differ by at most $1$. So $\|1_S-1_T\|_\infty=1$.

**2.** Suppose $z\in B(1_S,\tfrac12)\cap B(1_T,\tfrac12)$ with $S\ne T$. Then $1=\|1_S-1_T\|\le\|1_S-z\|+\|z-1_T\|<\tfrac12+\tfrac12=1$, a contradiction.

**3.** Let $D\subset\ell^\infty$ be dense. For each $S\subset\mathbb{N}$ the open ball $B(1_S,\tfrac12)$ is non-empty, so contains some $\phi(S)\in D$. By (2), $S\ne T$ implies $\phi(S)\ne\phi(T)$: the map $\phi:\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})\to D$ is injective. Since $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ is uncountable (Cantor's diagonal argument), $D$ is uncountable.

**Remark.** Separability passes to subspaces of metric spaces (a fact worth proving), so $\ell^\infty$ contains no separable-ness obstruction in the other direction: e.g. $c_0$ and $\ell^1$ are separable, but the big space $\ell^\infty$ is not. The same argument shows that an uncountable discrete metric space is not separable.

@@@ mt-tp-008-open-and-closed-sets-in-c01.md
---
title: Open and closed sets in C[0,1]
category: metric/mt-topology
level: m1
difficulty: 2
order: 25
tags: C[0,1], uniform norm, closed sets, open sets, polynomials
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

In $C[0,1]$ with the sup norm decide whether each set is open, closed, both or neither, and prove it.

1. $A=\{f: f(1/2)=0\}$.
2. $B=\{f: f(x)>0\text{ for all }x\in[0,1]\}$.
3. $C=\{f:\|f\|_\infty\le1\}$ and $D=\{f:\|f\|_\infty<1\}$.
4. $E=\{f:\int_0^1f=0\}$.
5. $F=\{f:\exists x\in[0,1],\ f(x)=0\}$.
6. The set $\mathcal{P}$ of polynomial functions.

## Hint

Evaluation at a point and the integral are continuous in the sup norm: $|f(x_0)-g(x_0)|\le\|f-g\|_\infty$ and $|\int f-\int g|\le\|f-g\|_\infty$. For (2) a continuous positive function has a positive minimum. For (6) use $e^x$ and a function with a kink.

## Solution

**Idea.** Use continuity of $f\mapsto f(x_0)$, $f\mapsto\int f$, $f\mapsto\|f\|_\infty$ to see closed sets as preimages of closed sets, and compactness of $[0,1]$ for the rest.

**1.** Evaluation $\mathrm{ev}:f\mapsto f(1/2)$ satisfies $|\mathrm{ev}(f)-\mathrm{ev}(g)|\le\|f-g\|_\infty$, so it is continuous; $A=\mathrm{ev}^{-1}(\{0\})$ is closed. It is not open: $f\in A$ and $f+\eta$ ($\eta>0$ constant) is in the ball $B(f,2\eta)$ but not in $A$.

**2.** Let $f\in B$ and $m=\min f>0$ (extreme value theorem). If $\|g-f\|_\infty<m$ then $g(x)>f(x)-m\ge0$. So $B(f,m)\subset B$: $B$ is open. It is not closed: $f_n=1/n$ lies in $B$ and converges uniformly to $0\notin B$.

**3.** $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ is continuous ($|\|f\|-\|g\||\le\|f-g\|$), so $C$ is closed and $D$ is open. $C$ is not open (the constant $1$ is in $C$ but $(1+\eta)\cdot1$ is in every ball around it), and $D$ is not closed ($(1-\tfrac1n)\to1\notin D$).

**4.** $E$ is the preimage of $\{0\}$ under $f\mapsto\int_0^1f$, which is continuous because $|\int f-\int g|\le\|f-g\|_\infty$. So $E$ is closed. Not open: $0\in E$ and $\eta\in B(0,2\eta)$ has integral $\eta\ne0$.

**5.** $F$ is closed. Let $f_n\in F$, $f_n\to f$ uniformly, $f_n(x_n)=0$. By Bolzano-Weierstrass some subsequence $x_{n_k}\to x\in[0,1]$. Then $|f(x_{n_k})|=|f(x_{n_k})-f_{n_k}(x_{n_k})|\le\|f-f_{n_k}\|_\infty\to0$ and, $f$ being continuous, $f(x)=\lim f(x_{n_k})=0$. So $f\in F$. It is not open: $0\in F$ but $\eta\notin F$ for $\eta>0$ small. (Its complement is $B\cup(-B)$, by the intermediate value theorem.)

**6.** $\mathcal{P}$ is not closed: the partial sums $\sum_{k\le N}x^k/k!$ converge uniformly on $[0,1]$ to $e^x$, which is not a polynomial. It is not open either: for a polynomial $p$ and $\eta>0$, the function $p+\eta\,|x-\tfrac12|$ has distance $\eta/2$ from $p$ but is not differentiable at $\tfrac12$, hence is not a polynomial. (By Weierstrass, $\mathcal{P}$ is dense, so its closure is everything.)

**Remark.** Closed sets are defined by "$\le$" or "$=$" conditions that survive uniform limits, open sets by strict conditions that persist under small perturbations. In an infinite-dimensional space this heuristic requires care, e.g. positivity needs compactness of $[0,1]$.

@@@ mt-tp-009-c0-inside-l-infinity.md
---
title: The subspace c_0 of l^infinity
category: metric/mt-topology
level: m1
difficulty: 3
order: 26
tags: l-infinity, c_0, closed subspace, dense subspace, empty interior
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Let $c_{00}\subset c_0\subset\ell^\infty$ be the sequences which are eventually $0$, resp. converge to $0$, with the sup norm.

1. Prove that $c_0$ is closed in $\ell^\infty$.
2. Prove that $c_{00}$ is dense in $c_0$ but not closed in $\ell^\infty$, and find its closure in $\ell^\infty$.
3. Prove that $c_0$ has empty interior in $\ell^\infty$.

## Hint

(1) $\varepsilon/2$ argument. (2) Truncate the sequence. (3) Perturb $x$ by the constant sequence $(1,1,1,\dots)$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Uniform convergence preserves "tends to $0$"; truncations are uniformly close because the tail is small.

**1.** Let $x^{(k)}\in c_0$ with $\|x^{(k)}-x\|_\infty\to0$, $x\in\ell^\infty$. Given $\varepsilon>0$ choose $k$ with $\|x-x^{(k)}\|_\infty<\varepsilon/2$ and then $N$ with $|x^{(k)}_n|<\varepsilon/2$ for $n>N$. For $n>N$, $|x_n|\le|x_n-x^{(k)}_n|+|x^{(k)}_n|<\varepsilon$. Hence $x_n\to0$, i.e. $x\in c_0$.

**2.** For $x\in c_0$ let $x^{[N]}=(x_1,\dots,x_N,0,0,\dots)\in c_{00}$. Then $\|x-x^{[N]}\|_\infty=\sup_{n>N}|x_n|\to0$ as $N\to\infty$, because $x_n\to0$. So $c_{00}$ is dense in $c_0$. Since $c_0$ is closed in $\ell^\infty$ by (1), the closure of $c_{00}$ in $\ell^\infty$ is exactly $c_0$: it is contained in $c_0$ and contains $c_0$. As $c_{00}\ne c_0$ (e.g. $(1/n)_n\in c_0\setminus c_{00}$), $c_{00}$ is not closed.

**3.** Let $x\in c_0$ and $r>0$. Put $y=x+\tfrac r2(1,1,1,\dots)$. Then $\|y-x\|_\infty=\tfrac r2<r$ but $y_n\to\tfrac r2\ne0$, so $y\notin c_0$. No ball around a point of $c_0$ lies in $c_0$, so $\operatorname{int}c_0=\emptyset$.

**Remark.** So $c_0$ is a closed set with empty interior, i.e. nowhere dense in $\ell^\infty$ (see the problem on nowhere dense sets). More generally a proper closed subspace of a normed space always has empty interior.

@@@ mt-tp-010-isolated-points.md
---
title: Isolated points and countability
category: metric/mt-topology
level: l2
difficulty: 3
order: 27
tags: isolated points, open sets, countability, density
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

A point $a$ of a metric space $X$ is *isolated* if $\{a\}$ is open, i.e. $B(a,r)=\{a\}$ for some $r>0$.

1. Let $S=\{1/n:n\ge1\}\subset\mathbb{R}$. Show every point of $S$ is isolated in $S$, but not in $S\cup\{0\}$.
2. Show that if $X$ has no isolated point, every non-empty open set of $X$ is infinite.
3. Show that a subset $A\subset\mathbb{R}^p$, all of whose points are isolated points of $A$ (with the induced metric), is countable.

## Hint

(2) A finite set of points can be separated from any one of its points by a small ball. (3) Attach to each $a\in A$ a ball with rational centre and radius that meets $A$ only at $a$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Isolation is a local property giving, for each point, a ball "private" to it; in $\mathbb{R}^p$ there are only countably many balls with rational data.

**1.** For $n\ge1$, $B(1/n,r)\cap S=\{1/n\}$ for $r=\tfrac1n-\tfrac1{n+1}$ (the nearest other points are $1/(n\pm1)$, at distance at least $\tfrac1n-\tfrac1{n+1}$; the other neighbour is further away). In $S\cup\{0\}$ the point $0$ has $B(0,r)\ni\tfrac1n$ for $n>1/r$, so $0$ is not isolated.

**2.** Suppose $U\ne\emptyset$ is open and finite, $U=\{u_1,\dots,u_m\}$. Choose $r_1>0$ with $B(u_1,r_1)\subset U$. Since $u_1$ is not isolated, $B(u_1,r)\ne\{u_1\}$ for every $r$: in particular the ball $B(u_1,\min(r_1,d_{\min}))$, where $d_{\min}$ is the smallest distance from $u_1$ to the other $u_j$ ($d_{\min}=\infty$ if $m=1$), contains a point different from $u_1$ and in $U$, but at distance less than every $d(u_1,u_j)$, $j\ne1$. That point is not in $U$, a contradiction. Hence $U$ is infinite.

**3.** For each $a\in A$ there is $r_a>0$ with $B(a,r_a)\cap A=\{a\}$. Choose a ball $B'_a=B(q_a,s_a)$ with $q_a\in\mathbb{Q}^p$, $s_a\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}$ such that $a\in B'_a\subset B(a,r_a)$ (take $s_a$ rational with $0<s_a<r_a/2$ and $q_a$ rational with $|q_a-a|<s_a$; then $B(q_a,s_a)\subset B(a,r_a)$ by the triangle inequality, as $|y-a|<2s_a<r_a$). Then $B'_a\cap A=\{a\}$, so $a\mapsto B'_a$ is injective. The family of balls with rational centre and radius is countable, hence $A$ is countable.

**Remark.** Part (3) fails in non-separable spaces (the discrete metric on an uncountable set). Also (2) with Baire's theorem shows that a non-empty complete metric space without isolated points is uncountable.

@@@ mt-tp-011-nowhere-dense-sets-and-the-cantor-set.md
---
title: Nowhere dense sets and the Cantor set
category: metric/mt-topology
level: m1
difficulty: 3
order: 28
tags: nowhere dense, Cantor set, closure, interior
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

A subset $A$ of a metric space $X$ is *nowhere dense* if $\operatorname{int}\overline{A}=\emptyset$.

1. Show that $A$ is nowhere dense iff $X\setminus\overline{A}$ is dense in $X$.
2. Show that a finite union of nowhere dense sets is nowhere dense.
3. Show that $\mathbb{Z}$ is nowhere dense in $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ is not.
4. Let $C_0=[0,1]$ and let $C_{n+1}$ be obtained from $C_n$ by removing the open middle third of each of its intervals. Show that the Cantor set $C=\bigcap_nC_n$ is closed and nowhere dense in $\mathbb{R}$.

## Hint

(1) Use $\operatorname{int}B=X\setminus\overline{X\setminus B}$. (2) Given an open set $V$, remove $\overline{A}$ then $\overline{B}$ and keep an open set. (4) $C_n$ is a union of $2^n$ intervals of length $3^{-n}$.

## Solution

**Idea.** "Nowhere dense" means that the closure of $A$ contains no ball at all: inside any open set one can find a smaller open set avoiding $A$.

**1.** With $B=\overline{A}$: $\operatorname{int}\overline{A}=X\setminus\overline{X\setminus\overline{A}}$. So $\operatorname{int}\overline{A}=\emptyset$ iff $\overline{X\setminus\overline{A}}=X$, i.e. iff $X\setminus\overline{A}$ is dense.

**2.** It is enough to treat $A$ and $B$ (then induct). Let $V$ be a non-empty open set. Since $A$ is nowhere dense, $V\not\subset\overline{A}$ (otherwise $V\subset\operatorname{int}\overline{A}$), so $W=V\setminus\overline{A}$ is non-empty and open. Likewise $W\not\subset\overline{B}$, so $W'=W\setminus\overline{B}$ is non-empty and open. Then $W'\subset V$ is disjoint from $\overline{A}\cup\overline{B}=\overline{A\cup B}$. So no non-empty open set $V$ is contained in $\overline{A\cup B}$: $\operatorname{int}\overline{A\cup B}=\emptyset$.

**3.** $\mathbb{Z}$ is closed and contains no interval, so $\operatorname{int}\overline{\mathbb{Z}}=\emptyset$. On the other hand $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}=\mathbb{R}$ has non-empty interior.

**4.** Each $C_n$ is a finite union of closed intervals, hence closed, so $C$ is closed and $\overline{C}=C$. Suppose $C$ contained an interval $(a,b)$ with $a<b$. Pick $n$ with $3^{-n}<b-a$. Then $(a,b)\subset C_n$, but $C_n$ is a union of intervals of length $3^{-n}$ separated by gaps (removed open middle thirds) so the connected set $(a,b)$ would have to lie in a single interval of $C_n$ of length $3^{-n}<b-a$, which is absurd. So $C$ has empty interior; being closed, it is nowhere dense.

**Remark.** The Cantor set is uncountable yet "small" topologically. A closed set is nowhere dense iff it has empty interior. Note that a union of *countably* many nowhere dense sets can be everything ($\mathbb{Q}=\bigcup\{q\}$), so (2) does not extend to infinite unions; Baire's theorem is the correct substitute.

@@@ mt-tp-012-closed-sets-are-g-delta.md
---
title: Closed sets are G-delta sets, open sets are F-sigma sets
category: metric/mt-topology
level: m1
difficulty: 2
order: 29
tags: G-delta, F-sigma, closed sets, distance function
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

A $G_\delta$ set is a countable intersection of open sets; an $F_\sigma$ set is a countable union of closed sets. Let $X$ be a metric space.

1. Show that every closed set $F\subset X$ is a $G_\delta$.
2. Deduce that every open set is an $F_\sigma$.
3. Show that in $\mathbb{R}$ the set $\mathbb{Q}$ is an $F_\sigma$ and $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ is a $G_\delta$.

## Hint

Take the open "thickenings" $U_n=\{x:d(x,F)<1/n\}$.

## Solution

**Idea.** A closed set is the set of points at distance $0$ from itself; replace "$=0$" by "$<1/n$" for all $n$.

**1.** If $F=\emptyset$ it is open, hence $G_\delta$. Otherwise let $U_n=\{x\in X:d(x,F)<1/n\}$. It is open: if $d(x,F)<1/n$ pick $a\in F$ with $d(x,a)<1/n$; for $y\in B(x,1/n-d(x,a))$ we get $d(y,F)\le d(y,a)<1/n$, so the ball lies in $U_n$. Moreover $\bigcap_nU_n=\{x:d(x,F)=0\}=\overline{F}=F$ (see the problem on the distance to a set).

**2.** If $U$ is open then $X\setminus U$ is closed, hence $X\setminus U=\bigcap_nU_n$ with $U_n$ open, and $U=\bigcup_n(X\setminus U_n)$, a countable union of closed sets.

**3.** $\mathbb{Q}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb{Q}}\{q\}$ is a countable union of closed sets (points are closed). Hence $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}=\bigcap_{q}(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{q\})$ is a countable intersection of open sets.

**Remark.** The converse question is subtle: $\mathbb{Q}$ is $F_\sigma$ but, as shown in the Baire problems below, it is not a $G_\delta$. So the classes $F_\sigma$ and $G_\delta$ are genuinely different.

@@@ mt-tp-013-baire-category-theorem.md
---
title: The Baire category theorem
category: metric/mt-topology
level: m1
difficulty: 4
order: 30
tags: Baire, complete metric space, dense open sets, nested balls
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Let $(X,d)$ be a non-empty complete metric space.

1. Prove: if $(U_n)_{n\ge1}$ are dense open subsets of $X$, then $\bigcap_nU_n$ is dense in $X$.
2. Deduce that $X$ is not a countable union of closed sets with empty interior.
3. Deduce that if $X$ has no isolated point, then $X$ is uncountable. In particular $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable.

## Hint

Given a non-empty open set $V$, build nested closed balls $B_f(x_n,r_n)$ with $r_n\to0$, with $B_f(x_{n+1},r_{n+1})\subset B(x_n,r_n)\cap U_{n+1}$, and use completeness on the centres.

## Solution

**Idea.** Density of $U_n$ lets us enter $U_n$ inside any open set; shrinking balls produce a Cauchy sequence whose limit lies in every $U_n$.

**1.** Let $V\ne\emptyset$ be open. We show $V\cap\bigcap_nU_n\ne\emptyset$. Since $U_1$ is dense, $V\cap U_1$ is non-empty open: pick $x_1$ in it and $0<r_1<1$ with $B_f(x_1,r_1)\subset V\cap U_1$. Inductively, $B(x_n,r_n)\cap U_{n+1}$ is non-empty and open (density of $U_{n+1}$); choose $x_{n+1}$ in it and $0<r_{n+1}<\tfrac1{n+1}$ with $B_f(x_{n+1},r_{n+1})\subset B(x_n,r_n)\cap U_{n+1}$. For $m\ge n$ we have $x_m\in B(x_n,r_n)$, so $d(x_m,x_n)<r_n<\tfrac1n$: the sequence is Cauchy. By completeness $x_m\to x$. For each $n$, all $x_m$ with $m\ge n$ lie in the closed set $B_f(x_n,r_n)$, hence so does $x$. Thus $x\in B_f(x_n,r_n)\subset U_n$ for all $n$, and $x\in B_f(x_1,r_1)\subset V$.

**2.** If $X=\bigcup_nF_n$ with $F_n$ closed and $\operatorname{int}F_n=\emptyset$, then $U_n=X\setminus F_n$ is open and dense (a closed set has empty interior iff its complement is dense). By (1), $\bigcap_nU_n\ne\emptyset$ (as $X\ne\emptyset$ is dense in itself), but $\bigcap U_n=X\setminus\bigcup F_n=\emptyset$, a contradiction.

**3.** Suppose $X=\{x_1,x_2,\dots\}$ is countable. Each singleton $\{x_k\}$ is closed, and has empty interior since $x_k$ is not isolated. Then $X=\bigcup\{x_k\}$ contradicts (2). For $\mathbb{R}$, which is complete with no isolated point, we find that $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable.

**Remark.** Completeness is essential: $\mathbb{Q}$ is a countable union of points. A subset that contains a countable intersection of dense open sets is called *residual*; Baire says that residual sets are dense, which is why "generic" statements can be proved by exhibiting a residual set.

@@@ mt-tp-014-q-is-not-a-g-delta-set.md
---
title: The rationals are not a G-delta set
category: metric/mt-topology
level: m1
difficulty: 3
order: 31
tags: Baire, G-delta, rationals, irrationals
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Use the Baire category theorem: in a non-empty complete metric space, a countable intersection of dense open sets is dense.

1. Show that $\mathbb{Q}$ is not a $G_\delta$ in $\mathbb{R}$.
2. Deduce that $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ is not an $F_\sigma$.
3. Show that there is no sequence of open sets $(U_n)$ with $\bigcap_nU_n=\mathbb{Q}$, and also none with $\bigcap_nU_n=\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]$ among open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$.

## Hint

If $\mathbb{Q}=\bigcap U_n$, each $U_n$ is dense. Also $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{q\}$ is dense open for each rational $q$.

## Solution

**Idea.** If $\mathbb{Q}$ were $G_\delta$, we could intersect it with the dense open sets $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{q\}$ and obtain a dense set that is empty.

**1.** Suppose $\mathbb{Q}=\bigcap_{n}U_n$ with $U_n$ open. Each $U_n\supset\mathbb{Q}$ is dense. Enumerate $\mathbb{Q}=\{q_1,q_2,\dots\}$ and let $V_k=\mathbb{R}\setminus\{q_k\}$, open and dense. The family $(U_n)\cup(V_k)$ is a countable family of dense open sets, so by Baire its intersection is dense, hence non-empty. But
$$\bigcap_nU_n\cap\bigcap_kV_k=\mathbb{Q}\cap(\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset.$$
Contradiction.

**2.** If $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}=\bigcup F_n$ with $F_n$ closed, then $\mathbb{Q}=\bigcap(\mathbb{R}\setminus F_n)$ would be a $G_\delta$, contradicting (1).

**3.** The first is (1). For the second, suppose $\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]=\bigcap U_n$ with $U_n$ open. Then $U_n\cap(0,1)$ is open and dense in $(0,1)$. Now $(0,1)$ is homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}$ (a complete metric structure exists, e.g. via $\tan(\pi(x-\tfrac12))$), or directly one can run the argument above in the complete space $[0,1]$: the sets $U_n\cap[0,1]$ and $[0,1]\setminus\{q_k\}$ are dense open in $[0,1]$, and their intersection is empty, contradicting Baire in $[0,1]$.

**Remark.** The sets $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ are both dense and "complementary", but only the irrationals are $G_\delta$. This is the key to the next problem.

@@@ mt-tp-015-points-of-continuity-form-a-g-delta.md
---
title: The set of continuity points is a G-delta
category: metric/mt-topology
level: m1
difficulty: 4
order: 32
tags: oscillation, continuity points, G-delta, Baire
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Let $f:X\to\mathbb{R}$ be any function on a metric space $X$. For $x\in X$ and $\delta>0$ put
$$\omega_f(x,\delta)=\sup\{|f(y)-f(z)|:\ y,z\in B(x,\delta)\},\qquad \omega_f(x)=\inf_{\delta>0}\omega_f(x,\delta).$$

1. Show that $f$ is continuous at $x$ iff $\omega_f(x)=0$.
2. Show that $\{x:\omega_f(x)<\tfrac1n\}$ is open for each $n$.
3. Conclude that the set of continuity points of $f$ is a $G_\delta$.
4. Show that there is no function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ which is continuous exactly at the rational numbers.

## Hint

For (2) a small ball around a nearby point stays inside the big ball. For (4) combine (3) with the fact that $\mathbb{Q}$ is not a $G_\delta$ (a consequence of Baire's theorem).

## Solution

**Idea.** The oscillation measures how much $f$ jumps near $x$; its strict sub-level sets are open because a nearby point sees a subset of the same neighbourhood.

**1.** Suppose $\omega_f(x)=0$ and let $\varepsilon>0$. There is $\delta$ with $\omega_f(x,\delta)<\varepsilon$; taking $z=x$ gives $|f(y)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ for $y\in B(x,\delta)$: $f$ is continuous at $x$. Conversely if $f$ is continuous at $x$, given $\varepsilon>0$ take $\delta$ with $|f(y)-f(x)|<\varepsilon/3$ on $B(x,\delta)$; then $|f(y)-f(z)|<2\varepsilon/3$ for $y,z$ in the ball, so $\omega_f(x)\le\omega_f(x,\delta)\le2\varepsilon/3<\varepsilon$. As $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, $\omega_f(x)=0$.

**2.** If $\omega_f(x)<\tfrac1n$, there is $\delta>0$ with $\omega_f(x,\delta)<\tfrac1n$. For $y\in B(x,\delta)$ set $\delta'=\delta-d(x,y)>0$; then $B(y,\delta')\subset B(x,\delta)$, so $\omega_f(y)\le\omega_f(y,\delta')\le\omega_f(x,\delta)<\tfrac1n$. Hence $B(x,\delta)\subset\{\omega_f<\tfrac1n\}$.

**3.** By (1), the set of continuity points is $\{\omega_f=0\}=\bigcap_{n\ge1}\{\omega_f<\tfrac1n\}$, a countable intersection of open sets by (2).

**4.** If $f$ were continuous exactly on $\mathbb{Q}$, by (3) $\mathbb{Q}$ would be a $G_\delta$, which is impossible.

**Remark.** There is a function continuous exactly at the irrationals (Thomae's function $f(p/q)=1/q$, $f(\text{irrational})=0$), consistent with the fact that $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ is a $G_\delta$. The oscillation function is also the right tool to prove that the set of discontinuity points of any function is $F_\sigma$.

@@@ mt-tp-016-equivalent-bounded-metrics.md
---
title: Replacing a metric by a bounded one
category: metric/mt-topology
level: l2
difficulty: 2
order: 33
tags: equivalent metrics, bounded metric, Cauchy sequences, completeness
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and $e(x,y)=\min(d(x,y),1)$.

1. Prove that $e$ is a metric on $X$.
2. Show that $d$ and $e$ have the same open sets, the same convergent sequences and the same Cauchy sequences. In particular $(X,d)$ is complete iff $(X,e)$ is.
3. Is boundedness a topological property? Explain.

## Hint

$B_e(x,r)=B_d(x,r)$ for $r\le1$. For the triangle inequality distinguish whether $d(x,y)$ or $d(y,z)$ is at least $1$.

## Solution

**Idea.** Only small distances matter for topology; capping distances at $1$ changes nothing locally.

**1.** Positivity, symmetry and $e(x,y)=0\iff x=y$ are clear. Triangle inequality: if $e(x,y)=1$ or $e(y,z)=1$, then $e(x,y)+e(y,z)\ge1\ge e(x,z)$. Otherwise $e(x,y)=d(x,y)$ and $e(y,z)=d(y,z)$, so $e(x,z)\le d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)=e(x,y)+e(y,z)$.

**2.** For $0<r\le1$ we have $B_e(x,r)=B_d(x,r)$, since $e(x,y)<r\le1$ iff $d(x,y)<r$. A set $U$ is open for a metric iff each point has a ball of some radius inside $U$, and one may always shrink the radius to be at most $1$. So $U$ is $d$-open iff $e$-open. Convergence $x_n\to x$ is $d(x_n,x)<\varepsilon$ for $\varepsilon<1$ eventually, i.e. $e(x_n,x)<\varepsilon$; the same argument (with $\varepsilon<1$) applies to the Cauchy condition. Completeness follows.

**3.** No. The metric $e$ is bounded by $1$, $d$ possibly not, yet they define the same topology. So "bounded" depends on the metric, not only on the topology; by contrast compactness, connectedness, and closedness are topological. (Completeness is not topological either, see the next problem, but it is preserved by this particular change.)

**Remark.** The metric $d/(1+d)$ is another bounded replacement with the same properties. This explains why one can freely assume metrics bounded by $1$ in many constructions, such as countable products of metric spaces.

@@@ mt-tp-017-completeness-is-not-a-topological-property.md
---
title: Completeness is not topological
category: metric/mt-topology
level: m1
difficulty: 3
order: 34
tags: equivalent metrics, completeness, Cauchy sequences, arctan
date: 2026-11-17
---

## Statement

On $\mathbb{R}$ define $\rho(x,y)=|\arctan x-\arctan y|$.

1. Show that $\rho$ is a metric.
2. Show that $\rho$ and the usual metric $|x-y|$ have the same convergent sequences, hence (using closures by sequences) the same closed sets and the same open sets.
3. Show that $(\mathbb{R},\rho)$ is not complete, whereas $(\mathbb{R},|\cdot|)$ is.
4. Is $[0,+\infty)$ compact in $(\mathbb{R},\rho)$?

## Hint

Since $\arctan$ is an increasing bijection onto $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ with continuous inverse $\tan$, $\rho$ is the usual distance of the images. The sequence $n$ is $\rho$-Cauchy.

## Solution

**Idea.** The map $\arctan:\mathbb{R}\to(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2)$ is a homeomorphism, and $\rho$ is the distance transported from the open interval, which is not complete.
